steps.title: fine·good·okay
steps.goal: 비슷한 답의 느낌 차이 알기
steps.scene_desc: 12월 초 평일 저녁, 동네 카페 창가 자리. 퇴근길의 지우가 지친 얼굴로 노트북 가방을 멘 채 의자에 앉고, 맞은편 클로이가 핫초코 두 잔을 앞에 두고 고개를 갸웃하며 지우 얼굴을 살핌. 창밖은 어둡고 창가에 작은 전구 장식. 간판·메뉴판에 글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Fine, Good, or Okay?" (fine·good·okay). Goal: 비슷한 답의 느낌 차이 알기. Today's scene: 12월 초 평일 저녁, 동네 카페 창가 자리. 퇴근길의 지우가 지친 얼굴로 노트북 가방을 멘 채 의자에 앉고, 맞은편 클로이가 핫초코 두 잔을 앞에 두고 고개를 갸웃하며 지우 얼굴을 살핌. 창밖은 어둡고 창가에 작은 전구 장식. 간판·메뉴판에 글자 없음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Chloe, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I’m fine.".

steps.when: 말투에 따라 뜻이 달라요. 밝게 말하면 *정말 괜찮다*, 낮고 짧게 끝을 떨어뜨리면 *별로 안 괜찮으니 더 묻지 말아 달라*는 신호가 될 수 있어요.
steps.extra: I’m fine. Just a little tired.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I’m fine." (괜찮아요.). When to use it: 말투에 따라 뜻이 달라요. 밝게 말하면 정말 괜찮다, 낮고 짧게 끝을 떨어뜨리면 별로 안 괜찮으니 더 묻지 말아 달라는 신호가 될 수 있어요. Note: I’m fine. Just a little tired.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I'm fine. I stayed up late to be productive, then spent twenty minutes looking for my glasses on my face. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I’m good.".

steps.when: 안부에 가볍고 친근하게 답해요. 무언가를 권할 때 “I’m good.”이라고 하면 *사양*(No, thanks)이에요.
steps.extra: “More coffee?” “I’m good, thanks.”
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I’m good." (잘 지내요. / (권할 때) 괜찮아요, 됐어요.). When to use it: 안부에 가볍고 친근하게 답해요. 무언가를 권할 때 “I’m good.”이라고 하면 사양(No, thanks)이에요. Note: “More coffee?” “I’m good, thanks.”.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): More cake? I'm good, thanks. I already had one piece for dessert and one for emotional support. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I’m okay.".

steps.when: fine·good보다 *조금 가라앉은 기분*으로 들릴 때가 많아요. 그래서 듣는 사람이 한 번 더 물어보기도 해요.
steps.extra: I’m okay. It’s been a long week.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I’m okay." (그럭저럭 괜찮아요.). When to use it: fine·good보다 조금 가라앉은 기분으로 들릴 때가 많아요. 그래서 듣는 사람이 한 번 더 물어보기도 해요. Note: I’m okay. It’s been a long week.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I'm okay. It has been a long week, and my plant looks more energetic than I do. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("How Are You, Really? · 12월 초 평일 저녁, 동네 카페에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: How Are You, Really? · 12월 초 평일 저녁, 동네 카페에서

lines.en: Jiwoo, over here! I got you a hot chocolate. So, how are you?
lines.ko: 지우 씨, 여기요! 핫초코 시켜 놨어요. 그래서, 어떻게 지내요?

lines.en: {{I’m fine.}}
lines.ko: 괜찮아요.

lines.en: Hmm. That was a flat “fine.” Your voice dropped, and you didn’t even look up.
lines.ko: 흠. 밋밋한 ‘fine’이네요. 목소리가 뚝 떨어지고, 고개도 안 들었잖아요.

lines.en: Was it that obvious? Honestly? Not great. I’ve worked late four nights in a row.
lines.ko: 그렇게 티가 났어요? 솔직히요? 별로예요. 나흘 연속 야근했어요.

lines.en: Four nights? No wonder. A “fine” like that often means “Please don’t ask.”
lines.ko: 나흘이요? 그럴 만하네요. 그런 ‘fine’은 ‘더 묻지 말아 줘’라는 뜻일 때가 많아요.

lines.en: Really? In my first English textbook, it was always “I’m fine, thank you. And you?”
lines.ko: 정말요? 제 첫 영어 교과서에서는 늘 ‘I’m fine, thank you. And you?’였는데요.

lines.en: Ha! People do say “{{Fine, thanks. And you?}}” But it’s just a greeting. The tone tells you the real answer.
lines.ko: 하! ‘Fine, thanks. And you?’라고들 하죠. 그런데 그건 인사일 뿐이에요. 진짜 대답은 말투가 알려 줘요.

lines.en: So when I really am fine, what should I say?
lines.ko: 그럼 제가 정말 괜찮을 때는 뭐라고 해요?

lines.en: Try “{{I’m good!}}” in a bright voice. Or “{{I’m doing great, thanks}}” on a really good day.
lines.ko: 밝은 목소리로 ‘I’m good!’ 해 봐요. 정말 좋은 날엔 ‘I’m doing great, thanks.’도 좋고요.

lines.en: And “{{I’m okay}}”?
lines.ko: 그럼 ‘I’m okay’는요?

lines.en: That’s closer to “so-so,” so people often ask more. And “{{I’ve been better}}” is an understatement. It means things are pretty bad.
lines.ko: 그건 ‘그저 그래요’에 가까워서 더 물어보곤 해요. ‘I’ve been better’는 일부러 약하게 하는 말이에요. 꽤 안 좋다는 뜻이죠.

lines.en: Then right now, I’ve been better. But {{I’ll survive.}} The project ends next Friday.
lines.ko: 그럼 지금 저는 별로예요. 그래도 버틸 거예요. 프로젝트가 다음 주 금요일에 끝나거든요.

lines.en: “I’ll survive!” Just like a drama hero. OK, dinner’s on me next Friday. Then I want a bright “I’m good!”
lines.ko: ‘I’ll survive!’ 드라마 주인공 같네요. 좋아요, 다음 주 금요일 저녁은 제가 살게요. 그때는 밝은 ‘I’m good!’ 들려줘요.

items: Jiwoo has worked late four nights in a row.
Chloe says “I’ve been better” means things are great.
steps.teach:
Quiz about the scene, now that the learner has heard it and read it in both roles. First ask two short, easy questions about what happens in it (who, what, where or how often), one per turn, with the answers in the lines below. Any answer that shows they understood is right, in any words or in Korean: say so and go on. If it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Never turn an answer into a repeat drill here: if their English has a slip, just say the right sentence back once in your reaction and go on. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too.
Then the true/false check. The statements on the learner's screen, each with its answer and the scene line that shows it. The answers are for you only: never say an answer or a line number before the learner has answered:
1. Jiwoo has worked late four nights in a row. → True (line 4)
2. Chloe says “I’ve been better” means things are great. → False (line 11)
3. Jiwoo’s project ends next Friday. → True (line 12)
The scene they are about:
1. Chloe: "Jiwoo, over here! I got you a hot chocolate. So, how are you?" (지우 씨, 여기요! 핫초코 시켜 놨어요. 그래서, 어떻게 지내요?)
2. Jiwoo: "I’m fine." (괜찮아요.)
3. Chloe: "Hmm. That was a flat “fine.” Your voice dropped, and you didn’t even look up." (흠. 밋밋한 ‘fine’이네요. 목소리가 뚝 떨어지고, 고개도 안 들었잖아요.)
4. Jiwoo: "Was it that obvious? Honestly? Not great. I’ve worked late four nights in a row." (그렇게 티가 났어요? 솔직히요? 별로예요. 나흘 연속 야근했어요.)
5. Chloe: "Four nights? No wonder. A “fine” like that often means “Please don’t ask.”" (나흘이요? 그럴 만하네요. 그런 ‘fine’은 ‘더 묻지 말아 줘’라는 뜻일 때가 많아요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Really? In my first English textbook, it was always “I’m fine, thank you. And you?”" (정말요? 제 첫 영어 교과서에서는 늘 ‘I’m fine, thank you. And you?’였는데요.)
7. Chloe: "Ha! People do say “Fine, thanks. And you?” But it’s just a greeting. The tone tells you the real answer." (하! ‘Fine, thanks. And you?’라고들 하죠. 그런데 그건 인사일 뿐이에요. 진짜 대답은 말투가 알려 줘요.)
8. Jiwoo: "So when I really am fine, what should I say?" (그럼 제가 정말 괜찮을 때는 뭐라고 해요?)
9. Chloe: "Try “I’m good!” in a bright voice. Or “I’m doing great, thanks” on a really good day." (밝은 목소리로 ‘I’m good!’ 해 봐요. 정말 좋은 날엔 ‘I’m doing great, thanks.’도 좋고요.)
10. Jiwoo: "And “I’m okay”?" (그럼 ‘I’m okay’는요?)
11. Chloe: "That’s closer to “so-so,” so people often ask more. And “I’ve been better” is an understatement. It means things are pretty bad." (그건 ‘그저 그래요’에 가까워서 더 물어보곤 해요. ‘I’ve been better’는 일부러 약하게 하는 말이에요. 꽤 안 좋다는 뜻이죠.)
12. Jiwoo: "Then right now, I’ve been better. But I’ll survive. The project ends next Friday." (그럼 지금 저는 별로예요. 그래도 버틸 거예요. 프로젝트가 다음 주 금요일에 끝나거든요.)
13. Chloe: "“I’ll survive!” Just like a drama hero. OK, dinner’s on me next Friday. Then I want a bright “I’m good!”" (‘I’ll survive!’ 드라마 주인공 같네요. 좋아요, 다음 주 금요일 저녁은 제가 살게요. 그때는 밝은 ‘I’m good!’ 들려줘요.)
Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). A one-word answer (True, False, 맞아요) is enough; never ask for a full sentence. Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: Things are great
Things are so-so
Things are hard
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: I’m good! I just ___. / Honestly? Not great. ___. Table (Things are great → Things are so-so):
- I’m good! → I’m okay.
- I’m doing great, thanks. → Not too bad.
- Can’t complain. → Same old, same old.
- Couldn’t be better. → It’s been a long week.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I'm good! I just bought vegetables. Then I came home and ordered noodles anyway. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I’m *fine*! ↗ 높고 밝게 → 정말 괜찮아요. 
I’m fine. ↘ 낮고 짧게, 끝을 뚝 → 별로예요(더 묻지 말아 줘요). 
이 대화의 연습 패턴이에요. 실제 뜻은 억양과 함께 강세·표정·상황으로 전해져요.

I’m doing great > I’m good > I’m fine / I’m okay > I’ve been better 
사람과 말투에 따라 달라요. 순서보다 목소리와 표정을 함께 들어요.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 같은 말, 다른 뜻 — 억양(intonation): I’m fine! ↗ 높고 밝게 → 정말 괜찮아요. / I’m fine. ↘ 낮고 짧게, 끝을 뚝 → 별로예요(더 묻지 말아 줘요). / 이 대화의 연습 패턴이에요. 실제 뜻은 억양과 함께 강세·표정·상황으로 전해져요.
- 기분의 정도 (대략): I’m doing great > I’m good > I’m fine / I’m okay > I’ve been better / 사람과 말투에 따라 달라요. 순서보다 목소리와 표정을 함께 들어요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I been better. → I’ve been better. (현재완료라 have(’ve)가 꼭 있어야 해요.)
- I’m doing greatly. → I’m doing great. (안부 대답에서는 great(greatly ×).)
- I’m hanging on there. → I’m hanging in there. (정해진 덩어리 표현이라 in there.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I'm doing great sounds bright. I'm okay sounds softer. Like I found my keys after searching with them in my hand. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) so-so / a long week → A: How are you? B: I’m okay. It’s been a long week.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) so-so / a long week → A: How are you? B: I’m okay. It’s been a long week. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): so-so / a long week | great / good news today | not great / missed the bus twice | nothing new / work, home, work.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "Fine, Good, or Okay?" (fine·good·okay); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I’m fine." / "I’m good." / "I’m okay.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 좋거나 무난할 때: "I’m doing great, thanks." (아주 잘 지내요, 고마워요., 보통); "Can’t complain." (불만 없어요. 잘 지내요., 친근); "Not too bad." (나쁘지 않아요., 친근)
- 그저 그럴 때: "Fine, thanks. And you?" (잘 지내요, 고마워요. 당신은요?(인사), 보통); "Same old, same old." (늘 똑같죠, 뭐., 친근); "Hanging in there." (그럭저럭 버티고 있어요., 친근)
- 힘들 때: "I’ve been better." (좋았던 때도 있었죠.(지금은 별로예요), 보통); "Honestly? Not great." (솔직히요? 별로예요., 친근); "I’ll survive." (버틸 거예요. 괜찮아질 거예요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Can't complain. I tried once, but even I got bored. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

I’m *FINE*. fine에 세게 힘을 주고 끝을 내리면 → 짜증, ‘그만 물어’

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- (말투) 억양이 보내는 신호: I’m FINE. fine에 세게 힘을 주고 끝을 내리면 → 짜증, ‘그만 물어’ / I’m fi-ine. ↗ 길게 늘이며 올리면 → 장난스럽게 ‘괜찮다니까’ / 미묘한(subtle) 차이라 표정과 상황(context)도 같이 봐요.

Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Hey, how are you? B: I’ve been ___. Long week. / A: Oh no. Hang in ___. B: Thanks. I’ll ___. / A: More coffee? B: I’m ___, thanks. / 낱말 상자: better · there · survive · good
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: intonation (억양(말소리의 높낮이)), inflection ((목소리의) 높낮이 변화, 억양 변화), tone (말투, 어조), subtle (미묘한, 알아채기 어려운), literal (글자 그대로의), ambiguous ((뜻이) 애매한, 두 가지 이상으로 읽히는), convey ((생각·느낌을) 전하다), signal (신호; 신호를 보내다), understatement (실제보다 약하게 말하기, 절제된 표현), sincere (진심 어린), genuine (진짜의; 진심에서 나온), context (맥락, (말이 나온) 상황).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Context matters. 'I'm fine' at a picnic is nice. 'I'm fine' at the dentist means nobody believes you. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.

Word list on screen: connotation ((낱말에 따라오는) 느낌, 함축) — "“Cheap” can have a negative connotation."; implication (숨은 뜻, 함의) — "The implication was clear. She was tired."; euphemism (완곡어(불편한 말을 부드럽게 바꾼 말)) — "“Not great” can be a euphemism for “terrible.”"; nuance (미묘한 차이, 뉘앙스) — "the nuance of “fine”"; emphasis (강조, (말의) 힘) — "Put the emphasis on “good.”"; polite (공손한, 예의 바른) — "a polite smile"; mood (기분) — "I could hear her mood in her voice.".

Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "How do people usually answer “How are you?” in your language? Is the answer always true?" (hint on screen: Usually we say ___. It’s (not) always true, because ___.)
- "Which answer sounds most like you today? Why?" (hint on screen: Today I’d say “___,” because ___.)

- "A friend says “I’m fine” in a flat voice. What do you say next?" (hint on screen: Are you sure? You don’t sound ___. / Want to ___?)

steps.title: The Tone Test
steps.text: Before they left the café, Chloe gave Jiwoo a quick tone test. She said “I’m fine” three times. The first was bright and high. The second was flat and short. The third was long and slow, with a sigh at the end. “Same words, different signals,” Chloe said. “The literal meaning stays the same, but the intonation changes everything.” Jiwoo guessed all three — really fine, please don’t ask, and very tired. Chloe said the difference can be subtle, so it helps to look at the context, too. Jiwoo laughed. “So ‘I’m fine’ is the most ambiguous sentence in English?” “One of them,” Chloe said. The next Friday, the project ended. When Chloe called, Jiwoo answered in a bright voice. “I’m good!” This time, she meant it.
steps.gloss: literal 글자 그대로의 · intonation 억양 · subtle 미묘한 · context 맥락, 상황 · ambiguous 애매한 · mean it 진심으로 말하다
questions: What were the three meanings of Chloe’s “I’m fine”?
How did Jiwoo answer Chloe’s call the next Friday?

steps.teach:

1. Chloe (you): "Jiwoo, over here! I got you a hot chocolate. So, how are you?" (지우 씨, 여기요! 핫초코 시켜 놨어요. 그래서, 어떻게 지내요?)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "I’m fine." (괜찮아요.)
3. Chloe (you): "Hmm. That was a flat “fine.” Your voice dropped, and you didn’t even look up." (흠. 밋밋한 ‘fine’이네요. 목소리가 뚝 떨어지고, 고개도 안 들었잖아요.)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "Was it that obvious? Honestly? Not great. I’ve worked late four nights in a row." (그렇게 티가 났어요? 솔직히요? 별로예요. 나흘 연속 야근했어요.)

8. Jiwoo (learner): "So when I really am fine, what should I say?" (그럼 제가 정말 괜찮을 때는 뭐라고 해요?)

10. Jiwoo (learner): "And “I’m okay”?" (그럼 ‘I’m okay’는요?)
11. Chloe (you): "That’s closer to “so-so,” so people often ask more. And “I’ve been better” is an understatement. It means things are pretty bad." (그건 ‘그저 그래요’에 가까워서 더 물어보곤 해요. ‘I’ve been better’는 일부러 약하게 하는 말이에요. 꽤 안 좋다는 뜻이죠.)
12. Jiwoo (learner): "Then right now, I’ve been better. But I’ll survive. The project ends next Friday." (그럼 지금 저는 별로예요. 그래도 버틸 거예요. 프로젝트가 다음 주 금요일에 끝나거든요.)
13. Chloe (you): "“I’ll survive!” Just like a drama hero. OK, dinner’s on me next Friday. Then I want a bright “I’m good!”" (‘I’ll survive!’ 드라마 주인공 같네요. 좋아요, 다음 주 금요일 저녁은 제가 살게요. 그때는 밝은 ‘I’m good!’ 들려줘요.)
In one short sentence, say what is on the screen now and invite them to start. Do not say the learner's line before they try: remembering it is the point of this part, so this is the one exception to saying a sentence first. If they get stuck, give only the next word or two as a hint. If a word was missing or wrong, say the whole line once inside double quotes and let them try once more, then go on. steps.teach: Wrap up like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how it felt to say the scene by heart, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today (for example a line they remembered well), say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 사과가 아닌 sorry
steps.goal: sorry의 여러 쓰임 익히기
steps.scene_desc: 12월 말 저녁, 붐비는 동네 전통 시장 골목. 벤이 장바구니를 든 남자와 살짝 부딪혀 둘 다 미안하다는 손짓을 하고, 목도리를 두른 지우가 옆에서 웃음. 뒤로 호떡 노점에서 김이 오르고 사람들이 북적임. 간판·가격표에 글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Sorry, Sorry, Sorry" (사과가 아닌 sorry). Goal: sorry의 여러 쓰임 익히기. Today's scene: 12월 말 저녁, 붐비는 동네 전통 시장 골목. 벤이 장바구니를 든 남자와 살짝 부딪혀 둘 다 미안하다는 손짓을 하고, 목도리를 두른 지우가 옆에서 웃음. 뒤로 호떡 노점에서 김이 오르고 사람들이 북적임. 간판·가격표에 글자 없음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Ben, Shopper, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Sorry, could you say that again?".

steps.en: Sorry, could you say that again?
steps.when: 잘 못 들었을 때 써요. 사과가 아니라 *다시 말해 달라는 부탁*을 부드럽게 여는 말이에요. 끝을 살짝 올려요.

Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). A one-word answer (True, False, 맞아요) is enough; never ask for a full sentence. Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: When …
Say …
It’s really …
rows: Sorry, could you say that again?
I’m sorry, but I can’t make it.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: Oh, sorry to hear that. ___? / I’m sorry, but ___. Table (When … → Say …):
- you didn’t hear well → Sorry, could you say that again?
- a friend has bad news → Oh, sorry to hear that.
- you have to say no → I’m sorry, but I can’t make it.
- you bump into someone → Oops, sorry!
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I’m sorry, but I can’t make it. My calendar looks confident, but I do not. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
Oops, *sorry*! 사과 
*Sorry to* hear that. 공감 
*Sorry,* could you say that again? 부탁 앞 쿠션 
*I’m sorry, but* I can’t. 거절·반대 앞 쿠션

Sorry *for* the wait. for + 명사·-ing 
Sorry *to* bother you. to + 동사원형 
I’m sorry *(that)* you missed it. (that) + 문장
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- sorry가 하는 일(function) 네 가지: Oops, sorry! 사과 / Sorry to hear that. 공감 / Sorry, could you say that again? 부탁 앞 쿠션 / I’m sorry, but I can’t. 거절·반대 앞 쿠션
- sorry for / sorry to / sorry (that): Sorry for the wait. for + 명사·-ing / Sorry to bother you. to + 동사원형 / I’m sorry (that) you missed it. (that) + 문장
Common mistakes on screen:
- Sorry for hear that. → Sorry to hear that. (공감은 sorry to + 동사원형.)
- Sorry for late. → Sorry for being late. (for 뒤에는 명사나 -ing.)
- No need to apology. → No need to apologize. (to 뒤라 동사 apologize(apology는 명사).)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Sorry for being late. I spent ten minutes looking for my glasses, and they were on my head. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) My flight was canceled. / sympathy → A: My flight was canceled. B: Oh no, sorry to hear that.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) My flight was canceled. / sympathy → A: My flight was canceled. B: Oh no, sorry to hear that. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): My flight was canceled. / sympathy | Can you work on Saturday? / a soft “no” | (It’s noisy.) / a request | You stepped on my foot. / an apology.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: Sorry, could you say that again?
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Sorry, Sorry, Sorry" (사과가 아닌 sorry); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Sorry, could you say that again?" / "Sorry to hear that." / "I’m sorry, but ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: 미안하다고는 하지만, 사실 후회 안 해요.(장난)
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 사과가 아닌 sorry: "Sorry, after you." (죄송해요, 먼저 가세요., 보통); "Sorry, is this seat taken?" (실례지만, 여기 자리 있어요?, 보통); "Sorry, I didn’t catch that." (죄송한데, 잘 못 들었어요., 보통); "Sorry, but that’s not right." (죄송하지만, 그건 맞지 않아요., 보통)
- 사과할 때·받을 때: "Sorry for the wait." (기다리게 해서 죄송해요., 정중); "I owe you an apology." (제가 사과드려야겠어요., 정중); "Apology accepted." (사과 받아 줄게요., 보통)
- 사과할 필요 없을 때: "No need to apologize." (사과할 필요 없어요., 보통); "Sorry, not sorry." (미안하다고는 하지만, 사실 후회 안 해요.(장난), 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Sorry, after you. I said that to an automatic door this morning, then walked into the wall beside it. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Picture words on screen. New: apologetic (미안해하는, 사과하는 (표정·말투)), cultural (문화의, 문화적인), function (기능, (말의) 쓰임), excessive (지나친, 너무 많은), gesture (몸짓; (마음을 보여 주는) 행동), etiquette (예절, 에티켓), reflex (반사적인 반응, 저절로 나오는 행동), overapologize (지나치게 사과하다), remorse (깊은 후회, 뉘우침), interrupt ((말·일에) 끼어들다, 방해하다), mistake (실수), forgive (용서하다).

Then call next_step.

steps.title: Sorry, Not Sorry
steps.text: The line at the hotteok stand was long, but it moved fast. “Sorry for the wait!” the vendor said with a smile. Jiwoo almost said “Sorry” back, out of pure reflex. Instead, she said, “Thanks! It smells amazing.” They found a crowded bench with one free spot. “Sorry, is this seat taken?” Jiwoo asked a woman with a big shopping bag. The woman smiled and moved her bag. Ben gave Jiwoo a thumbs-up. That sorry had a real function. On the way home, Jiwoo thought about the two sorries she had really needed, one to ask Ben to repeat himself and one to ask about the seat. She also counted her hotteoks. She had bought three, one more than she’d planned. “Sorry, not sorry,” she told Ben, holding up the bag. Ben laughed. “Now you’re just showing off.”
steps.gloss: vendor 노점 상인 · out of reflex 반사적으로 · free spot 빈자리 · thumbs-up 엄지척 · show off 자랑하다

It smells amazing.” They found a crowded bench with one free spot. “Sorry, is this seat taken?” Jiwoo asked a woman with a big shopping bag. The woman smiled and moved her bag. Ben gave Jiwoo a thumbs-up. That sorry had a real function. On the way home, Jiwoo thought about the two sorries she had really needed, one to ask Ben to repeat himself and one to ask about the seat. She also counted her hotteoks. She had bought three, one more than she’d planned. “Sorry, not sorry,” she told Ben, holding up the bag. Ben laughed. “Now you’re just showing off.”" Words: vendor 노점 상인 · out of reflex 반사적으로 · free spot 빈자리 · thumbs-up 엄지척 · show off 자랑하다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Jiwoo say to the vendor instead of “Sorry”?" / "Why did Jiwoo say “Sorry, not sorry”?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.

Ha! See? That “sorry” was perfect. You didn’t catch it, so you asked politely. That’s not an apology.
lines.ko: 하! 봐요. 방금 그 sorry는 완벽했어요. 못 알아들어서 공손하게 물었잖아요. 그건 사과가 아니에요.

lines.en: 그럼 어떤 sorry가 지나친 거예요?
The ones for things that aren’t your fault. Instead of “Sorry, I’m complaining,” try “Thanks for listening.” But to say no, “{{I’m sorry, but}} I can’t” is just right.
lines.ko: 내 잘못이 아닌 일에 하는 거요. ‘미안해요, 불평만 하네요’ 대신 ‘들어 줘서 고마워요’라고 해요. 거절할 때는 ‘죄송하지만 안 돼요’가 딱 맞고요.

lines.en: 알겠어요. 들어 줘서 고마워요. 그리고 그 많은 sorry는 정식으로 사과할게요.
Ha! {{Apology accepted.}} That one sounded sincere. Now, hotteok time!
lines.ko: 하! 사과 받아 줄게요. 그건 진심으로 들렸어요. 자, 이제 호떡 먹으러 가요!

steps.hint: 한국어 뜻만 보고 내 줄을 영어로 말해요
steps.teach:
Memory practice 3: now the learner's lines show only their Korean meaning. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Ben, Shopper exactly as written. The full lines, for you only:
1. Ben (you): "Wow, it’s packed today! Oops … sorry!" (와, 오늘 사람 진짜 많네요! 앗, 죄송해요!)
2. Shopper (you): "Oh, sorry! My fault." (아, 죄송해요! 제 잘못이에요.)
3. Ben (you): "No, no. Sorry, after you." (아니에요. 죄송해요, 먼저 가세요.)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "Sorry I’m late, Ben. My subway stopped for twenty minutes. Sorry!" (늦어서 미안해요, 벤. 지하철이 20분이나 멈춰 있었어요. 미안해요!)
5. Ben (you): "Oh, sorry to hear that. But no need to apologize. It wasn’t your fault." (아, 안됐네요. 그래도 사과할 필요 없어요. 지우 씨 잘못이 아니잖아요.)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "And so crowded. Sorry, I’m complaining. Oh … I did it again." (사람도 엄청 많았고요. 미안해요, 불평만 하네요. 아 … 또 그랬네요.)
7. Ben (you): "Three sorries in thirty seconds! Soon you’ll owe me an apology for apologizing." (30초 만에 sorry가 세 번이에요! 이러다 사과한 걸로 사과해야겠어요.)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "Sorry, could you say that again? That vendor is so loud." (죄송한데, 다시 말해 줄래요? 저 상인 목소리가 너무 커서요.)
9. Ben (you): "Ha! See? That “sorry” was perfect. You didn’t catch it, so you asked politely. That’s not an apology." (하! 봐요. 방금 그 sorry는 완벽했어요. 못 알아들어서 공손하게 물었잖아요. 그건 사과가 아니에요.)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "So which sorries are too much?" (그럼 어떤 sorry가 지나친 거예요?)
11. Ben (you): "The ones for things that aren’t your fault. Instead of “Sorry, I’m complaining,” try “Thanks for listening.” But to say no, “I’m sorry, but I can’t” is just right." (내 잘못이 아닌 일에 하는 거요. ‘미안해요, 불평만 하네요’ 대신 ‘들어 줘서 고마워요’라고 해요. 거절할 때는 ‘죄송하지만 안 돼요’가 딱 맞고요.)
12. Jiwoo (learner): "Got it. Thanks for listening. And I owe you an apology for all those sorries." (알겠어요. 들어 줘서 고마워요. 그리고 그 많은 sorry는 정식으로 사과할게요.)
13. Ben (you): "Ha! Apology accepted. That one sounded sincere. Now, hotteok time!" (하! 사과 받아 줄게요. 그건 진심으로 들렸어요. 자, 이제 호떡 먹으러 가요!)
In one short sentence, say what is on the screen now and invite them to start. Do not say the learner's line before they try: remembering it is the point of this part, so this is the one exception to saying a sentence first. If they get stuck, give only the next word or two as a hint. If a word was missing or wrong, say the whole line once inside double quotes and let them try once more, then go on. Go in order, one line at a time. After the last line, react in a word or two, with no comment on how they sounded.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

steps.label: 마무리
steps.teach: Wrap up like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how it felt to say the scene by heart, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today (for example a line they remembered well), say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

lessons.title: 말 흐리기

steps.title: 말 흐리기
steps.goal: 일부러 흐리게 말하는 표현을 알아듣고 쓰기
steps.scene_desc: 1월 첫 토요일 저녁, 클로이가 사는 동네 골목. 목도리를 두른 클로이가 하품을 참으며 두 손으로 ‘대략 이만큼’을 그려 보이고, 지우가 웃으며 나란히 걸음. 가로등과 작은 가게들(간판 글자 없이), 차가운 공기에 입김
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Kind of Fun, or Something" (말 흐리기). Goal: 일부러 흐리게 말하는 표현을 알아듣고 쓰기. Today's scene: 1월 첫 토요일 저녁, 클로이가 사는 동네 골목. 목도리를 두른 클로이가 하품을 참으며 두 손으로 ‘대략 이만큼’을 그려 보이고, 지우가 웃으며 나란히 걸음. 가로등과 작은 가게들, 차가운 공기에 입김. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Jiwoo, Chloe. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "It was kind of ___.".

steps.when: 느낌을 *약하게·흐리게* 말해요. 딱 잘라 말하기 애매하거나 부담 없이 말하고 싶을 때 써요. 말할 때는 kinda처럼 짧게.
steps.extra: It was kind of fun, actually.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "It was kind of ___." (좀 ~했어요.). When to use it: 느낌을 약하게·흐리게 말해요. 딱 잘라 말하기 애매하거나 부담 없이 말하고 싶을 때 써요. 말할 때는 kinda처럼 짧게. Note: It was kind of fun, actually.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): It was kind of fun, actually. I tried one home workout, then celebrated like I had finished a marathon. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "___ or something like that.".

steps.when: 정확하지 않다는 걸 알려요. 이름·숫자가 잘 기억나지 않을 때도 써요.
steps.extra: He was a magician or something like that.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "___ or something like that." (~나 뭐 그런 거요.). When to use it: 정확하지 않다는 걸 알려요. 이름·숫자가 잘 기억나지 않을 때도 써요. Note: He was a magician or something like that.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): It was a cooking class or something like that. I mostly learned that smoke appears very quickly. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "You know what I mean?".

steps.when: 다 설명하지 않고 상대의 *공감*을 구해요. 너무 자주 쓰면 말버릇처럼 들려요.
steps.extra: It was fun but tiring. You know what I mean?
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "You know what I mean?" (무슨 말인지 알죠?). When to use it: 다 설명하지 않고 상대의 공감을 구해요. 너무 자주 쓰면 말버릇처럼 들려요. Note: It was fun but tiring. You know what I mean?
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): My room looked clean for about five minutes. Then one shirt appeared on the chair. You know what I mean? Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Last Night’s Party · 1월 첫 토요일 저녁, 클로이 집 근처 골목에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Last Night’s Party · 1월 첫 토요일 저녁, 클로이 집 근처 골목에서

lines.en: Chloe! You look sleepy. Late night?
lines.ko: 클로이 씨! 졸려 보여요. 늦게 잤어요?

lines.en: Kind of. A coworker had a housewarming party last night. {{It was kind of}} fun. {{It was sort of weird}}, too.
lines.ko: 좀요. 회사 동료가 어젯밤에 집들이를 했거든요. 좀 재밌었어요. 좀 이상하기도 했고요.

lines.en: Weird how?
lines.ko: 어떻게 이상했는데요?

lines.en: Well, {{there were like fifty people there}}, in a tiny apartment. And there was a magician, {{or something like that}}.
lines.ko: 음, 작은 집에 한 쉰 명쯤 있었어요. 그리고 마술사가 있었어요, 뭐 그 비슷한 사람이요.

lines.en: A magician at a housewarming party?
lines.ko: 집들이에 마술사요?

lines.en: I know! {{It’s a bit of a long story}}. {{We had snacks and stuff}}, played some games, {{things like that}}. {{You know what I mean?}}
lines.ko: 그러니까요! 얘기하자면 좀 길어요. 간식 같은 거 먹고, 게임도 좀 하고, 그런 거요. 무슨 말인지 알죠?

lines.en: Not really! “Like fifty,” “or something,” “and stuff” … That’s so vague.
lines.ko: 잘 모르겠어요! ‘한 쉰 명’, ‘뭐 그런’, ‘같은 거’ … 너무 흐릿해요.

lines.en: Ha! That’s the point. With friends, I don’t need exact numbers. Vague words keep it casual. And listen. In “like FIFty,” “like” is quick and soft.
lines.ko: 하! 그게 핵심이에요. 친구끼리는 정확한 숫자가 필요 없잖아요. 흐릿한 말이 대화를 편하게 해 줘요. 그리고 들어 봐요. ‘like FIFty’에서 like는 빠르고 약해요.

lines.en: So should I talk like that, too?
lines.ko: 그럼 저도 그렇게 말해야 해요?

lines.en: With friends, sure. But not in a work report. If your team asks how many users tested the app, “like fifty” won’t work.
lines.ko: 친구끼리는 그럼요. 하지만 업무 보고에서는 안 돼요. 앱 테스트에 사용자 몇 명이 참여했냐고 팀이 물으면 ‘한 쉰 명’은 안 통해요.

lines.en: Right. At work, I’d say, “Forty-eight users tested it.”
lines.ko: 맞아요. 회사에서는 ‘사용자 48명이 테스트했습니다’라고 하겠죠.

lines.en: Exactly. Oh, and the magician? He was kind of great. He pulled a card out of my scarf, or {{something along those lines}}.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 아, 그리고 마술사요? 좀 대단했어요. 제 목도리에서 카드를 꺼냈어요, 뭐 대충 그런 식으로요.

lines.en: See? That’s vague, too!
lines.ko: 봐요. 그것도 흐릿하잖아요!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Last Night’s Party · 1월 첫 토요일 저녁, 클로이 집 근처 골목에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:

7. Jiwoo: "Not really! “Like fifty,” “or something,” “and stuff” … That’s so vague." (잘 모르겠어요! ‘한 쉰 명’, ‘뭐 그런’, ‘같은 거’ … 너무 흐릿해요.)
8. Chloe: "Ha! That’s the point. With friends, I don’t need exact numbers. Vague words keep it casual. And listen. In “like FIFty,” “like” is quick and soft." (하! 그게 핵심이에요. 친구끼리는 정확한 숫자가 필요 없잖아요. 흐릿한 말이 대화를 편하게 해 줘요. 그리고 들어 봐요. ‘like FIFty’에서 like는 빠르고 약해요.)
9. Jiwoo: "So should I talk like that, too?" (그럼 저도 그렇게 말해야 해요?)
10. Chloe: "With friends, sure. But not in a work report. If your team asks how many users tested the app, “like fifty” won’t work." (친구끼리는 그럼요. 하지만 업무 보고에서는 안 돼요. 앱 테스트에 사용자 몇 명이 참여했냐고 팀이 물으면 ‘한 쉰 명’은 안 통해요.)
11. Jiwoo: "Right. At work, I’d say, “Forty-eight users tested it.”" (맞아요. 회사에서는 ‘사용자 48명이 테스트했습니다’라고 하겠죠.)
12. Chloe: "Exactly. Oh, and the magician? He was kind of great. He pulled a card out of my scarf, or something along those lines." (바로 그거예요. 아, 그리고 마술사요? 좀 대단했어요. 제 목도리에서 카드를 꺼냈어요, 뭐 대충 그런 식으로요.)
13. Jiwoo: "See? That’s vague, too!" (봐요. 그것도 흐릿하잖아요!)
Give one short, natural reaction to the scene (a few words) and say in one short sentence that you will now read it together. Do not ask any question about what happened yet: the quiz comes later, after the role reading. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:
Role reading of the same scene. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Chloe exactly as written, word for word. Never change, add or skip a line, and never read the learner's lines for them first.
1. Jiwoo (learner): "Chloe! You look sleepy. Late night?" (클로이 씨! 졸려 보여요. 늦게 잤어요?)
2. Chloe (you): "Kind of. A coworker had a housewarming party last night. It was kind of fun. It was sort of weird, too." (좀요. 회사 동료가 어젯밤에 집들이를 했거든요. 좀 재밌었어요. 좀 이상하기도 했고요.)
3. Jiwoo (learner): "Weird how?" (어떻게 이상했는데요?)
4. Chloe (you): "Well, there were like fifty people there, in a tiny apartment. And there was a magician, or something like that." (음, 작은 집에 한 쉰 명쯤 있었어요. 그리고 마술사가 있었어요, 뭐 그 비슷한 사람이요.)
5. Jiwoo (learner): "A magician at a housewarming party?" (집들이에 마술사요?)
6. Chloe (you): "I know! It’s a bit of a long story. We had snacks and stuff, played some games, things like that. You know what I mean?" (그러니까요! 얘기하자면 좀 길어요. 간식 같은 거 먹고, 게임도 좀 하고, 그런 거요. 무슨 말인지 알죠?)
7. Jiwoo (learner): "Not really! “Like fifty,” “or something,” “and stuff” … That’s so vague." (잘 모르겠어요! ‘한 쉰 명’, ‘뭐 그런’, ‘같은 거’ … 너무 흐릿해요.)
8. Chloe (you): "Ha! That’s the point. With friends, I don’t need exact numbers. Vague words keep it casual. And listen. In “like FIFty,” “like” is quick and soft." (하! 그게 핵심이에요. 친구끼리는 정확한 숫자가 필요 없잖아요. 흐릿한 말이 대화를 편하게 해 줘요. 그리고 들어 봐요. ‘like FIFty’에서 like는 빠르고 약해요.)
9. Jiwoo (learner): "So should I talk like that, too?" (그럼 저도 그렇게 말해야 해요?)
10. Chloe (you): "With friends, sure. But not in a work report. If your team asks how many users tested the app, “like fifty” won’t work." (친구끼리는 그럼요. 하지만 업무 보고에서는 안 돼요. 앱 테스트에 사용자 몇 명이 참여했냐고 팀이 물으면 ‘한 쉰 명’은 안 통해요.)
11. Jiwoo (learner): "Right. At work, I’d say, “Forty-eight users tested it.”" (맞아요. 회사에서는 ‘사용자 48명이 테스트했습니다’라고 하겠죠.)
12. Chloe (you): "Exactly. Oh, and the magician? He was kind of great. He pulled a card out of my scarf, or something along those lines." (바로 그거예요. 아, 그리고 마술사요? 좀 대단했어요. 제 목도리에서 카드를 꺼냈어요, 뭐 대충 그런 식으로요.)
13. Jiwoo (learner): "See? That’s vague, too!" (봐요. 그것도 흐릿하잖아요!)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Chloe. The learner speaks first: call highlight_line with 1 and invite them to start. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, react to the scene in a word or two (not a comment on how they sounded), then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short quiz about the scene.

Never turn an answer into a repeat drill here: if their English has a slip, just say the right sentence back once in your reaction and go on. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too.

Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. frame: It was kind of ___. There were like ___ people.
We ___ and stuff, or something like that.
head: How was it?
How many people?
What did you do?
rows: We ate and talked, things like that.
We watched a show or something.
It was okay, more or less.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: It was kind of ___. There were like ___ people. / We ___ and stuff, or something like that. Table (How was it? → How many people?):
- It was kind of fun. → There were like twenty.
- It was sort of weird. → Thirty-ish, maybe.
- It was kind of long. → Roughly a hundred.
- It was okay, more or less. → Not many. Ten or so.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): It was sort of weird. There were like thirty-ish people, and we clapped and stuff. I missed the rhythm after two seconds. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

*like* + 숫자 한 ~쯤(친근) · *roughly* + 숫자 대략 
숫자·시간 + *-ish* ~쯤 · eight-ish 8시쯤

… *and stuff* / … *things like that* ~ 같은 것들 
… *or something (like that)* ~나 뭐 그런 거

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 흐리게 만드는 말(hedge): kind of / sort of + 형용사 좀, 어느 정도 / like + 숫자 한 ~쯤(친근) · roughly + 숫자 대략 / 숫자·시간 + -ish ~쯤 · eight-ish 8시쯤
- 끝에 붙이는 말: … and stuff / … things like that ~ 같은 것들 / … or something (like that) ~나 뭐 그런 거 / 업무 보고·이메일에서는 정확한 숫자와 이름으로 말해요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- It was kind of a fun. → It was kind of fun. (fun은 여기서 형용사처럼 써서 a 없이.)
- We had snacks and stuffs. → We had snacks and stuff. (stuff는 셀 수 없는 명사라 -s 없이.)
- There were roughly of a hundred people. → There were roughly a hundred people. (roughly는 숫자 바로 앞에 써요(of ×).)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I got home at eight-ish and made dinner and stuff. By dinner, I mean toast and one very tired egg. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) fun / twenty people → A: How was the party? B: It was kind of fun. There were like twenty people, or something like that.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) fun / twenty people → A: How was the party? B: It was kind of fun. There were like twenty people, or something like that. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): fun / twenty people | weird / a magician | long / three speeches | quiet / board games.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "Kind of Fun, or Something" (말 흐리기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "It was kind of ___." / "___ or something like that." / "You know what I mean?". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: There were like fifty people there.

Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. steps.teach:
Picture words on screen. New: vague (흐릿한, 애매한), approximate (대략의, 어림의), hedge ((단정하지 않고) 말을 흐리다, 확답을 피하다), filler (군말(um, like처럼 말 사이를 채우는 말)), ish (~쯤, ~스러운(eight-ish 8시쯤)), roughly (대략, 대충), stuff (것들, 물건(셀 수 없음)), thing (것, 일), whatever (뭐든지, 아무거나), imprecise (정확하지 않은), softener (말을 부드럽게 하는 말), casual (격식 없는, 편한).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): My directions were vague. I said the café was kind of near the station, and then I got lost before my friend did. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

steps.title: Vague on Saturday, Exact on Monday
steps.text: At dinner that night, Grace asked Chloe about the party. Chloe gave the same answer. “Like fifty people, a magician, snacks and stuff.” Everyone laughed. Then Ben asked Jiwoo about her week. “It was kind of busy,” she said. “Lots of meetings, things like that.” Chloe gave her a quick nod. On Monday morning, though, Jiwoo switched modes. In the team meeting, Maya asked about the user test. Jiwoo didn’t say “roughly fifty people” or “ten-ish minutes.” She said, “Forty-eight users tested the new map screen. Thirty-one finished the task in under a minute.” Maya smiled. “Clear and exact. Thanks.” Jiwoo realized that vague words aren’t lazy. They’re a tool. In a casual chat, they sound friendly. In a report, they just sound imprecise.
steps.gloss: switch modes 방식을 바꾸다 · user test 사용자 테스트 · exact 정확한 · lazy 게으른 · imprecise 정확하지 않은
questions: How did Jiwoo describe her week at dinner?
What did Jiwoo say about the user test on Monday?

steps.scene_desc: 1월 첫 토요일 저녁, 클로이가 사는 동네 골목. 목도리를 두른 클로이가 하품을 참으며 두 손으로 ‘대략 이만큼’을 그려 보이고, 지우가 웃으며 나란히 걸음. 가로등과 작은 가게들(간판 글자 없이), 차가운 공기에 입김
steps.label: 대화 외우기
steps.teach:
This is the start of Part 3 of "Kind of Fun, or Something" (말 흐리기); it may be a different day. Today the learner practises saying the scene from this lesson by heart. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of one or two exchanges. React to what they say.
2) Then, in a new turn, say in one or two short sentences that today you will practise the scene ("Last Night’s Party · 1월 첫 토요일 저녁, 클로이 집 근처 골목에서") until they can say it by heart: first listen once, then say their lines with fewer and fewer words on the screen. Do not ask if they are ready more than once.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays the scene once more — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Last Night’s Party · 1월 첫 토요일 저녁, 클로이 집 근처 골목에서

lines.en: Chloe! You look sleepy. Late night?
lines.ko: 클로이 씨! 졸려 보여요. 늦게 잤어요?

lines.en: Kind of. A coworker had a housewarming party last night. {{It was kind of}} fun. {{It was sort of weird}}, too.
lines.ko: 좀요. 회사 동료가 어젯밤에 집들이를 했거든요. 좀 재밌었어요. 좀 이상하기도 했고요.

lines.en: Weird how?
lines.ko: 어떻게 이상했는데요?

lines.en: Well, {{there were like fifty people there}}, in a tiny apartment. And there was a magician, {{or something like that}}.
lines.ko: 음, 작은 집에 한 쉰 명쯤 있었어요. 그리고 마술사가 있었어요, 뭐 그 비슷한 사람이요.

lines.en: A magician at a housewarming party?
lines.ko: 집들이에 마술사요?

lines.en: I know! {{It’s a bit of a long story}}. {{We had snacks and stuff}}, played some games, {{things like that}}. {{You know what I mean?}}
lines.ko: 그러니까요! 얘기하자면 좀 길어요. 간식 같은 거 먹고, 게임도 좀 하고, 그런 거요. 무슨 말인지 알죠?

lines.en: Not really! “Like fifty,” “or something,” “and stuff” … That’s so vague.
lines.ko: 잘 모르겠어요! ‘한 쉰 명’, ‘뭐 그런’, ‘같은 거’ … 너무 흐릿해요.

lines.en: Ha! That’s the point. With friends, I don’t need exact numbers. Vague words keep it casual. And listen. In “like FIFty,” “like” is quick and soft.
lines.ko: 하! 그게 핵심이에요. 친구끼리는 정확한 숫자가 필요 없잖아요. 흐릿한 말이 대화를 편하게 해 줘요. 그리고 들어 봐요. ‘like FIFty’에서 like는 빠르고 약해요.

lines.ko: 그럼 저도 그렇게 말해야 해요?

lines.ko: 친구끼리는 그럼요. 하지만 업무 보고에서는 안 돼요. 앱 테스트에 사용자 몇 명이 참여했냐고 팀이 물으면 ‘한 쉰 명’은 안 통해요.

lines.ko: 맞아요. 회사에서는 ‘사용자 48명이 테스트했습니다’라고 하겠죠.

lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 아, 그리고 마술사요? 좀 대단했어요. 제 목도리에서 카드를 꺼냈어요, 뭐 대충 그런 식으로요.

7. Jiwoo (you): "Not really! “Like fifty,” “or something,” “and stuff” … That’s so vague." (잘 모르겠어요! ‘한 쉰 명’, ‘뭐 그런’, ‘같은 거’ … 너무 흐릿해요.)
8. Chloe (learner): "Ha! That’s the point. With friends, I don’t need exact numbers. Vague words keep it casual. And listen. In “like FIFty,” “like” is quick and soft." (하! 그게 핵심이에요. 친구끼리는 정확한 숫자가 필요 없잖아요. 흐릿한 말이 대화를 편하게 해 줘요. 그리고 들어 봐요. ‘like FIFty’에서 like는 빠르고 약해요.)
9. Jiwoo (you): "So should I talk like that, too?" (그럼 저도 그렇게 말해야 해요?)
10. Chloe (learner): "With friends, sure. But not in a work report. If your team asks how many users tested the app, “like fifty” won’t work." (친구끼리는 그럼요. 하지만 업무 보고에서는 안 돼요. 앱 테스트에 사용자 몇 명이 참여했냐고 팀이 물으면 ‘한 쉰 명’은 안 통해요.)
11. Jiwoo (you): "Right. At work, I’d say, “Forty-eight users tested it.”" (맞아요. 회사에서는 ‘사용자 48명이 테스트했습니다’라고 하겠죠.)
12. Chloe (learner): "Exactly. Oh, and the magician? He was kind of great. He pulled a card out of my scarf, or something along those lines." (바로 그거예요. 아, 그리고 마술사요? 좀 대단했어요. 제 목도리에서 카드를 꺼냈어요, 뭐 대충 그런 식으로요.)
13. Jiwoo (you): "See? That’s vague, too!" (봐요. 그것도 흐릿하잖아요!)
In one short sentence, say what is on the screen now and invite them to start. Do not say the learner's line before they try: remembering it is the point of this part, so this is the one exception to saying a sentence first. If they get stuck, give only the next word or two as a hint. If a word was missing or wrong, say the whole line once inside double quotes and let them try once more, then go on. Go in order, one line at a time. After the last line, react in a word or two, with no comment on how they sounded.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

steps.label: 마무리
steps.teach: Wrap up like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how it felt to say the scene by heart, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today (for example a line they remembered well), say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.
