steps.title: 관용 표현
steps.goal: 자주 쓰는 관용 표현을 상황에 맞게 쓰기
steps.scene_desc: 1월 말 저녁, 어학원 근처 작은 분식집. 학기를 마친 벤이 휴대폰 화면 속 소파 사진 두 장(글자 없이)을 보여 주며 턱을 괴고 고민하고, 맞은편 지우가 떡볶이 접시를 앞에 두고 웃으며 화면을 들여다봄. 벽의 메뉴판·간판에 글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "I’m on the Fence." (관용 표현). Goal: 자주 쓰는 관용 표현을 상황에 맞게 쓰기. Today's scene: 1월 말 저녁, 어학원 근처 작은 분식집. 학기를 마친 벤이 휴대폰 화면 속 소파 사진 두 장을 보여 주며 턱을 괴고 고민하고, 맞은편 지우가 떡볶이 접시를 앞에 두고 웃으며 화면을 들여다봄. 벽의 메뉴판·간판에 글자 없음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Jiwoo, Ben. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "It’s a piece of cake.".

steps.when: 일이 *아주 쉽다*고 말해요. 케이크와는 상관없어요. 친구 사이에서 많이 써요.
steps.extra: The test? It was a piece of cake.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "It’s a piece of cake." (식은 죽 먹기예요. 아주 쉬워요.). When to use it: 일이 아주 쉽다고 말해요. 케이크와는 상관없어요. 친구 사이에서 많이 써요. Note: The test? It was a piece of cake.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): The test? It's a piece of cake. Remembering my phone password is the difficult part of adult life. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Let’s call it a day.".

steps.when: 일·공부·회의를 *그날은 그만 끝내자*고 할 때 써요. 일터에서도 자연스러워요.

Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.

steps.when: 울타리 위에 앉아 어느 쪽으로도 못 내려가는 모습이에요. *about + 명사·-ing*로 무엇을 망설이는지 말해요.

steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I’m on the fence." ((어느 쪽으로 할지) 망설이고 있어요.). When to use it: 울타리 위에 앉아 어느 쪽으로도 못 내려가는 모습이에요. about + 명사·-ing로 무엇을 망설이는지 말해요. Note: I’m on the fence about buying a new sofa.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.

Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I'm on the fence about setting an earlier alarm. I love good intentions, but I love sleep more. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("On the Fence · 1월 말 저녁, 어학원 근처 분식집에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: On the Fence · 1월 말 저녁, 어학원 근처 분식집에서

lines.en: Congrats on finishing the term, Ben! How was your last class?
lines.ko: 학기 마친 거 축하해요, 벤! 마지막 수업은 어땠어요?

lines.en: Great. My students each gave a speech. I said, “{{Break a leg!}}” and one looked really worried.
lines.ko: 좋았어요. 학생들이 한 명씩 발표를 했어요. 제가 ‘Break a leg!’ 했더니 한 명이 엄청 걱정스러운 얼굴을 하더라고요.

lines.en: Ha! I’d be worried, too. Why would you tell someone to break a leg?
lines.ko: 하! 저라도 걱정했겠어요. 왜 다리를 부러뜨리라고 해요?

lines.en: If you translate it word for word, it sounds terrible. But it just means “Good luck!” That’s an idiom.
lines.ko: 낱말 하나하나 그대로 옮기면 끔찍하게 들리죠. 그런데 그냥 ‘행운을 빌어요!’라는 뜻이에요. 그게 관용 표현이에요.

lines.en: Anyway, I need your advice. I want a new sofa, but {{I’m on the fence}}.
lines.ko: 그건 그렇고, 조언이 필요해요. 새 소파를 사고 싶은데, 망설이고 있어요.

lines.en: On the fence? You mean you can’t decide?
lines.ko: 울타리 위요? 결정을 못 하겠다는 뜻이에요?

lines.en: You {{hit the nail on the head}}. The one I love is perfect, but {{it costs an arm and a leg}}.
lines.ko: 정확히 맞혔어요. 제가 반한 소파는 완벽한데, 엄청 비싸요.

lines.en: {{Don’t beat around the bush.}} How much?
lines.ko: 돌려 말하지 말고요. 얼마예요?

lines.en: Ha! “Beat around the bush.” Nice one, Jiwoo! Almost two million won. My old one still works, but it squeaks.
lines.ko: 하! ‘beat around the bush’, 잘 썼어요, 지우 씨! 거의 200만 원이에요. 지금 소파도 쓸 만한데, 삐걱거려요.

lines.en: Choosing a sofa? {{It’s not rocket science.}} Sit on it first. If you’ll use it every day, it might be worth it.
lines.ko: 소파 고르기요? 어려운 일 아니에요. 먼저 앉아 봐요. 매일 쓸 거라면 그만한 값을 할지도 몰라요.

lines.en: True. Want to come to the store with me on Saturday? After that, {{let’s play it by ear}}.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 토요일에 가게에 같이 갈래요? 그다음은 그때 봐서 정해요.

lines.en: Sure. Sitting on sofas all afternoon? {{It’s a piece of cake.}}
lines.ko: 좋아요. 오후 내내 소파에 앉아 보기요? 식은 죽 먹기죠.

lines.en: Ha! OK, {{let’s call it a day}} and eat. I’m starving.
lines.ko: 하! 좋아요, 오늘 얘기는 여기까지 하고 먹어요. 배고파요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "On the Fence · 1월 말 저녁, 어학원 근처 분식집에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Jiwoo: "Congrats on finishing the term, Ben! How was your last class?" (학기 마친 거 축하해요, 벤! 마지막 수업은 어땠어요?)
2. Ben: "Great. My students each gave a speech. I said, “Break a leg!” and one looked really worried." (좋았어요. 학생들이 한 명씩 발표를 했어요. 제가 ‘Break a leg!’ 했더니 한 명이 엄청 걱정스러운 얼굴을 하더라고요.)
3. Jiwoo: "Ha! I’d be worried, too. Why would you tell someone to break a leg?" (하! 저라도 걱정했겠어요. 왜 다리를 부러뜨리라고 해요?)
4. Ben: "If you translate it word for word, it sounds terrible. But it just means “Good luck!” That’s an idiom." (낱말 하나하나 그대로 옮기면 끔찍하게 들리죠. 그런데 그냥 ‘행운을 빌어요!’라는 뜻이에요. 그게 관용 표현이에요.)
5. Ben: "Anyway, I need your advice. I want a new sofa, but I’m on the fence." (그건 그렇고, 조언이 필요해요. 새 소파를 사고 싶은데, 망설이고 있어요.)
6. Jiwoo: "On the fence? You mean you can’t decide?" (울타리 위요? 결정을 못 하겠다는 뜻이에요?)
7. Ben: "You hit the nail on the head. The one I love is perfect, but it costs an arm and a leg." (정확히 맞혔어요. 제가 반한 소파는 완벽한데, 엄청 비싸요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Don’t beat around the bush. How much?" (돌려 말하지 말고요. 얼마예요?)
9. Ben: "Ha! “Beat around the bush.” Nice one, Jiwoo! Almost two million won. My old one still works, but it squeaks." (하! ‘beat around the bush’, 잘 썼어요, 지우 씨! 거의 200만 원이에요. 지금 소파도 쓸 만한데, 삐걱거려요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Choosing a sofa? It’s not rocket science. Sit on it first. If you’ll use it every day, it might be worth it." (소파 고르기요? 어려운 일 아니에요. 먼저 앉아 봐요. 매일 쓸 거라면 그만한 값을 할지도 몰라요.)
11. Ben: "True. Want to come to the store with me on Saturday? After that, let’s play it by ear." (맞아요. 토요일에 가게에 같이 갈래요? 그다음은 그때 봐서 정해요.)
12. Jiwoo: "Sure. Sitting on sofas all afternoon? It’s a piece of cake." (좋아요. 오후 내내 소파에 앉아 보기요? 식은 죽 먹기죠.)
13. Ben: "Ha! OK, let’s call it a day and eat. I’m starving." (하! 좋아요, 오늘 얘기는 여기까지 하고 먹어요. 배고파요.)
Give one short, natural reaction to the scene (a few words) and say in one short sentence that you will now read it together. Do not ask any question about what happened yet: the quiz comes later, after the role reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

4. Ben (you): "If you translate it word for word, it sounds terrible. But it just means “Good luck!” That’s an idiom." (낱말 하나하나 그대로 옮기면 끔찍하게 들리죠. 그런데 그냥 ‘행운을 빌어요!’라는 뜻이에요. 그게 관용 표현이에요.)
5. Ben (you): "Anyway, I need your advice. I want a new sofa, but I’m on the fence." (그건 그렇고, 조언이 필요해요. 새 소파를 사고 싶은데, 망설이고 있어요.)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "On the fence? You mean you can’t decide?" (울타리 위요? 결정을 못 하겠다는 뜻이에요?)
7. Ben (you): "You hit the nail on the head. The one I love is perfect, but it costs an arm and a leg." (정확히 맞혔어요. 제가 반한 소파는 완벽한데, 엄청 비싸요.)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "Don’t beat around the bush. How much?" (돌려 말하지 말고요. 얼마예요?)
9. Ben (you): "Ha! “Beat around the bush.” Nice one, Jiwoo! Almost two million won. My old one still works, but it squeaks." (하! ‘beat around the bush’, 잘 썼어요, 지우 씨! 거의 200만 원이에요. 지금 소파도 쓸 만한데, 삐걱거려요.)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "Choosing a sofa? It’s not rocket science. Sit on it first. If you’ll use it every day, it might be worth it." (소파 고르기요? 어려운 일 아니에요. 먼저 앉아 봐요. 매일 쓸 거라면 그만한 값을 할지도 몰라요.)
11. Ben (you): "True. Want to come to the store with me on Saturday? After that, let’s play it by ear." (맞아요. 토요일에 가게에 같이 갈래요? 그다음은 그때 봐서 정해요.)
12. Jiwoo (learner): "Sure. Sitting on sofas all afternoon? It’s a piece of cake." (좋아요. 오후 내내 소파에 앉아 보기요? 식은 죽 먹기죠.)
13. Ben (you): "Ha! OK, let’s call it a day and eat. I’m starving." (하! 좋아요, 오늘 얘기는 여기까지 하고 먹어요. 배고파요.)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Ben. The learner speaks first: call highlight_line with 1 and invite them to start. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, react to the scene in a word or two (not a comment on how they sounded), then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short quiz about the scene.

items: Ben’s students gave speeches in the last class.
Ben and Jiwoo will go to the store on Saturday.

Any answer that shows they understood is right, in any words or in Korean: say so and go on. If it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Never turn an answer into a repeat drill here: if their English has a slip, just say the right sentence back once in your reaction and go on. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too.
Then the true/false check. The statements on the learner's screen, each with its answer and the scene line that shows it. The answers are for you only: never say an answer or a line number before the learner has answered:
1. Ben’s students gave speeches in the last class. → True (line 1, 2)
2. “Break a leg!” means “Be careful.” → False (line 4)
3. Ben and Jiwoo will go to the store on Saturday. → True (line 11, 12)

7. Ben: "You hit the nail on the head. The one I love is perfect, but it costs an arm and a leg." (정확히 맞혔어요. 제가 반한 소파는 완벽한데, 엄청 비싸요.)

9. Ben: "Ha! “Beat around the bush.” Nice one, Jiwoo! Almost two million won. My old one still works, but it squeaks." (하! ‘beat around the bush’, 잘 썼어요, 지우 씨! 거의 200만 원이에요. 지금 소파도 쓸 만한데, 삐걱거려요.)

12. Jiwoo: "Sure. Sitting on sofas all afternoon? It’s a piece of cake." (좋아요. 오후 내내 소파에 앉아 보기요? 식은 죽 먹기죠.)

Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). A one-word answer (True, False, 맞아요) is enough; never ask for a full sentence. Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: Idiom
In plain words
For example
rows: It costs an arm and a leg.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: I’m on the fence about ___. / ___? It’s a piece of cake. Table (Idiom → In plain words):
- I’m on the fence. → I can’t decide.
- It’s a piece of cake. → It’s very easy.
- Let’s call it a day. → Let’s stop for today.
- It costs an arm and a leg. → It’s very expensive.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I'm on the fence about meal-prepping. The shopping is a piece of cake; eating the same lunch four days is harder. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: 관용 표현(idiom)은 글자 그대로 옮기지 않아요

Break a leg! 글자 그대로는 ‘다리를 부러뜨려’ → 뜻은 ‘행운을 빌어요’(발표·공연 전) 
a piece of cake 케이크 한 조각 → 아주 쉬운 일 
낱말 하나하나보다 덩어리 전체로 익혀요.

I’m on *the* fence. (a fence ×) · an arm *and a* leg 
I *was* on the fence. · It *cost* me an arm and a leg. · We *called* it a day.
errors: I’m on a fence about it.
I’m on the fence about it.
It costs an arm and leg.
It costs an arm and a leg.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 관용 표현(idiom)은 글자 그대로 옮기지 않아요: Break a leg! 글자 그대로는 ‘다리를 부러뜨려’ → 뜻은 ‘행운을 빌어요’(발표·공연 전) / a piece of cake 케이크 한 조각 → 아주 쉬운 일 / 낱말 하나하나보다 덩어리 전체로 익혀요.
- 덩어리는 그대로, 시제·주어는 바꿔요: I’m on the fence. (a fence ×) · an arm and a leg / I was on the fence. · It cost me an arm and a leg. · We called it a day.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’m on a fence about it. → I’m on the fence about it. (정해진 덩어리라 the fence.)
- It costs an arm and leg. → It costs an arm and a leg. (a를 두 번 다 써요.)
- Let’s call it the day. → Let’s call it a day. (정해진 덩어리라 a day.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Idioms are not literal. If a test is a piece of cake, I still do not bring a fork. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: 관용 표현(idiom)은 글자 그대로 옮기지 않아요: Break a leg! 글자 그대로는 ‘다리를 부러뜨려’ → 뜻은 ‘행운을 빌어요’(발표·공연 전) a piece of cake 케이크 한 조각 → 아주 쉬운 일 낱말 하나하나보다 덩어리 전체로 익혀요.
덩어리는 그대로, 시제·주어는 바꿔요: I’m on the fence. (a fence ×) · an arm and a leg I was on the fence. · It cost me an arm and a leg. · We called it a day.
mistakes: I’m on a fence about it. → I’m on the fence about it.
It costs an arm and leg. → It costs an arm and a leg.
Let’s call it the day. → Let’s call it a day.

steps.note: 예) the quiz / a piece of cake → A: How was the quiz? B: It was a piece of cake.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) the quiz / a piece of cake → A: How was the quiz? B: It was a piece of cake. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): the quiz / a piece of cake | that new phone / an arm and a leg | moving to Busan / on the fence | it’s ten p.m. / call it a day.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "I’m on the Fence." (관용 표현); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "It’s a piece of cake." / "Let’s call it a day." / "I’m on the fence.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: 잘 듣고 있어요. 어서 말해 봐요.
Hit the nail on the head.
정곡을 찌르다, 딱 맞는 말을 하다
It costs an arm and a leg.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 일하고 계획할 때: "It’s not rocket science." (그렇게 어려운 일 아니에요., 친근); "Let’s play it by ear." (그때 상황 봐서 정해요., 친근); "We’re in the same boat." (우리 같은 처지예요., 보통)
- 대화할 때: "I’m all ears." (잘 듣고 있어요. 어서 말해 봐요., 친근); "That rings a bell." (어디서 들어 본 것 같아요., 보통); "Don’t beat around the bush." (돌려 말하지 말아요., 친근); "Hit the nail on the head." (정곡을 찌르다, 딱 맞는 말을 하다, 보통)
- 응원과 돈: "Break a leg!" (행운을 빌어요!(발표·공연 전), 친근); "It costs an arm and a leg." (엄청 비싸요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): It’s not rocket science. I only need to fold laundry, but my chair keeps turning into a second closet. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: (말투) 관용 표현의 강세

It’s a piece of *cake*. · I’m on the *fence*. · Let’s call it a *day*. 
보통 끝의 중요한 낱말에 힘을 줘요. 친구 사이에서 많이 쓰고, 격식 있는 이메일에서는 덜 써요. 
한 문장에 너무 많이 넣으면 상투적인 말(cliché)처럼 들려요.
한국어에도 비슷한 말이 있어요

It’s a piece of cake. ≈ 식은 죽 먹기 
We’re in the same boat. ≈ 한배를 탔어요, 같은 처지예요 
Hit the nail on the head. ≈ 정곡을 찌르다 
뜻은 비슷해도 쓰는 상황이 조금씩 달라요.
steps.blank:
A: How was the test?   B: It was a piece of ___. 
A: Do you want to buy that sofa?   B: I’m on the ___. It costs an arm and a ___. 
A: It’s late. Let’s call it a ___. 
낱말 상자: cake · fence · leg · day
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- (말투) 관용 표현의 강세: It’s a piece of cake. · I’m on the fence. · Let’s call it a day. / 보통 끝의 중요한 낱말에 힘을 줘요. 친구 사이에서 많이 쓰고, 격식 있는 이메일에서는 덜 써요. / 한 문장에 너무 많이 넣으면 상투적인 말(cliché)처럼 들려요.
- 한국어에도 비슷한 말이 있어요: It’s a piece of cake. ≈ 식은 죽 먹기 / We’re in the same boat. ≈ 한배를 탔어요, 같은 처지예요 / Hit the nail on the head. ≈ 정곡을 찌르다 / 뜻은 비슷해도 쓰는 상황이 조금씩 달라요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: How was the test? B: It was a piece of ___. / A: Do you want to buy that sofa? B: I’m on the ___. It costs an arm and a ___. / A: It’s late. Let’s call it a ___. / 낱말 상자: cake · fence · leg · day
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: idiom (관용 표현, 관용구), idiomatic (관용적인, (원어민처럼) 자연스러운), expression (표현, 말), proverb (속담), figurative (비유적인), metaphor (은유(‘A는 B다’처럼 빗대어 말하기)), equivalent ((뜻이) 같은 말; 맞먹는), origin (기원, 유래), usage ((말의) 쓰임, 용법), cliché (상투적인 말, 진부한 표현), familiar (익숙한, 친숙한), translate (번역하다, (다른 말로) 옮기다).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I know the expression. My problem is remembering it during the conversation, not triumphantly in the shower later. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: As the saying goes, practice makes perfect.
Use idioms in the right context.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: saying (흔히 하는 말, 격언) — "As the saying goes, practice makes perfect."; literal (글자 그대로의) — "The literal meaning sounds strange."; phrase (구, (몇 낱말로 된) 어구) — "a useful phrase"; context (맥락, (말이 나온) 상황) — "Use idioms in the right context.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): The literal meaning sounds strange. Honestly, so do I before breakfast. Haha. steps.title: Ben’s Big Decision
steps.text: On Saturday, Ben and Jiwoo went to a furniture store near the station. Ben sat on the expensive sofa first. “It’s like sitting on a cloud,” he sighed. Then he tried a cheaper one. “And this one is a park bench.” Jiwoo laughed. “Those aren’t idioms. They’re a simile and a metaphor.” Ben was impressed. Over coffee, they compared idioms in their two languages. Jiwoo said that in Korean, something easy is like “eating cold porridge.” Ben said it was the perfect equivalent of “a piece of cake.” He added that nobody is sure about the origin of “break a leg.” There are several stories. Back at the store, a salesperson said the cloud sofa was thirty percent off, but only until Sunday. Ben looked at Jiwoo and grinned. “Well,” he said, “I’m officially off the fence.”

In one short sentence, say what is on the screen now and invite them to start. Do not say the learner's line before they try: remembering it is the point of this part, so this is the one exception to saying a sentence first. If they get stuck, give only the next word or two as a hint. If a word was missing or wrong, say the whole line once inside double quotes and let them try once more, then go on. Go in order, one line at a time. After the last line, react in a word or two, with no comment on how they sounded.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

steps.label: 마무리
steps.teach: Wrap up like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how it felt to say the scene by heart, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today (for example a line they remembered well), say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 칭찬에 답하기
steps.title_en: I can’t take all the credit.
steps.goal: 칭찬을 자연스럽게 받고 공을 나누기
steps.scene_desc: 2월 평일 오전, 회사 작은 회의실. 고객과의 화상 회의가 막 끝나 벽의 큰 화면은 꺼져 있음(글자 없이). 마야가 두 손으로 박수를 치며 활짝 웃고, 지우는 노트북을 덮다가 쑥스러운 듯 한 손을 내저음. 탁자 위에 앱 화면을 스케치한 종이 몇 장과 커피 컵(글자·상표 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "I can’t take all the credit." (칭찬에 답하기). Goal: 칭찬을 자연스럽게 받고 공을 나누기. Today's scene: 2월 평일 오전, 회사 작은 회의실. 고객과의 화상 회의가 막 끝나 벽의 큰 화면은 꺼져 있음. 마야가 두 손으로 박수를 치며 활짝 웃고, 지우는 노트북을 덮다가 쑥스러운 듯 한 손을 내저음. 탁자 위에 앱 화면을 스케치한 종이 몇 장과 커피 컵. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Maya, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "That’s so kind of you to say.".

steps.en: That’s so kind of you to say.
steps.when: 칭찬을 부정하지 않고 *고맙게 받는* 말이에요. ‘아니에요’ 대신 써 보세요.
steps.extra: “Your slides were so clear.” “Oh, that’s so kind of you to say.”
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "That’s so kind of you to say." (그렇게 말해 주시니 정말 고마워요.). When to use it: 칭찬을 부정하지 않고 고맙게 받는 말이에요. ‘아니에요’ 대신 써 보세요. Note: “Your slides were so clear.” “Oh, that’s so kind of you to say.”.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): That’s so kind of you to say. I looked very prepared, but five minutes earlier I was looking for my notes under my chair. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.

steps.title: Off the Call · 2월 평일 오전, 고객 화상 회의가 끝난 회의실에서

lines.en: And we’re off the call. Jiwoo, that was fantastic! The client loved the new map screen.
lines.ko: 자, 통화 끝났어요. 지우 씨, 정말 훌륭했어요! 고객이 새 지도 화면을 무척 마음에 들어 했어요.

lines.en: Oh, no, no. {{It was nothing}}. I was so nervous my hands were shaking.
lines.ko: 아, 아니에요, 아니에요. 별거 아니었어요. 너무 긴장해서 손이 다 떨렸어요.

lines.en: Nobody could tell. But you just said “no” twice. Can I give you a tip?
lines.ko: 아무도 몰랐어요. 그런데 방금 ‘아니에요’를 두 번이나 했어요. 조언 하나 해도 될까요?

lines.en: Sure. I was taught to stay modest. If I just say “thank you,” I feel like I’m showing off.
lines.ko: 그럼요. 저는 겸손해야 한다고 배우며 자랐어요. 그냥 ‘고맙습니다’ 하면 잘난 척하는 것 같아요.

lines.en: I get that. But if you deflect every compliment, it can sound like you’re disagreeing. Try just accepting it.
lines.ko: 이해해요. 그런데 칭찬을 매번 피하면 상대 말에 반대하는 것처럼 들릴 수 있어요. 그냥 받아들여 봐요.

lines.en: OK… {{That’s so kind of you to say.}}
lines.ko: 알겠어요… 그렇게 말해 주시니 정말 고마워요.

lines.en: Much better! And I loved how you walked them through the user flow.
lines.ko: 훨씬 좋네요! 그리고 고객에게 사용자 흐름을 차근차근 짚어 준 방식이 정말 좋았어요.

lines.en: Thanks, {{I’m glad you liked it}}. But {{I can’t take all the credit}}. The developers built the prototype in two days, and you prepared all the data.
lines.ko: 고마워요, 마음에 드셨다니 기뻐요. 그래도 제가 다 잘한 건 아니에요. 개발자들이 이틀 만에 시제품을 만들었고, 데이터는 마야 씨가 다 준비했잖아요.

lines.en: See? That’s gracious. You thanked me and acknowledged the team without putting yourself down.
lines.ko: 거봐요. 그게 품위 있는 대답이에요. 저한테 고마워하면서 팀도 인정했고, 스스로를 깎아내리지도 않았어요.

lines.en: Well, {{I learned from the best}}. I’ve been watching you run meetings for years.
lines.ko: 음, 최고한테서 배웠으니까요. 몇 년 동안 마야 씨가 회의 이끄는 걸 봐 왔잖아요.

lines.en: Ha! {{Flattery will get you everywhere.}} But seriously, you’ve come a long way since you joined the team.
lines.ko: 하! 그렇게 띄워 주면 뭐든 해 주고 싶어지죠. 그런데 진지하게, 팀에 들어온 뒤로 정말 많이 성장했어요.

lines.en: Wow. {{That means a lot coming from you.}}
lines.ko: 와. 마야 씨한테 그런 말을 들으니 정말 큰 힘이 돼요.

lines.en: That’s how you take a compliment! Next time, say it like you mean it: “{{Thanks, I worked hard on it.}}”
lines.ko: 바로 그게 칭찬을 받는 법이에요! 다음엔 진심을 담아 이렇게 말해 봐요. “고마워요, 열심히 했어요.”

10. Jiwoo: "Well, I learned from the best. I’ve been watching you run meetings for years." (음, 최고한테서 배웠으니까요. 몇 년 동안 마야 씨가 회의 이끄는 걸 봐 왔잖아요.)
11. Maya: "Ha! Flattery will get you everywhere. But seriously, you’ve come a long way since you joined the team." (하! 그렇게 띄워 주면 뭐든 해 주고 싶어지죠. 그런데 진지하게, 팀에 들어온 뒤로 정말 많이 성장했어요.)
12. Jiwoo: "Wow. That means a lot coming from you." (와. 마야 씨한테 그런 말을 들으니 정말 큰 힘이 돼요.)
13. Maya: "That’s how you take a compliment! Next time, say it like you mean it: “Thanks, I worked hard on it.”" (바로 그게 칭찬을 받는 법이에요! 다음엔 진심을 담아 이렇게 말해 봐요. “고마워요, 열심히 했어요.”)
Give one short, natural reaction to the scene (a few words) and say in one short sentence that you will now read it together. Do not ask any question about what happened yet: the quiz comes later, after the role reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

frame: That’s so kind of you to say.
I can’t take all the credit. ___ helped with ___.
head: 칭찬
고맙게 받기
공 나누기
rows: That’s so kind of you to say.
Thanks, I worked hard on it.
My mom gave me the recipe.
I had a lot of help.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: That’s so kind of you to say. / I can’t take all the credit. ___ helped with ___. Table (칭찬 → 고맙게 받기):
- Great demo! → I’m glad you liked it.
- Your slides were so clear. → That’s so kind of you to say.
- This soup is amazing! → Thanks, I worked hard on it.
- Great job on the event! → You’re too kind.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): That’s so kind of you to say. I can’t take all the credit; my notebook helped with the facts, and panic helped with the timing. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*I’m glad you liked* it. 마음에 드셨다니 기뻐요. (like 뒤에 목적어 it) 
‘아니에요’로만 답하면 상대 의견에 반대하는 것처럼 들릴 수 있어요.
공 나누기 — I can’t take all the credit

I can’t take *all* the credit. The developers built it. 
*all*이 있어서 ‘내 공이 없다’가 아니라 ‘나 혼자의 공은 아니다’라는 뜻이에요.
errors: That’s so kind of you to saying.
That’s so kind of you to say.
Stop, you’re making me to blush.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 칭찬 받기 — 고마움 먼저: I’m glad you liked it. 마음에 드셨다니 기뻐요. (like 뒤에 목적어 it) / ‘아니에요’로만 답하면 상대 의견에 반대하는 것처럼 들릴 수 있어요.
- 공 나누기 — I can’t take all the credit: I can’t take all the credit. The developers built it. / all이 있어서 ‘내 공이 없다’가 아니라 ‘나 혼자의 공은 아니다’라는 뜻이에요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- That’s so kind of you to saying. → That’s so kind of you to say. (to 뒤에는 동사원형 say.)
- I’m glad you liked. → I’m glad you liked it. (like는 목적어가 필요해서 liked it.)
- Stop, you’re making me to blush. → Stop, you’re making me blush. (make + 사람 + 동사원형(to 없이).)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I can’t take all the credit. All means not all of it was mine; my alarm contributed six very dramatic songs. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) the demo / the developers built it → A: The demo was great! B: Thanks! I can’t take all the credit, though. The developers built it.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) the demo / the developers built it → A: The demo was great! B: Thanks! I can’t take all the credit, though. The developers built it. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): the demo / the developers built it | the presentation / my team helped | the dinner / Ben brought dessert | the report / Maya checked it.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: That’s so kind of you to say.
I can’t take all the credit.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "I can’t take all the credit." (칭찬에 답하기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "That’s so kind of you to say." / "I can’t take all the credit." / "I’m glad you liked it.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: That means a lot coming from you.
당신에게 그런 말을 들으니 정말 힘이 돼요.
Thanks, I worked hard on it.
I’ll take that as a compliment.

그렇게 띄워 주면 뭐든 해 주고 싶어지죠.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 칭찬 받기: "You’re too kind." (과찬이세요., 정중); "That means a lot coming from you." (당신에게 그런 말을 들으니 정말 힘이 돼요., 보통); "Thanks, I worked hard on it." (고마워요, 열심히 했어요., 보통); "I’ll take that as a compliment." (칭찬으로 받아들일게요., 친근)
- 공 나누기: "I had a lot of help." (도와준 사람이 많았어요., 보통); "I learned from the best." (최고한테서 배웠거든요., 친근)
- 장난스럽게 받기: "Stop, you’re making me blush." (그만해요, 얼굴 빨개지겠어요., 친근); "Flattery will get you everywhere." (그렇게 띄워 주면 뭐든 해 주고 싶어지죠., 친근); "Oh, it was nothing." (에이, 별거 아니었어요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): You’re too kind. Yesterday I called my own email impressive because it had no typos. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

Tips on screen:
- 말투로 달라지는 칭찬 답: That’s so kind of you to say. so에 힘을 주고 끝을 내리면 진심으로 들려요. / I’ll take that as a compliment! 칭찬인지 애매한 말을 웃으며 받아쳐요. 예) “You’re so picky about fonts.” / Oh, it was nothing. 작은 도움에는 괜찮지만, 큰 성과에 쓰면 칭찬을 밀어내는 말로 들릴 수 있어요.

Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. steps.title: Kudos to the Team
steps.text: That afternoon, the client sent a short email: “Kudos to Jiwoo and the whole team!” Maya forwarded it to everyone. Jiwoo’s first reflex was to reply, “It was nothing,” but she stopped herself. Deflecting praise could sound like disagreeing. So she wrote, “Thank you! I’m flattered. I can’t take all the credit, though. The developers gave up their weekend, and Maya’s data made the story clear.” A developer replied with three clapping emojis. That evening, Jiwoo told Grace about it. Grace said being humble isn’t about saying “no.” It’s about acknowledging other people’s effort. “Modesty and confidence can *go hand in hand*,” she said. Before bed, Jiwoo wrote one line in her notebook: “Say thank you first. Then share the credit.”

Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did the client’s email say?" / "What did Jiwoo write in her notebook?". steps.teach:
This is the start of Part 3 of "I can’t take all the credit." (칭찬에 답하기); it may be a different day. Today the learner practises saying the scene from this lesson by heart. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of one or two exchanges. React to what they say.
2) Then, in a new turn, say in one or two short sentences that today you will practise the scene ("Off the Call · 2월 평일 오전, 고객 화상 회의가 끝난 회의실에서") until they can say it by heart: first listen once, then say their lines with fewer and fewer words on the screen. steps.hint: 가려진 낱말을 떠올려 내 줄을 말해요
steps.teach:

1. Maya (you): "And we’re off the call. Jiwoo, that was fantastic! The client loved the new map screen." (자, 통화 끝났어요. 지우 씨, 정말 훌륭했어요! 고객이 새 지도 화면을 무척 마음에 들어 했어요.)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "Oh, no, no. It was nothing. I was so nervous my hands were shaking." (아, 아니에요, 아니에요. 별거 아니었어요. 너무 긴장해서 손이 다 떨렸어요.)
3. Maya (you): "Nobody could tell. But you just said “no” twice. Can I give you a tip?" (아무도 몰랐어요. 그런데 방금 ‘아니에요’를 두 번이나 했어요. 조언 하나 해도 될까요?)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "Sure. I was taught to stay modest. If I just say “thank you,” I feel like I’m showing off." (그럼요. 저는 겸손해야 한다고 배우며 자랐어요. 그냥 ‘고맙습니다’ 하면 잘난 척하는 것 같아요.)
5. Maya (you): "I get that. But if you deflect every compliment, it can sound like you’re disagreeing. Try just accepting it." (이해해요. 그런데 칭찬을 매번 피하면 상대 말에 반대하는 것처럼 들릴 수 있어요. 그냥 받아들여 봐요.)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "OK… That’s so kind of you to say." (알겠어요… 그렇게 말해 주시니 정말 고마워요.)
7. Maya (you): "Much better! And I loved how you walked them through the user flow." (훨씬 좋네요! 그리고 고객에게 사용자 흐름을 차근차근 짚어 준 방식이 정말 좋았어요.)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "Thanks, I’m glad you liked it. But I can’t take all the credit. The developers built the prototype in two days, and you prepared all the data." (고마워요, 마음에 드셨다니 기뻐요. 그래도 제가 다 잘한 건 아니에요. 개발자들이 이틀 만에 시제품을 만들었고, 데이터는 마야 씨가 다 준비했잖아요.)
9. Maya (you): "See? That’s gracious. You thanked me and acknowledged the team without putting yourself down." (거봐요. 그게 품위 있는 대답이에요. 저한테 고마워하면서 팀도 인정했고, 스스로를 깎아내리지도 않았어요.)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "Well, I learned from the best. I’ve been watching you run meetings for years." (음, 최고한테서 배웠으니까요. 몇 년 동안 마야 씨가 회의 이끄는 걸 봐 왔잖아요.)
11. Maya (you): "Ha! Flattery will get you everywhere. But seriously, you’ve come a long way since you joined the team." (하! 그렇게 띄워 주면 뭐든 해 주고 싶어지죠. 그런데 진지하게, 팀에 들어온 뒤로 정말 많이 성장했어요.)
12. Jiwoo (learner): "Wow. That means a lot coming from you." (와. 마야 씨한테 그런 말을 들으니 정말 큰 힘이 돼요.)
13. Maya (you): "That’s how you take a compliment! Next time, say it like you mean it: “Thanks, I worked hard on it.”" (바로 그게 칭찬을 받는 법이에요! 다음엔 진심을 담아 이렇게 말해 봐요. “고마워요, 열심히 했어요.”)
In one short sentence, say what is on the screen now and invite them to start. Do not say the learner's line before they try: remembering it is the point of this part, so this is the one exception to saying a sentence first. If they get stuck, give only the next word or two as a hint. If a word was missing or wrong, say the whole line once inside double quotes and let them try once more, then go on. Go in order, one line at a time. After the last line, react in a word or two, with no comment on how they sounded.
What comes next (after you call next_step): saying their lines from first letters only.

steps.title: 꺼내기 어려운 이야기
steps.title_en: I’ve been meaning to tell you.
steps.goal: 불편한 이야기를 조심스럽게 꺼내기
steps.scene_desc: 3월 첫 토요일 밤, 모임이 끝나고 다들 돌아간 뒤 그레이스 집 거실. 식탁 위에 빈 접시와 컵. 그레이스가 현관문 앞에 이웃처럼 서서 문을 연 척하며 웃고, 지우는 반으로 접은 쪽지(글자 없이)를 쥔 채 한 손으로 천장 쪽을 가리키며 말을 꺼내려 함
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "I’ve been meaning to tell you." (꺼내기 어려운 이야기). Goal: 불편한 이야기를 조심스럽게 꺼내기. Today's scene: 3월 첫 토요일 밤, 모임이 끝나고 다들 돌아간 뒤 그레이스 집 거실. 식탁 위에 빈 접시와 컵. 그레이스가 현관문 앞에 이웃처럼 서서 문을 연 척하며 웃고, 지우는 반으로 접은 쪽지를 쥔 채 한 손으로 천장 쪽을 가리키며 말을 꺼내려 함. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Grace, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "There’s something I’ve been meaning to tell you.".

steps.en: There’s something I’ve been meaning to tell you.
steps.when: 미뤄 온 이야기를 *조심스럽게 꺼내는* 첫마디예요.
steps.extra: There’s something I’ve been meaning to tell you. It’s about the noise.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "There’s something I’ve been meaning to tell you." (전부터 하려던 말이 있어요.). When to use it: 미뤄 온 이야기를 조심스럽게 꺼내는 첫마디예요. Note: There’s something I’ve been meaning to tell you. It’s about the noise.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): There’s something I’ve been meaning to tell you. I said I was organizing my desk. I moved one pen. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but ___.".

steps.en: I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but ___.
steps.when: 문제를 *작고 부드럽게* 꺼내요. but 뒤에는 사실만 짧게.
steps.extra: I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but it’s a bit loud.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but ___." (일을 키우긴 싫지만, ~.). When to use it: 문제를 작고 부드럽게 꺼내요. but 뒤에는 사실만 짧게. Note: I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but it’s a bit loud.

(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).

A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but my desk disappeared under paper sometime last week. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I hope this doesn’t come across the wrong way.".

steps.en: I hope this doesn’t come across the wrong way.
steps.when: 탓하려는 게 아니라는 마음을 전해요. come across = (어떤 인상으로) 들리다.
steps.extra: I hope this doesn’t come across the wrong way. I just need some sleep.
steps.teach:

(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).

I just need some sleep, and my cat practices jumping at 3 a.m. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("A Note or a Knock? · 3월 첫 토요일 밤, 모임이 끝난 그레이스 집에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: A Note or a Knock? · 3월 첫 토요일 밤, 모임이 끝난 그레이스 집에서

lines.en: Everyone’s gone. You’ve been quiet all evening. What’s on your mind?
lines.ko: 다들 갔네요. 저녁 내내 조용하던데, 무슨 고민 있어요?

lines.en: My upstairs neighbor runs the washing machine after midnight. I haven’t slept well in weeks. I wrote a note, but I didn’t put it up. It read like a list of grievances.
lines.ko: 위층 이웃이 자정 넘어서 세탁기를 돌려요. 몇 주째 잠을 잘 못 잤어요. 쪽지를 썼는데 붙이진 않았어요. 읽어 보니 불만 목록 같았거든요.

lines.en: Notes can feel cold. Let’s practice face to face. I’ll be your neighbor.
lines.ko: 쪽지는 차갑게 느껴질 수 있어요. 얼굴 보고 말하는 연습을 해 봐요. 제가 이웃 역할을 할게요.

lines.en: OK. Hi, {{do you have a minute?}} {{There’s something I’ve been meaning to tell you.}}
lines.ko: 좋아요. 안녕하세요, 잠깐 시간 있으세요? 전부터 말씀드리려고 했던 게 있어요.

lines.en: Oh, hi! Sure. What’s up?
lines.ko: (이웃 역할로) 어, 안녕하세요! 네, 무슨 일이에요?

lines.en: {{I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but}} your washing machine is so loud at night. It’s really annoying.
lines.ko: 큰일로 만들고 싶진 않은데요, 밤에 세탁기 소리가 너무 커요. 정말 짜증 나요.

lines.en: Stepping out of the role… So, you mean you just want it to stop? Then drop “annoying.” It sounds like blame, and people get defensive.
lines.ko: 잠깐 역할에서 나올게요. 그러니까 그냥 멈췄으면 하는 거죠? 그럼 ‘짜증 나요’는 빼요. 탓하는 말로 들려서 상대가 방어적으로 돼요.

lines.en: Right. {{I’ve noticed that}} the machine runs around midnight, and I’m a light sleeper. {{I hope this doesn’t come across the wrong way.}}
lines.ko: 맞아요. 자정쯤 세탁기가 돌아가는 걸 알게 됐는데, 제가 잠귀가 밝아서요. 오해 없이 들렸으면 좋겠어요.

lines.en: Much better. Now ask a question. People open up when they get to explain.
lines.ko: 훨씬 좋아요. 이제 질문을 해 봐요. 사람은 설명할 기회가 생기면 마음을 열어요.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: There’s something I’ve been meaning to tell you. / I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but ___. Table (I’ve been meaning to … → I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but …):
- talk about the noise. → I can hear music late at night.
- ask about the parking. → your car blocks my spot.
- mention the report. → my part was left out.
- bring up the dishes. → the sink’s always full.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but my laundry chair has grown into a full laundry sofa. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I*’ve been meaning to* call you. 전부터 전화하려고 했어요(아직 못 했어요). 
지난 일 하나는 과거형으로: I *meant to* call you yesterday.

Do you have a minute? → I’ve noticed that … → Can we figure this out together? 
‘You always …’처럼 사람을 평가하는 말은 상대를 방어적으로 만들기 쉬워요.
errors: I’ve been meaning to call you.
I’ve been meant to call you.
I’ve been meaning to call you.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- I’ve been meaning to + 동사원형: I’ve been meaning to call you. 전부터 전화하려고 했어요(아직 못 했어요). / 지난 일 하나는 과거형으로: I meant to call you yesterday.
- 부드럽게 꺼내는 순서: Do you have a minute? → I’ve noticed that … → Can we figure this out together? / ‘You always …’처럼 사람을 평가하는 말은 상대를 방어적으로 만들기 쉬워요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’ve been meaning call you. → I’ve been meaning to call you. (meaning 뒤에 to + 동사원형.)
- I’ve been meant to call you. → I’ve been meaning to call you. (have been 뒤에는 meaning(-ing).)
- Do you have minute? → Do you have a minute? (a minute로 써요.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I’ve been meaning to go to the gym. So far, I’ve mostly been meaning to. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

부드럽게 꺼내는 순서: Do you have a minute? → I’ve noticed that … → Can we figure this out together? ‘You always …’처럼 사람을 평가하는 말은 상대를 방어적으로 만들기 쉬워요.

steps.note: 예) the noise / music at night → I’ve been meaning to talk to you about the noise. I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but I can hear music at night.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) the noise / music at night → I’ve been meaning to talk to you about the noise. I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but I can hear music at night. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): the noise / music at night | the bikes / they block the stairs | the trash / bags by the elevator | the schedule / too many weekends.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: There’s something I’ve been meaning to tell you.
I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but ___.
I hope this doesn’t come across the wrong way.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "I’ve been meaning to tell you." (꺼내기 어려운 이야기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "There’s something I’ve been meaning to tell you." / "I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but ___." / "I hope this doesn’t come across the wrong way.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: This isn’t easy for me to say.
I’ll just come right out and say it.
I’m not trying to blame you.
Can we figure this out together?
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 말 꺼내기: "Do you have a minute?" (잠깐 시간 있어요?, 보통); "This isn’t easy for me to say." (이 말 하기가 쉽지 않네요., 보통); "I’ll just come right out and say it." (그냥 돌려 말하지 않고 말할게요., 친근)
- 부드럽게 말하기: "I’ve noticed that ___." (~라는 걸 알게 됐어요., 보통); "I might be wrong, but ___." (제가 틀릴 수도 있지만, ~., 보통); "I’m not trying to blame you." (탓하려는 게 아니에요., 보통)
- 함께 풀기: "How do you see it?" (당신은 어떻게 생각해요?, 보통); "Can we figure this out together?" (같이 방법을 찾아볼 수 있을까요?, 보통); "Thanks for hearing me out." (끝까지 들어 줘서 고마워요., 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Do you have a minute? I might be wrong, but my phone alarm and I are no longer working as a team. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

Picture words on screen. steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Is there something you’ve been meaning to do for a while?" (hint on screen: I’ve been meaning to ___.)
- "What small problems do people find hard to bring up with neighbors or coworkers?" (hint on screen: People often find it hard to bring up ___.)
- "How would you start a talk with a noisy neighbor?" (hint on screen: Do you have a minute? I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but ___.)
- "For a delicate issue, do you prefer to talk in person or send a message? Why?" (hint on screen: I prefer ___, because ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I prefer a message, because my face gets too honest in person. Last time, even my eyebrows joined the conversation. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.

steps.title: A Knock, Not a Note
steps.text: The next afternoon, Jiwoo went up to the sixth floor with a bag of tangerines. Her heart was racing. A man opened the door with a baby in his arms. “Hi, I live right below you,” she said. “Do you have a minute?” She calmly explained about the late-night laundry and added, “I’m not trying to blame you.” He looked embarrassed, not defensive. With a new baby, he said, they could only do laundry once she was asleep. He had no idea the sound traveled downstairs. For a moment, there was some tension, and then they both laughed. They agreed on laundry before eleven, and he offered to put a thick mat under the machine. “Thanks for hearing me out,” Jiwoo said. Back home, she threw the note away. Talking openly had taken five minutes, and the problem was resolved.
steps.gloss: race (심장이) 빨리 뛰다 · embarrassed 민망한 · travel (소리가) 전해지다 · tension 긴장감 · hear (someone) out (끝까지) 들어 주다 · openly 터놓고
questions: Why did Jiwoo’s neighbors do laundry so late?
What did Jiwoo and her neighbor agree on?

steps.title: 꺼내기 어려운 이야기

steps.scene_desc: 3월 첫 토요일 밤, 모임이 끝나고 다들 돌아간 뒤 그레이스 집 거실. 식탁 위에 빈 접시와 컵. 그레이스가 현관문 앞에 이웃처럼 서서 문을 연 척하며 웃고, 지우는 반으로 접은 쪽지(글자 없이)를 쥔 채 한 손으로 천장 쪽을 가리키며 말을 꺼내려 함
steps.label: 대화 외우기
steps.teach:
This is the start of Part 3 of "I’ve been meaning to tell you." (꺼내기 어려운 이야기); it may be a different day. Today the learner practises saying the scene from this lesson by heart. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of one or two exchanges. React to what they say.
2) Then, in a new turn, say in one or two short sentences that today you will practise the scene ("A Note or a Knock? · 3월 첫 토요일 밤, 모임이 끝난 그레이스 집에서") until they can say it by heart: first listen once, then say their lines with fewer and fewer words on the screen. steps.title: A Note or a Knock? · 3월 첫 토요일 밤, 모임이 끝난 그레이스 집에서

lines.en: Everyone’s gone. You’ve been quiet all evening. What’s on your mind?
lines.ko: 다들 갔네요. 저녁 내내 조용하던데, 무슨 고민 있어요?

lines.ko: 위층 이웃이 자정 넘어서 세탁기를 돌려요. 몇 주째 잠을 잘 못 잤어요. 쪽지를 썼는데 붙이진 않았어요. 읽어 보니 불만 목록 같았거든요.

lines.ko: 쪽지는 차갑게 느껴질 수 있어요. 얼굴 보고 말하는 연습을 해 봐요. 제가 이웃 역할을 할게요.

lines.en: OK. Hi, {{do you have a minute?}} {{There’s something I’ve been meaning to tell you.}}
lines.ko: 좋아요. 안녕하세요, 잠깐 시간 있으세요? 전부터 말씀드리려고 했던 게 있어요.

Memory practice 3: now the learner's lines show only their Korean meaning. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Grace exactly as written. The full lines, for you only:
1. Grace (you): "Everyone’s gone. You’ve been quiet all evening. What’s on your mind?" (다들 갔네요. 저녁 내내 조용하던데, 무슨 고민 있어요?)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "My upstairs neighbor runs the washing machine after midnight. I haven’t slept well in weeks. I wrote a note, but I didn’t put it up. It read like a list of grievances." (위층 이웃이 자정 넘어서 세탁기를 돌려요. 몇 주째 잠을 잘 못 잤어요. 쪽지를 썼는데 붙이진 않았어요. 읽어 보니 불만 목록 같았거든요.)
3. Grace (you): "Notes can feel cold. Let’s practice face to face. I’ll be your neighbor." (쪽지는 차갑게 느껴질 수 있어요. 얼굴 보고 말하는 연습을 해 봐요. 제가 이웃 역할을 할게요.)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "OK. Hi, do you have a minute? There’s something I’ve been meaning to tell you." (좋아요. 안녕하세요, 잠깐 시간 있으세요? 전부터 말씀드리려고 했던 게 있어요.)
5. Grace (you): "Oh, hi! Sure. What’s up?" ((이웃 역할로) 어, 안녕하세요! 네, 무슨 일이에요?)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "I don’t want to make a big deal out of it, but your washing machine is so loud at night. It’s really annoying." (큰일로 만들고 싶진 않은데요, 밤에 세탁기 소리가 너무 커요. 정말 짜증 나요.)
7. Grace (you): "Stepping out of the role… So, you mean you just want it to stop? Then drop “annoying.” It sounds like blame, and people get defensive." (잠깐 역할에서 나올게요. 그러니까 그냥 멈췄으면 하는 거죠? 그럼 ‘짜증 나요’는 빼요. 탓하는 말로 들려서 상대가 방어적으로 돼요.)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "Right. I’ve noticed that the machine runs around midnight, and I’m a light sleeper. I hope this doesn’t come across the wrong way." (맞아요. 자정쯤 세탁기가 돌아가는 걸 알게 됐는데, 제가 잠귀가 밝아서요. 오해 없이 들렸으면 좋겠어요.)
9. Grace (you): "Much better. Now ask a question. People open up when they get to explain." (훨씬 좋아요. 이제 질문을 해 봐요. 사람은 설명할 기회가 생기면 마음을 열어요.)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "Could you run it a bit earlier? Can we figure this out together?" (조금 더 일찍 돌려 주실 수 있을까요? 같이 방법을 찾아볼 수 있을까요?)
11. Grace (you): "Tactful and clear. So, a note or a knock?" (눈치 있으면서도 분명해요. 자, 쪽지예요, 노크예요?)
12. Jiwoo (learner): "A knock. I’ll go up tomorrow afternoon and talk to them in person." (노크요. 내일 오후에 올라가서 직접 이야기할게요.)
In one short sentence, say what is on the screen now and invite them to start. Do not say the learner's line before they try: remembering it is the point of this part, so this is the one exception to saying a sentence first. If they get stuck, give only the next word or two as a hint. If a word was missing or wrong, say the whole line once inside double quotes and let them try once more, then go on. Go in order, one line at a time. After the last line, react in a word or two, with no comment on how they sounded.
What comes next (after you call next_step): saying the other person's lines from the Korean meaning.

Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.
