steps.title: 부드럽게 거절하기
steps.title_en: Can I take a rain check?
steps.goal: 무례하지 않게 거절하고 다음을 기약하기
steps.scene_desc: 3월 말 평일 오후, 회사 탕비실. 창밖에 봄 햇살. 마야가 휴대폰 속 산 사진(글자 없이)을 보여 주며 신나게 웃고, 지우는 머그잔을 든 채 미안한 듯 웃으며 다른 손을 가슴에 얹음. 뒤쪽에 냉장고와 커피 머신(상표·글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Can I take a rain check?" (부드럽게 거절하기). Goal: 무례하지 않게 거절하고 다음을 기약하기. Today's scene: 3월 말 평일 오후, 회사 탕비실. 창밖에 봄 햇살. 마야가 휴대폰 속 산 사진을 보여 주며 신나게 웃고, 지우는 머그잔을 든 채 미안한 듯 웃으며 다른 손을 가슴에 얹음. 뒤쪽에 냉장고와 커피 머신. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Maya, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I’d love to, but ___.".

steps.when: 먼저 *마음은 있다*는 걸 보여 주고 거절해요. but 뒤 이유는 짧게 하나만.
steps.extra: I’d love to, but I have family plans that day.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I’d love to, but ___." (정말 그러고 싶은데, ~.). When to use it: 먼저 마음은 있다는 걸 보여 주고 거절해요. but 뒤 이유는 짧게 하나만. Note: I’d love to, but I have family plans that day.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I’d love to, but I promised myself an early night. I usually break that promise by midnight. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I’m going to have to pass this time.".

steps.en: I’m going to have to pass this time.
steps.when: *going to have to*가 ‘사정상 어쩔 수 없다’는 느낌을 줘서 부드러워요. *this time*이 다음 여지를 남겨요.
steps.extra: Thanks for asking, but I’m going to have to pass this time.

steps.en: Can I take a rain check?

steps.title: Next Time, for Sure · 3월 말 평일 오후, 회사 탕비실에서

lines.en: Jiwoo! The team’s going hiking this Saturday. Just an easy trail, then lunch. You in?
lines.ko: 지우 씨! 이번 토요일에 팀이 등산 가요. 쉬운 코스 걷고 점심 먹을 거예요. 같이 갈래요?

lines.en: Oh, {{I’d love to, but}} it’s my dad’s birthday. My whole family’s having lunch together.
lines.ko: 아, 정말 가고 싶은데, 그날 아빠 생신이에요. 온 가족이 같이 점심을 먹기로 했어요.

lines.en: Aw, family comes first. No worries at all.
lines.ko: 아, 가족이 먼저죠. 전혀 걱정 마요.

lines.en: Sorry. I feel bad saying no again. I missed the team dinner last month, too.
lines.ko: 미안해요. 또 거절하려니 마음이 안 좋네요. 지난달 팀 회식도 빠졌잖아요.

lines.en: Don’t be. Saying no is a skill. Saying yes to everything can burn you out.
lines.ko: 그러지 마요. 거절하는 것도 기술이에요. 뭐든 다 한다고 하면 지쳐 버릴 수 있어요.

lines.en: That’s me at work these days. {{I’ve got a lot on my plate right now.}} The client wants the new screens by April.
lines.ko: 요즘 회사에서 제가 딱 그래요. 지금 할 일이 산더미예요. 고객이 4월까지 새 화면을 원하거든요.

lines.en: Then don’t overcommit. You can say “{{I’m going to have to pass this time}},” even to me.
lines.ko: 그럼 무리해서 다 맡지 마요. 저한테도 ‘이번엔 빠져야 할 것 같아요’라고 해도 돼요.

lines.en: Even to my manager? Wouldn’t that sound rude?
lines.ko: 매니저한테도요? 무례하게 들리지 않을까요?

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: I’d love to, but ___. / Can I take a rain check? Table (초대 → I’d love to, but …):
- Drinks tonight? → I’ve got an early meeting.
- Join our book club? → I’ve got a lot on my plate.
- Futsal on Sunday? → I’ve got family plans.
- One more project? → I don’t have the bandwidth.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I’d love to, but I don’t have the bandwidth. My brain has three tabs open, and two are frozen. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*Thanks for thinking of me.* *I’d love to, but* I have plans. *Maybe another time?* 
이유는 하나면 충분해요. 변명(excuse)이 길면 오히려 덜 진심으로 들릴 수 있어요.
I’m going to have to ~ · I wish I could

I’m *going to have to* pass. 빠져야 할 것 같아요(사정상 어쩔 수 없다는 느낌). 
*I wish I could.* 그러고 싶은데 못 해요(뒤의 come 등은 생략).
errors: I’d love to, but I can’t to go.
I’d love to, but I can’t go.
I’m going to have to passing this time.
I’m going to have to pass this time.
지금 할 수 없는 일을 바랄 때 wish 뒤에는 *could*.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 부드러운 거절의 순서: Thanks for thinking of me. I’d love to, but I have plans. Maybe another time? / 이유는 하나면 충분해요. 변명(excuse)이 길면 오히려 덜 진심으로 들릴 수 있어요.
- I’m going to have to ~ · I wish I could: I’m going to have to pass. 빠져야 할 것 같아요(사정상 어쩔 수 없다는 느낌). / I wish I could. 그러고 싶은데 못 해요(뒤의 come 등은 생략).
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’d love to, but I can’t to go. → I’d love to, but I can’t go. (can’t 뒤에는 동사원형(to 없이).)
- I’m going to have to passing this time. → I’m going to have to pass this time. (have to 뒤에는 동사원형 pass.)
- I wish I can. → I wish I could. (지금 할 수 없는 일을 바랄 때 wish 뒤에는 could.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I’m going to have to pass this time. If I add one more plan, I may need two Mondays. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: 부드러운 거절의 순서: Thanks for thinking of me. I’d love to, but I have plans. Maybe another time? 이유는 하나면 충분해요. 변명(excuse)이 길면 오히려 덜 진심으로 들릴 수 있어요.
I’m going to have to ~ · I wish I could: I’m going to have to pass. 빠져야 할 것 같아요(사정상 어쩔 수 없다는 느낌). I wish I could. 그러고 싶은데 못 해요(뒤의 come 등은 생략).
mistakes: I’d love to, but I can’t to go. → I’d love to, but I can’t go.
I’m going to have to passing this time. → I’m going to have to pass this time.
I wish I can. → I wish I could.

steps.note: 예) join us for lunch / I have a deadline → A: Want to join us for lunch? B: I’d love to, but I have a deadline. Can I take a rain check?
items: I’ve got a lot on my plate
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) join us for lunch / I have a deadline → A: Want to join us for lunch? B: I’d love to, but I have a deadline. Can I take a rain check? The items (the words the learner gets for each one): join us for lunch / I have a deadline | come to the party / I have a prior engagement | go hiking on Sunday / I’ve got family plans | help with the event / I’ve got a lot on my plate.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Can I take a rain check?" (부드럽게 거절하기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I’d love to, but ___." / "I’m going to have to pass this time." / "Can I take a rain check?". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 고마움 먼저: "That’s really kind of you, but ___." (정말 고마운 말이지만, ~., 정중); "Thanks for thinking of me." (생각해 줘서 고마워요., 보통)
- 아쉬움과 이유: "I’ve got a lot on my plate right now." (지금 할 일이 산더미예요., 친근); "I wish I could." (그러고 싶은데 못 해요., 보통); "I don’t think I can make it." (못 갈 것 같아요., 보통); "I’ll have to sit this one out." (이번 건 빠질게요., 친근)

Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Thanks for thinking of me. I’ve got a lot on my plate right now. Even my to-do list needs its own to-do list. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. steps.title: A Clear No
steps.text: On Saturday, Jiwoo had lunch with her family for her dad’s birthday. Her phone buzzed with photos from the hike: muddy shoes, a view of the city, and Maya waving from the top. Jiwoo didn’t feel guilty. She had declined politely, and Maya had been gracious about it. On Monday, a designer from another team asked her to join one more project. Jiwoo felt the old urge to say yes. Instead, she said, “Thanks for thinking of me. I don’t have the bandwidth right now, but let me get back to you in April.” He nodded. “That’s fair. Keep me posted.” Jiwoo realized that a clear no can be more considerate than a reluctant yes. That evening, Maya sent a message: “Next hike is in May. You’re *on the hook* now!” Jiwoo replied with a thumbs-up.
steps.gloss: buzz (휴대폰이) 울리다 · muddy 진흙투성이의 · guilty 죄책감이 드는 · urge (강한) 충동 · considerate 배려하는 · on the hook (약속에) 꼼짝없이 걸린
questions: Why didn’t Jiwoo go on the hike?
What did Jiwoo say to the designer from another team?

I don’t have the bandwidth right now, but let me get back to you in April.” He nodded. “That’s fair. Keep me posted.” Jiwoo realized that a clear no can be more considerate than a reluctant yes. That evening, Maya sent a message: “Next hike is in May. You’re on the hook now!” Jiwoo replied with a thumbs-up." Words: buzz (휴대폰이) 울리다 · muddy 진흙투성이의 · guilty 죄책감이 드는 · urge (강한) 충동 · considerate 배려하는 · on the hook (약속에) 꼼짝없이 걸린.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Why didn’t Jiwoo go on the hike?" / "What did Jiwoo say to the designer from another team?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.

lines.en: Jiwoo! The team’s going hiking this Saturday. Just an easy trail, then lunch. You in?
lines.ko: 지우 씨! 이번 토요일에 팀이 등산 가요. 쉬운 코스 걷고 점심 먹을 거예요. 같이 갈래요?

lines.en: Oh, {{I’d love to, but}} it’s my dad’s birthday. My whole family’s having lunch together.

lines.en: Aw, family comes first. No worries at all.

lines.en: Sorry. I feel bad saying no again. I missed the team dinner last month, too.
lines.ko: 미안해요. 또 거절하려니 마음이 안 좋네요. 지난달 팀 회식도 빠졌잖아요.

lines.en: Don’t be. Saying no is a skill. Saying yes to everything can burn you out.
lines.ko: 그러지 마요. 거절하는 것도 기술이에요. 뭐든 다 한다고 하면 지쳐 버릴 수 있어요.

lines.en: That’s me at work these days. {{I’ve got a lot on my plate right now.}} The client wants the new screens by April.
lines.ko: 요즘 회사에서 제가 딱 그래요. 지금 할 일이 산더미예요. 고객이 4월까지 새 화면을 원하거든요.

lines.en: Then don’t overcommit. You can say “{{I’m going to have to pass this time}},” even to me.

lines.ko: 매니저한테도요? 무례하게 들리지 않을까요?

lines.en: “A prior engagement”! Very formal. Great for an email, but with me, just say “I’ve got family plans.”
lines.ko: ‘선약’이라니! 아주 격식 있네요. 이메일에는 좋은데, 저한테는 그냥 ‘가족 약속이 있어요’라고 해요.

steps.label: 장면 다시 듣기
steps.teach:

1. Maya: "Jiwoo! The team’s going hiking this Saturday. Just an easy trail, then lunch. You in?" (지우 씨! 이번 토요일에 팀이 등산 가요. 쉬운 코스 걷고 점심 먹을 거예요. 같이 갈래요?)

steps.title: 깊은 위로
steps.title_en: Take all the time you need.
steps.goal: 어려운 일을 겪는 사람에게 마음을 담아 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 4월 초 저녁, 그레이스 집 거실. 소파에 나란히 앉은 그레이스와 지우가 그레이스의 휴대폰 속 사진(바닷가에서 파도를 쫓아 뛰는 갈색 개, 글자 없이)을 함께 봄. 그레이스는 휴지를 쥔 채 살며시 웃고, 지우는 그레이스 어깨에 가만히 손을 얹음. 탁자 위에 지우가 가져온 수프 냄비와 따뜻한 차 두 잔. 창밖은 어스름(글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Take all the time you need." (깊은 위로). Goal: 어려운 일을 겪는 사람에게 마음을 담아 말하기. Today's scene: 4월 초 저녁, 그레이스 집 거실. 소파에 나란히 앉은 그레이스와 지우가 그레이스의 휴대폰 속 사진을 함께 봄. 그레이스는 휴지를 쥔 채 살며시 웃고, 지우는 그레이스 어깨에 가만히 손을 얹음. 탁자 위에 지우가 가져온 수프 냄비와 따뜻한 차 두 잔. 창밖은 어스름. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Jiwoo, Grace. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I can’t imagine how hard this must be.".

steps.en: I can’t imagine how hard this must be.
steps.when: 상대의 아픔을 *안다고 말하지 않고* 마음을 전해요. must be = 틀림없이 ~일 거예요(추측).
steps.extra: I can’t imagine how hard this must be for your family.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I can’t imagine how hard this must be." (얼마나 힘들지 상상도 안 돼요.). When to use it: 상대의 아픔을 안다고 말하지 않고 마음을 전해요. must be = 틀림없이 ~일 거예요(추측). Note: I can’t imagine how hard this must be for your family.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I can't imagine how hard this must be for my family. Every time I cook, they quietly check if there is ramen. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Take all the time you need.".

steps.en: Take all the time you need.
steps.when: *서두르지 않아도 된다*고 말해요. 마음을 추스르거나 일을 미뤄도 된다는 뜻으로도 써요.
steps.extra: Don’t worry about the report. Take all the time you need.

It updated for forty minutes, then asked for another update. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). steps.en: I’m here if you need anything.
steps.when: 무언가를 하라는 게 아니라 *곁에 있겠다*는 마음을 전해요.
steps.extra: Call me anytime. I’m here if you need anything.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I’m here if you need anything." (필요한 게 있으면 언제든 말해요.). When to use it: 무언가를 하라는 게 아니라 곁에 있겠다는 마음을 전해요. Note: Call me anytime. I’m here if you need anything.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I'm here if you need anything. Unless you need help folding a fitted sheet. Then we both need help. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Biscuit · 4월 초 저녁, 그레이스 집 거실에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Biscuit · 4월 초 저녁, 그레이스 집 거실에서

lines.en: I brought some soup. Grace, {{I’m so sorry for your loss.}}
lines.ko: 수프 좀 가져왔어요. 그레이스, 정말 상심이 크겠어요.

lines.en: Mom called this morning. Biscuit passed away in his sleep. He was fifteen.
lines.ko: 아침에 엄마한테 전화가 왔어요. 비스킷이 자다가 조용히 떠났대요. 열다섯 살이었어요.

lines.en: Oh, Grace. {{I can’t imagine how hard this must be}}, so far from home.
lines.ko: 아, 그레이스. 고향에서 이렇게 멀리 있으니 얼마나 힘들지 상상도 안 돼요.

lines.en: I didn’t get to say goodbye. I should’ve gone home at Christmas.
lines.ko: 작별 인사를 못 했어요. 크리스마스에 집에 갔어야 했어요.

lines.en: {{There are no words.}} But he knew how much you loved him.
lines.ko: 무슨 말을 해야 할지 모르겠어요. 그래도 비스킷은 그레이스가 얼마나 사랑했는지 알았을 거예요.

lines.en: I hope so. Every Sunday on video calls, he’d tilt his head at my voice.
lines.ko: 그랬으면 좋겠어요. 일요일마다 영상 통화를 하면 비스킷이 제 목소리에 고개를 갸웃했어요.

lines.en: That’s so sweet. Want to show me some photos? {{Whenever you’re ready.}}
lines.ko: 정말 사랑스럽네요. 사진 보여 줄래요? 마음이 내킬 때요.

lines.en: Look, this is Biscuit as a puppy. He chewed up my favorite sneakers.
lines.ko: 봐요, 이게 강아지 때 비스킷이에요. 제가 아끼던 운동화를 다 물어뜯었어요.

lines.en: Look at those ears! And this one, at the beach?
lines.ko: 귀 좀 봐요! 그리고 이건 바닷가예요?

lines.en: His favorite place. He’d chase the waves for hours. Sorry, I keep crying.
lines.ko: 제일 좋아하던 곳이에요. 몇 시간이고 파도를 쫓아다녔어요. 미안해요, 자꾸 눈물이 나네요.

lines.en: Don’t apologize. {{It’s okay not to be okay.}} {{Take all the time you need.}}
lines.ko: 사과하지 마요. 괜찮지 않아도 괜찮아요. 필요한 만큼 천천히 해요.

lines.en: Thank you, Jiwoo. Honestly, just having you here helps.
lines.ko: 고마워요, 지우 씨. 솔직히 옆에 있어 주는 것만으로도 힘이 돼요.

lines.en: {{I’m here if you need anything.}} {{I’ll drop by with some food}} tomorrow. And {{be gentle with yourself}}, OK?

12. Grace: "Thank you, Jiwoo. Honestly, just having you here helps." (고마워요, 지우 씨. 솔직히 옆에 있어 주는 것만으로도 힘이 돼요.)
13. Jiwoo: "I’m here if you need anything. I’ll drop by with some food tomorrow. And be gentle with yourself, OK?" (필요한 거 있으면 언제든 말해요. 내일 먹을 거 들고 들를게요. 그리고 너무 자책하지 말아요, 알았죠?)

frame: I can’t imagine how hard this must be.
I’m here if you need anything.
head: I can’t imagine how …
this must be for …
I could …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: I can’t imagine how hard this must be. / I’m here if you need anything. Table (I can’t imagine how … → this must be for …):
- hard → you.
- painful → your family.
- lonely → you right now.
- exhausting → all of you.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I can't imagine how exhausting this must be for my family. I'm here if you need anything, they say, when I start fixing things. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I can’t imagine *how hard this must be*. 
I can’t imagine *what you’re going through*. 
의문사 뒤는 *주어 + 동사*(must this be ×).

You *must be* exhausted. 많이 지쳤겠어요. (상대 마음을 짐작해 공감) 
‘I know how you feel.’은 상대가 ‘내 마음을 어떻게 알아?’ 하고 느낄 수도 있어요.

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- I can’t imagine + how/what 절: I can’t imagine how hard this must be. / I can’t imagine what you’re going through. / 의문사 뒤는 주어 + 동사(must this be ×).
- must be = (틀림없이) ~일 거예요: You must be exhausted. 많이 지쳤겠어요. (상대 마음을 짐작해 공감) / ‘I know how you feel.’은 상대가 ‘내 마음을 어떻게 알아?’ 하고 느낄 수도 있어요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I can’t imagine how hard must this be. → I can’t imagine how hard this must be. (의문사 뒤는 주어 + 동사.)
- I’m so sorry for you loss. → I’m so sorry for your loss. (소유격 your.)
- It’s okay to not okay. → It’s okay not to be okay. (to be가 필요해요.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): After how, say subject plus verb. I can't imagine how tired my bus driver must be; he sighed at every stop. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: I can’t imagine + how/what 절: I can’t imagine how hard this must be. I can’t imagine what you’re going through. 의문사 뒤는 주어 + 동사(must this be ×).
must be = (틀림없이) ~일 거예요: You must be exhausted. 많이 지쳤겠어요. (상대 마음을 짐작해 공감) ‘I know how you feel.’은 상대가 ‘내 마음을 어떻게 알아?’ 하고 느낄 수도 있어요.

I’m so sorry for you loss. → I’m so sorry for your loss.
It’s okay to not okay. → It’s okay not to be okay.

steps.note: 예) hard / bring you some soup → I can’t imagine how hard this must be. I could bring you some soup.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) hard / bring you some soup → I can’t imagine how hard this must be. I could bring you some soup. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): hard / bring you some soup | painful / walk with you tomorrow | lonely / just sit with you | tough / call you tonight.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: I can’t imagine how hard this must be.
Take all the time you need.
I’m here if you need anything.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Take all the time you need." (깊은 위로); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I can’t imagine how hard this must be." / "Take all the time you need." / "I’m here if you need anything.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I’m so sorry for your loss.
You don’t have to go through this alone.
Is there anything I can do?
제가 할 수 있는 게 있을까요?
I’ll drop by with some food.
It’s okay not to be okay.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 처음 건네는 말: "I’m so sorry for your loss." (정말 상심이 크겠어요., 정중); "There are no words." (무슨 말을 해야 할지 모르겠어요., 보통); "I’m thinking of you." (늘 마음 쓰고 있어요., 보통)
- 곁에 있기: "You don’t have to go through this alone." (혼자 견디지 않아도 돼요., 보통); "Is there anything I can do?" (제가 할 수 있는 게 있을까요?, 보통); "I’ll drop by with some food." (먹을 거 들고 들를게요., 친근)
- 마음 놓게 하기: "It’s okay not to be okay." (괜찮지 않아도 괜찮아요., 친근); "Be gentle with yourself." (너무 자책하지 말아요., 보통); "Whenever you’re ready." (마음이 내킬 때 해요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I'll drop by with some food, I always say. Then I remember my cooking and stop by with fruit. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 목소리와 속도

위로할 때는 천천히, 낮고 부드럽게 말해요. 
I’m *so* sorry. so를 조금 길게 말하면 마음이 전해져요. 
Whenever you’re ready. 끝을 올리지 말고 조용히 내려요. 
말이 없어도 괜찮아요. 곁에 있어 주는 것(presence)도 위로예요.
(참고) 격식 있는 위로의 말

Please accept my *condolences*. · My deepest *sympathies*. 카드·메시지에 쓰는 격식 있는 조의 표현 
*funeral* 장례식 · *bereavement* (가족·가까운 이를) 잃음, 사별(격식 있는 말) 
반려동물을 떠나보낸 뒤 작은 추모(memorial)를 하는 가족도 있어요.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 목소리와 속도: 위로할 때는 천천히, 낮고 부드럽게 말해요. / I’m so sorry. so를 조금 길게 말하면 마음이 전해져요. / Whenever you’re ready. 끝을 올리지 말고 조용히 내려요. / 말이 없어도 괜찮아요. 곁에 있어 주는 것(presence)도 위로예요.
- (참고) 격식 있는 위로의 말: Please accept my condolences. · My deepest sympathies. 카드·메시지에 쓰는 격식 있는 조의 표현 / funeral 장례식 · bereavement (가족·가까운 이를) 잃음, 사별(격식 있는 말) / 반려동물을 떠나보낸 뒤 작은 추모(memorial)를 하는 가족도 있어요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Our old dog passed away last night. B: I’m so ___ for your loss. I can’t ___ how hard this must be. / A: Thank you. B: I’m ___ if you need anything. / 낱말 상자: sorry · imagine · here
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: loss ((소중한 존재를) 잃음, 상실), grief ((잃은 뒤의) 깊은 슬픔), sorrow (슬픔, 비통함), sympathy (안타까워하는 마음; 위로), condolence (조의, 애도(주로 condolences)), compassion ((아픈 사람을) 아끼고 돕고 싶은 마음), comfort (위로; 위로하다), gentle (부드러운, 다정한), burden (짐, 부담), heal ((상처·마음이) 낫다, 아물다), memorial (추모(하는 것), 기념물), solace (위안(이 되는 것)).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Too many shopping bags become a real burden. One orange rolled away like it had its own plans. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: healing (치유, 아물어 가는 과정) — "Healing takes time."; sympathies ((격식) 조의, 위로의 마음) — "Our sympathies are with you."; support (힘이 되어 줌; 지지하다) — "Thanks for your support."; empathy (공감(상대 입장이 되어 느낌)) — "She listened with empathy."; cope ((힘든 일을) 견디다, 대처하다) — "How are you coping?"; presence (곁에 있음, 존재) — "Your presence means a lot."; strength (힘, (마음의) 강인함) — "Friends gave her strength.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): How am I coping? I make a list, lose the list, and call that a system. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Your friend’s pet passed away. What would you say first?" (hint on screen: I’m so sorry for your loss. I can’t imagine ___.)
- "What can you do for a friend who is sad, besides talking?" (hint on screen: I could ___. / I’ll drop by with ___.)
- "What do you find comforting when you’re having a hard day?" (hint on screen: It helps when ___. / Just ___.)
- "How do people around you usually show sympathy?" (hint on screen: They usually ___. / Some people send ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Some people send kind messages to show sympathy. My aunt sends one heart and seventeen exclamation points. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: A Tree for Biscuit
steps.text: A week later, Grace’s parents planted a small apple tree in their garden as a memorial for Biscuit. Grace joined by video call, and Jiwoo sat beside her on the sofa. Her mom held up the phone so Grace could see the tree. “He always loved digging right here,” her dad said, and they all laughed for the first time in days. Afterward, Grace said grief comes and goes *in waves*. Some mornings she felt fine. Other times, a dog on the street made her cry. Jiwoo didn’t try to fix it. She just listened, and sometimes she brought dinner. “Your presence was a real solace,” Grace told her. “You didn’t give me advice. You just stayed.” That night, Jiwoo thought about it. Comforting someone isn’t about finding the perfect words. It’s about *being there*.
steps.gloss: memorial 추모(의 표시) · dig (땅을) 파다 · in waves 밀려왔다 밀려갔다 하며 · presence 곁에 있음 · solace 위안 · be there (for someone) 곁에 있어 주다
questions: What did Grace’s parents plant for Biscuit?
What did Jiwoo do instead of giving advice?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "A Tree for Biscuit". Text: "A week later, Grace’s parents planted a small apple tree in their garden as a memorial for Biscuit. Grace joined by video call, and Jiwoo sat beside her on the sofa. Her mom held up the phone so Grace could see the tree. “He always loved digging right here,” her dad said, and they all laughed for the first time in days. Afterward, Grace said grief comes and goes in waves. Some mornings she felt fine. Other times, a dog on the street made her cry. Jiwoo didn’t try to fix it. She just listened, and sometimes she brought dinner. “Your presence was a real solace,” Grace told her. “You didn’t give me advice. You just stayed.” That night, Jiwoo thought about it. Comforting someone isn’t about finding the perfect words. It’s about being there." Words: memorial 추모(의 표시) · dig (땅을) 파다 · in waves 밀려왔다 밀려갔다 하며 · presence 곁에 있음 · solace 위안 · be there (for someone) 곁에 있어 주다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Grace’s parents plant for Biscuit?" / "What did Jiwoo do instead of giving advice?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘I can’t imagine how hard this must be.’로 상대의 아픔에 공감할 수 있어요.

Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘I can’t imagine how hard this must be.’로 상대의 아픔에 공감할 수 있어요.

First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that next time we will practise saying today's scene by heart, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 깊은 위로
steps.title_en: Take all the time you need.
steps.goal: 오늘 장면의 대화를 외워서 말해 보기
steps.scene_desc: 4월 초 저녁, 그레이스 집 거실. 소파에 나란히 앉은 그레이스와 지우가 그레이스의 휴대폰 속 사진(바닷가에서 파도를 쫓아 뛰는 갈색 개, 글자 없이)을 함께 봄. 그레이스는 휴지를 쥔 채 살며시 웃고, 지우는 그레이스 어깨에 가만히 손을 얹음. 탁자 위에 지우가 가져온 수프 냄비와 따뜻한 차 두 잔. 창밖은 어스름(글자 없이)
steps.label: 대화 외우기
steps.teach:
This is the start of Part 3 of "Take all the time you need." (깊은 위로); it may be a different day. Today the learner practises saying the scene from this lesson by heart. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of one or two exchanges. React to what they say.
2) Then, in a new turn, say in one or two short sentences that today you will practise the scene ("Biscuit · 4월 초 저녁, 그레이스 집 거실에서") until they can say it by heart: first listen once, then say their lines with fewer and fewer words on the screen. Do not ask if they are ready more than once.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays the scene once more — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Biscuit · 4월 초 저녁, 그레이스 집 거실에서

lines.en: I brought some soup. Grace, {{I’m so sorry for your loss.}}
lines.ko: 수프 좀 가져왔어요. 그레이스, 정말 상심이 크겠어요.

lines.en: Mom called this morning. Biscuit passed away in his sleep. He was fifteen.
lines.ko: 아침에 엄마한테 전화가 왔어요. 비스킷이 자다가 조용히 떠났대요. 열다섯 살이었어요.

lines.en: Oh, Grace. {{I can’t imagine how hard this must be}}, so far from home.
lines.ko: 아, 그레이스. 고향에서 이렇게 멀리 있으니 얼마나 힘들지 상상도 안 돼요.

lines.en: I didn’t get to say goodbye. I should’ve gone home at Christmas.
lines.ko: 작별 인사를 못 했어요. 크리스마스에 집에 갔어야 했어요.

lines.en: {{There are no words.}} But he knew how much you loved him.
lines.ko: 무슨 말을 해야 할지 모르겠어요. 그래도 비스킷은 그레이스가 얼마나 사랑했는지 알았을 거예요.

lines.en: I hope so. Every Sunday on video calls, he’d tilt his head at my voice.
lines.ko: 그랬으면 좋겠어요. 일요일마다 영상 통화를 하면 비스킷이 제 목소리에 고개를 갸웃했어요.

lines.en: That’s so sweet. Want to show me some photos? {{Whenever you’re ready.}}
lines.ko: 정말 사랑스럽네요. 사진 보여 줄래요? 마음이 내킬 때요.

lines.en: Look, this is Biscuit as a puppy. He chewed up my favorite sneakers.
lines.ko: 봐요, 이게 강아지 때 비스킷이에요. 제가 아끼던 운동화를 다 물어뜯었어요.

lines.en: Look at those ears! And this one, at the beach?
lines.ko: 귀 좀 봐요! 그리고 이건 바닷가예요?

lines.en: His favorite place. He’d chase the waves for hours. Sorry, I keep crying.
lines.ko: 제일 좋아하던 곳이에요. 몇 시간이고 파도를 쫓아다녔어요. 미안해요, 자꾸 눈물이 나네요.

lines.en: Don’t apologize. {{It’s okay not to be okay.}} {{Take all the time you need.}}
lines.ko: 사과하지 마요. 괜찮지 않아도 괜찮아요. 필요한 만큼 천천히 해요.

lines.en: Thank you, Jiwoo. Honestly, just having you here helps.
lines.ko: 고마워요, 지우 씨. 솔직히 옆에 있어 주는 것만으로도 힘이 돼요.

lines.en: {{I’m here if you need anything.}} {{I’ll drop by with some food}} tomorrow. And {{be gentle with yourself}}, OK?
lines.ko: 필요한 거 있으면 언제든 말해요. 내일 먹을 거 들고 들를게요. 그리고 너무 자책하지 말아요, 알았죠?

steps.label: 장면 다시 듣기
steps.teach:
The app has just played the scene again in the characters' own voices:
1. Jiwoo: "I brought some soup. Grace, I’m so sorry for your loss." (수프 좀 가져왔어요. 그레이스, 정말 상심이 크겠어요.)
2. Grace: "Mom called this morning. Biscuit passed away in his sleep. He was fifteen." (아침에 엄마한테 전화가 왔어요. 비스킷이 자다가 조용히 떠났대요. 열다섯 살이었어요.)
3. Jiwoo: "Oh, Grace. I can’t imagine how hard this must be, so far from home." (아, 그레이스. 고향에서 이렇게 멀리 있으니 얼마나 힘들지 상상도 안 돼요.)
4. Grace: "I didn’t get to say goodbye. I should’ve gone home at Christmas." (작별 인사를 못 했어요. 크리스마스에 집에 갔어야 했어요.)
5. Jiwoo: "There are no words. But he knew how much you loved him." (무슨 말을 해야 할지 모르겠어요. 그래도 비스킷은 그레이스가 얼마나 사랑했는지 알았을 거예요.)
6. Grace: "I hope so. Every Sunday on video calls, he’d tilt his head at my voice." (그랬으면 좋겠어요. 일요일마다 영상 통화를 하면 비스킷이 제 목소리에 고개를 갸웃했어요.)
7. Jiwoo: "That’s so sweet. Want to show me some photos? Whenever you’re ready." (정말 사랑스럽네요. 사진 보여 줄래요? 마음이 내킬 때요.)
8. Grace: "Look, this is Biscuit as a puppy. He chewed up my favorite sneakers." (봐요, 이게 강아지 때 비스킷이에요. 제가 아끼던 운동화를 다 물어뜯었어요.)
9. Jiwoo: "Look at those ears! And this one, at the beach?" (귀 좀 봐요! 그리고 이건 바닷가예요?)
10. Grace: "His favorite place. He’d chase the waves for hours. Sorry, I keep crying." (제일 좋아하던 곳이에요. 몇 시간이고 파도를 쫓아다녔어요. 미안해요, 자꾸 눈물이 나네요.)
11. Jiwoo: "Don’t apologize. It’s okay not to be okay. Take all the time you need." (사과하지 마요. 괜찮지 않아도 괜찮아요. 필요한 만큼 천천히 해요.)
12. Grace: "Thank you, Jiwoo. Honestly, just having you here helps." (고마워요, 지우 씨. 솔직히 옆에 있어 주는 것만으로도 힘이 돼요.)
13. Jiwoo: "I’m here if you need anything. I’ll drop by with some food tomorrow. And be gentle with yourself, OK?" (필요한 거 있으면 언제든 말해요. 내일 먹을 거 들고 들를게요. 그리고 너무 자책하지 말아요, 알았죠?)

lines.ko: 작별 인사를 못 했어요. 크리스마스에 집에 갔어야 했어요.

lines.en: 무슨 말을 해야 할지 모르겠어요. 그래도 비스킷은 그레이스가 얼마나 사랑했는지 알았을 거예요.
I hope so. Every Sunday on video calls, he’d tilt his head at my voice.
lines.ko: 그랬으면 좋겠어요. 일요일마다 영상 통화를 하면 비스킷이 제 목소리에 고개를 갸웃했어요.

lines.en: 정말 사랑스럽네요. 사진 보여 줄래요? 마음이 내킬 때요.
Look, this is Biscuit as a puppy. He chewed up my favorite sneakers.
lines.ko: 봐요, 이게 강아지 때 비스킷이에요. 제가 아끼던 운동화를 다 물어뜯었어요.

lines.en: 귀 좀 봐요! 그리고 이건 바닷가예요?
His favorite place. He’d chase the waves for hours. Sorry, I keep crying.
lines.ko: 제일 좋아하던 곳이에요. 몇 시간이고 파도를 쫓아다녔어요. 미안해요, 자꾸 눈물이 나네요.

lines.en: 사과하지 마요. 괜찮지 않아도 괜찮아요. 필요한 만큼 천천히 해요.
Thank you, Jiwoo. Honestly, just having you here helps.
lines.ko: 고마워요, 지우 씨. 솔직히 옆에 있어 주는 것만으로도 힘이 돼요.

lines.en: 필요한 거 있으면 언제든 말해요. 내일 먹을 거 들고 들를게요. 그리고 너무 자책하지 말아요, 알았죠?

steps.hint: 한국어 뜻만 보고 내 줄을 영어로 말해요
steps.teach:
Memory practice 3: now the learner's lines show only their Korean meaning. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Grace exactly as written. The full lines, for you only:
1. Jiwoo (learner): "I brought some soup. Grace, I’m so sorry for your loss." (수프 좀 가져왔어요. 그레이스, 정말 상심이 크겠어요.)
2. Grace (you): "Mom called this morning. Biscuit passed away in his sleep. He was fifteen." (아침에 엄마한테 전화가 왔어요. 비스킷이 자다가 조용히 떠났대요. 열다섯 살이었어요.)
3. Jiwoo (learner): "Oh, Grace. I can’t imagine how hard this must be, so far from home." (아, 그레이스. 고향에서 이렇게 멀리 있으니 얼마나 힘들지 상상도 안 돼요.)
4. Grace (you): "I didn’t get to say goodbye. I should’ve gone home at Christmas." (작별 인사를 못 했어요. 크리스마스에 집에 갔어야 했어요.)
5. Jiwoo (learner): "There are no words. But he knew how much you loved him." (무슨 말을 해야 할지 모르겠어요. 그래도 비스킷은 그레이스가 얼마나 사랑했는지 알았을 거예요.)
6. Grace (you): "I hope so. Every Sunday on video calls, he’d tilt his head at my voice." (그랬으면 좋겠어요. 일요일마다 영상 통화를 하면 비스킷이 제 목소리에 고개를 갸웃했어요.)
7. Jiwoo (learner): "That’s so sweet. Want to show me some photos? Whenever you’re ready." (정말 사랑스럽네요. 사진 보여 줄래요? 마음이 내킬 때요.)
8. Grace (you): "Look, this is Biscuit as a puppy. He chewed up my favorite sneakers." (봐요, 이게 강아지 때 비스킷이에요. 제가 아끼던 운동화를 다 물어뜯었어요.)
9. Jiwoo (learner): "Look at those ears! And this one, at the beach?" (귀 좀 봐요! 그리고 이건 바닷가예요?)
10. Grace (you): "His favorite place. He’d chase the waves for hours. Sorry, I keep crying." (제일 좋아하던 곳이에요. 몇 시간이고 파도를 쫓아다녔어요. 미안해요, 자꾸 눈물이 나네요.)
11. Jiwoo (learner): "Don’t apologize. It’s okay not to be okay. Take all the time you need." (사과하지 마요. 괜찮지 않아도 괜찮아요. 필요한 만큼 천천히 해요.)
12. Grace (you): "Thank you, Jiwoo. Honestly, just having you here helps." (고마워요, 지우 씨. 솔직히 옆에 있어 주는 것만으로도 힘이 돼요.)
13. Jiwoo (learner): "I’m here if you need anything. I’ll drop by with some food tomorrow. And be gentle with yourself, OK?" (필요한 거 있으면 언제든 말해요. 내일 먹을 거 들고 들를게요. 그리고 너무 자책하지 말아요, 알았죠?)
In one short sentence, say what is on the screen now and invite them to start. Do not say the learner's line before they try: remembering it is the point of this part, so this is the one exception to saying a sentence first. If they get stuck, give only the next word or two as a hint. If a word was missing or wrong, say the whole line once inside double quotes and let them try once more, then go on. Go in order, one line at a time. After the last line, react in a word or two, with no comment on how they sounded.
What comes next (after you call next_step): saying the other person's lines from the Korean meaning.

steps.title: 말투 바꾸기
steps.goal: 같은 부탁을 상대에 맞게 격식을 바꿔 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 5월 중순 토요일 오후, 그레이스 집 거실. 소파에 앉은 지우가 무릎 위 노트북(화면에 글자 없이)을 보며 이야기하고, 맞은편 의자의 그레이스가 손가락 세 개를 펴 보이며(친구·동료·고객 세 단계) 웃으며 설명함. 스탠드 옆에 충전기, 탁자 위에 찻잔 두 개와 작은 화분. 글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Would you mind if I …?" (말투 바꾸기). Goal: 같은 부탁을 상대에 맞게 격식을 바꿔 말하기. Today's scene: 5월 중순 토요일 오후, 그레이스 집 거실. 소파에 앉은 지우가 무릎 위 노트북을 보며 이야기하고, 맞은편 의자의 그레이스가 손가락 세 개를 펴 보이며(친구·동료·고객 세 단계) 웃으며 설명함. 스탠드 옆에 충전기, 탁자 위에 찻잔 두 개와 작은 화분. 글자 없음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Grace, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Would you mind if I ___?".

steps.when: 고객·윗사람·처음 보는 사람에게 하는 *정중한* 부탁. 괜찮다는 대답은 *No, not at all.*(‘아니요, 전혀 꺼리지 않아요’)예요.
steps.extra: Would you mind if I recorded the meeting?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Would you mind if I ___?" (제가 ~해도 괜찮을까요?). When to use it: 고객·윗사람·처음 보는 사람에게 하는 정중한 부탁. 괜찮다는 대답은 No, not at all.(‘아니요, 전혀 꺼리지 않아요’)예요. Note: Would you mind if I recorded the meeting?
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Would you mind if I recorded the meeting? My notes start as English and finish as cave drawings. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Mind if I ___?".

steps.when: 친구·가까운 동료에게 *짧고 가볍게*. Do you를 빼고 말해요. 끝을 올려요.
steps.extra: Mind if I record this?
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "Mind if I ___?" (~해도 돼요?). When to use it: 친구·가까운 동료에게 짧고 가볍게. Do you를 빼고 말해요. 끝을 올려요. Note: Mind if I record this?

(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).

A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Mind if I record this? My memory is excellent for song lyrics and terrible for actual instructions. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "Let me put it another way.".

steps.en: Let me put it another way.
steps.when: 말이 너무 직설적이었거나 잘못 전해졌을 때 *표현을 바꿔* 다시 말해요.
steps.extra: That sounded too blunt. Let me put it another way.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "Let me put it another way." (다르게 말해 볼게요.). When to use it: 말이 너무 직설적이었거나 잘못 전해졌을 때 표현을 바꿔 다시 말해요. Note: That sounded too blunt. Let me put it another way.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).

A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Let me put it another way. I was trying to be clear, not accidentally sound like a robot. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Same Ask, Three Ways · 5월 중순 토요일 오후, 그레이스 집 거실에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Same Ask, Three Ways · 5월 중순 토요일 오후, 그레이스 집 거실에서

lines.en: So, the big client meeting is next Thursday. How are you feeling?
lines.ko: 그러니까 큰 고객 회의가 다음 주 목요일이죠. 기분은 어때요?

3. Grace: "Hmm, that sounds a bit blunt. It’s an announcement, not a request. Try “Would you mind if I recorded the meeting?”" (음, 좀 직설적으로 들려요. 부탁이 아니라 통보예요. ‘회의를 녹화해도 괜찮을까요?’라고 해 봐요.)
4. Jiwoo: "Would you mind if I recorded the meeting? It helps with my notes." (회의를 녹화해도 괜찮을까요? 기록하는 데 도움이 돼서요.)

11. Grace: "Let’s try it. I’m the client. … Too complicated? Hmm." (해 봐요. 제가 고객이에요. … 너무 복잡하다고요? 음.)
12. Jiwoo: "Oh, that came out wrong. Let me put it another way. What I’m trying to say is, could we start with three key screens and add more later?" (아, 말이 잘못 나왔네요. 다르게 말씀드릴게요. 제 말은, 핵심 화면 세 개로 시작하고 나중에 더하면 어떨까 하는 거예요.)

14. Jiwoo: "Formal, but still me. That’s the goal." (격식 있게, 그래도 저답게. 그게 목표예요.)

head: Friend · Mind if I …
Teammate · Is it OK if I …
Client · Would you mind if I …
rows: share my screen for a sec?
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: Would you mind if I ___? / Mind if I ___? Table (Friend · Mind if I … → Teammate · Is it OK if I …):
- record this? → record this call?
- leave early? → leave a bit early today?
- share my screen? → share my screen for a sec?
- send it tomorrow? → send it tomorrow morning?
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Is it OK if I send it tomorrow morning? After 10 p.m., my brain files a formal complaint. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: 격식 단계(register) — 같은 부탁, 세 가지 말투

Hey, can I grab …? 친구 → Is it OK if I …? 동료 → Would you mind if I …? 고객 
격식이 올라갈수록 말이 *길어지고* 과거형·could·might처럼 *한 걸음 물러선* 꼴을 써요.
Would you mind if I … ? — 동사 꼴과 대답

Would you mind if I *recorded* …? 지금 일이지만 과거형을 쓰면 더 조심스러워요. if I *record*도 써요. 
허락: *No, not at all.* / *Go ahead.* 
거절: Actually, I’d rather you didn’t.
errors: Would you mind if I joining?
Would you mind if I joined?
Mind if I to sit here?
if I 뒤에 to 없이 동사.
Let me put it other way.
Let me put it another way.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 격식 단계(register) — 같은 부탁, 세 가지 말투: Hey, can I grab …? 친구 → Is it OK if I …? 동료 → Would you mind if I …? 고객 / 격식이 올라갈수록 말이 길어지고 과거형·could·might처럼 한 걸음 물러선 꼴을 써요.
- Would you mind if I … ? — 동사 꼴과 대답: Would you mind if I recorded …? 지금 일이지만 과거형을 쓰면 더 조심스러워요. if I record도 써요. / 허락: No, not at all. / Go ahead. / 거절: Actually, I’d rather you didn’t.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Would you mind if I joining? → Would you mind if I joined? (if I 뒤에는 동사(-ing ×).)
- Mind if I to sit here? → Mind if I sit here? (if I 뒤에 to 없이 동사.)
- Let me put it other way. → Let me put it another way. (‘다른 한 방법’ → another.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Would you mind if I joined? Extra words make it more polite. Sadly, extra words do not make me more punctual. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) record the meeting / client → Would you mind if I recorded the meeting?
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) record the meeting / client → Would you mind if I recorded the meeting? The items (the words the learner gets for each one): record the meeting / client | borrow your pen / friend | leave a bit early / client | open the window / friend.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: Let me put it another way.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Would you mind if I …?" (말투 바꾸기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Would you mind if I ___?" / "Mind if I ___?" / "Let me put it another way.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I was wondering whether it might be possible to move the meeting.
혹시 회의를 옮길 수 있을지 여쭤봐도 될까요?

steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 정중하게 (고객·윗사람): "I was wondering whether it might be possible to move the meeting." (혹시 회의를 옮길 수 있을지 여쭤봐도 될까요?, 정중); "Could I trouble you for the latest file?" (번거로우시겠지만 최신 파일 좀 받을 수 있을까요?, 정중)
- 가볍게 (동료·친구): "Any chance I could join the call late?" (혹시 통화에 좀 늦게 들어가도 될까요?, 보통); "Is it cool if I bring a friend?" (친구 데려가도 괜찮아?, 친근); "Hey, can I grab a chair?" (저기, 의자 하나 가져가도 돼?, 친근)
- 말 바로잡기: "That came out wrong." (말이 잘못 나왔네요., 보통); "What I’m trying to say is, we need more time." (제 말은, 시간이 더 필요하다는 거예요., 보통); "Let me rephrase that." (다시 말씀드릴게요., 정중); "I didn’t mean it like that." (그런 뜻으로 한 말이 아니에요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I was wondering whether it might be possible to move the meeting. I accidentally booked two meetings and only one face. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

steps.title: Grace’s Three Rooms
steps.text: Grace shared a trick from her years in the travel business. “Picture three rooms: a kitchen, an office, and a meeting room. Same request, different register.” In the kitchen, slang and colloquial phrases are fine. In the office, a casual but respectful tone works. In the meeting room, choose your phrasing carefully, because blunt words can sound rude to a new audience. “Formal doesn’t mean cold,” Grace said. “It just means appropriate for the context.” The next Thursday, Jiwoo opened the client meeting with, “Would you mind if I recorded this?” “Not at all,” the client said. When one sentence came out wrong, she said, “*Let me rephrase that*,” and tried again. That evening, she texted Grace: “Back to my kitchen voice. Thank you!”

steps.label: 장면 다시 듣기
steps.teach:
The app has just played the scene again in the characters' own voices:
1. Grace: "So, the big client meeting is next Thursday. How are you feeling?" (그러니까 큰 고객 회의가 다음 주 목요일이죠. 기분은 어때요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Nervous. I want to record it for my notes. I wrote, “I will record this meeting.”" (긴장돼요. 메모하려고 녹화하고 싶어요. ‘이 회의를 녹화하겠습니다.’라고 써 놨어요.)
3. Grace: "Hmm, that sounds a bit blunt. It’s an announcement, not a request. Try “Would you mind if I recorded the meeting?”" (음, 좀 직설적으로 들려요. 부탁이 아니라 통보예요. ‘회의를 녹화해도 괜찮을까요?’라고 해 봐요.)
4. Jiwoo: "Would you mind if I recorded the meeting? It helps with my notes." (회의를 녹화해도 괜찮을까요? 기록하는 데 도움이 돼서요.)
5. Grace: "Perfect. If they say, “No, not at all,” that’s a yes." (완벽해요. 상대가 ‘No, not at all.’(전혀 꺼리지 않아요)이라고 하면 허락이에요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Tricky! But that’s way too formal for my teammates." (헷갈리네요! 그런데 팀 동료들한테 하기엔 너무 격식 차린 말이에요.)
7. Grace: "Right. With teammates, just “Mind if I record this?”" (맞아요. 동료에게는 그냥 ‘녹화해도 돼요?’면 돼요.)
8. Jiwoo: "And with you, it’s “Hey, can I grab your charger?” My phone just died." (그럼 그레이스 씨한테는 ‘저기, 충전기 좀 써도 돼요?’죠. 제 휴대폰이 방금 꺼졌어요.)
9. Grace: "Go ahead, it’s by the lamp. See? You already switch registers." (써요, 스탠드 옆에 있어요. 봐요, 벌써 말투의 격식을 바꾸잖아요.)
10. Jiwoo: "True. The hard part is the client’s plan. I want to say, “Your plan is too complicated.”" (그렇네요. 어려운 건 고객 쪽 계획이에요. ‘계획이 너무 복잡해요.’라고 말하고 싶어요.)
11. Grace: "Let’s try it. I’m the client. … Too complicated? Hmm." (해 봐요. 제가 고객이에요. … 너무 복잡하다고요? 음.)
12. Jiwoo: "Oh, that came out wrong. Let me put it another way. What I’m trying to say is, could we start with three key screens and add more later?" (아, 말이 잘못 나왔네요. 다르게 말씀드릴게요. 제 말은, 핵심 화면 세 개로 시작하고 나중에 더하면 어떨까 하는 거예요.)
13. Grace: "So, you mean simple first, then more? Much better. Respectful phrasing, and a clear point." (그러니까 먼저 단순하게, 그다음에 더하자는 거죠? 훨씬 나아요. 표현은 정중하고 요점은 분명해요.)
14. Jiwoo: "Formal, but still me. That’s the goal." (격식 있게, 그래도 저답게. 그게 목표예요.)
Give one short reaction in a few words and say in one short sentence that now they will practise their lines. Ask no question about it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): saying the learner's lines one by one.

3. Grace (you): "Hmm, that sounds a bit blunt. It’s an announcement, not a request. Try “Would you mind if I recorded the meeting?”" (음, 좀 직설적으로 들려요. 부탁이 아니라 통보예요. ‘회의를 녹화해도 괜찮을까요?’라고 해 봐요.)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "Would you mind if I recorded the meeting? It helps with my notes." (회의를 녹화해도 괜찮을까요? 기록하는 데 도움이 돼서요.)
5. Grace (you): "Perfect. If they say, “No, not at all,” that’s a yes." (완벽해요. 상대가 ‘No, not at all.’(전혀 꺼리지 않아요)이라고 하면 허락이에요.)

10. Jiwoo (learner): "True. The hard part is the client’s plan. I want to say, “Your plan is too complicated.”" (그렇네요. 어려운 건 고객 쪽 계획이에요. ‘계획이 너무 복잡해요.’라고 말하고 싶어요.)
11. Grace (you): "Let’s try it. I’m the client. … Too complicated? Hmm." (해 봐요. 제가 고객이에요. … 너무 복잡하다고요? 음.)
12. Jiwoo (learner): "Oh, that came out wrong. Let me put it another way. What I’m trying to say is, could we start with three key screens and add more later?" (아, 말이 잘못 나왔네요. 다르게 말씀드릴게요. 제 말은, 핵심 화면 세 개로 시작하고 나중에 더하면 어떨까 하는 거예요.)
13. Grace (you): "So, you mean simple first, then more? Much better. Respectful phrasing, and a clear point." (그러니까 먼저 단순하게, 그다음에 더하자는 거죠? 훨씬 나아요. 표현은 정중하고 요점은 분명해요.)
14. Jiwoo (learner): "Formal, but still me. That’s the goal." (격식 있게, 그래도 저답게. 그게 목표예요.)

steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "I’m afraid I won’t be able to …" (격식 있게 말하기). Goal: 공식 메일처럼 정중하게 말하기. Today's scene: 5월 말 평일 저녁, 동네 카페 창가 자리. 지우가 노트북을 대니얼 쪽으로 돌려 보여 주고, 대니얼은 자기 노트북을 옆에 둔 채 몸을 기울여 화면을 가리키며 웃음. 탁자 위에 아이스커피 두 잔과 메모지. 글자·상표 없음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Daniel, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I’m afraid I won’t be able to ___.".

Expression 1 of 3: "I’m afraid I won’t be able to ___." (유감스럽지만 ~하기 어렵겠습니다.). When to use it: 못 한다는 말을 정중하게. I’m afraid는 ‘무서워요’가 아니라 ‘유감이지만’이에요. can’t보다 부드러워요. Note: I’m afraid I won’t be able to meet on Wednesday.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.

Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.

lines.ko: 네. 다음 주 수요일 검토 회의를 옮겨야 해요. 테스트 결과가 준비가 안 될 거라서요. 초안은 ‘죄송, 수요일 못 만나요.’예요.

lines.ko: 친구한테 보내는 문자라면 괜찮아요. 고객에게는 ‘예정대로 수요일에 뵙기는 어려울 것 같습니다.’라고 해 봐요.

lines.en: Always? Can you think of a counterexample?
lines.ko: 늘요? 반례를 하나 떠올려 볼래요?
