steps.title: Slide Forty · 8월 오후, 대학의 빈 강의실에서

lines.en: … and finally, slide forty. Now I’ll elaborate on the implications.
lines.ko: … 마지막으로 40번째 슬라이드입니다. 이제 그 함의를 자세히 설명하겠습니다.

lines.en: Can I stop you there? That was thirty-five minutes. Isn’t the limit twenty?
lines.ko: 잠깐 끊어도 돼요? 35분 지났어요. 제한 시간이 20분 아니에요?

lines.en: It is. But every slide feels essential.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 그런데 슬라이드가 하나같이 꼭 필요한 것 같아요.

lines.en: The committee has read your thesis. What’s it about, in one sentence?
lines.ko: 심사위원들은 논문을 읽었잖아요. 한 문장으로 하면 무엇에 관한 거예요?

lines.en: It’s a mixed-methods analysis of modal choice for short urban trips.
lines.ko: 도시 단거리 이동에서의 교통수단 선택을 여러 연구 방법을 섞어 분석한 거예요.

lines.en: {{In plain English}}?
lines.ko: 쉬운 말로 하면요?

lines.en: Ha, fair. {{Basically}}, I asked people how they choose to walk, bike, or take the bus.
lines.ko: 하, 그렇네요. 쉽게 말하면, 걸을지, 자전거를 탈지, 버스를 탈지 어떻게 고르는지 사람들에게 물었어요.

lines.en: That’s the gist! And what did you find?
lines.ko: 그게 요지예요! 그래서 뭘 알아냈어요?

lines.en: {{The short version is}} that people in my study chose bikes when the route felt safe, not just fast.
lines.ko: 짧게 말하면, 제 연구에선 사람들이 길이 빠를 때만이 아니라 안전하게 느껴질 때 자전거를 골랐어요.

lines.en: Perfect. Put that on slide one. And jargon like “modal choice”? Cut it, or explain it once.
lines.ko: 완벽해요. 그걸 첫 슬라이드에 넣어요. ‘modal choice’ 같은 전문 용어는 빼거나 한 번만 설명해요.

lines.en: But how do you know they won’t miss the details? What’s your evidence?
lines.ko: 그래도 심사위원들이 세부 내용을 아쉬워하면요? 근거가 뭐예요?

lines.en: You lost me at slide twelve. That’s my evidence. {{Long story short}}, twenty slides, one message.
lines.ko: 12번째 슬라이드에서 제가 놓쳤어요. 그게 제 근거예요. 길게 말할 것 없이, 슬라이드 스무 장에 메시지 하나요.

lines.en: Fair point. {{In a nutshell}}, they want to see that I know my own work. {{The bottom line is}} clarity.
lines.ko: 일리 있네요. 한마디로 제가 제 연구를 잘 아는지 보고 싶은 거죠. 결국 중요한 건 명료함이에요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Slide Forty · 8월 오후, 대학의 빈 강의실에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Daniel: "… and finally, slide forty. Now I’ll elaborate on the implications." (… 마지막으로 40번째 슬라이드입니다. 이제 그 함의를 자세히 설명하겠습니다.)
2. Jiwoo: "Can I stop you there? That was thirty-five minutes. Isn’t the limit twenty?" (잠깐 끊어도 돼요? 35분 지났어요. 제한 시간이 20분 아니에요?)
3. Daniel: "It is. But every slide feels essential." (맞아요. 그런데 슬라이드가 하나같이 꼭 필요한 것 같아요.)
4. Jiwoo: "The committee has read your thesis. What’s it about, in one sentence?" (심사위원들은 논문을 읽었잖아요. 한 문장으로 하면 무엇에 관한 거예요?)
5. Daniel: "It’s a mixed-methods analysis of modal choice for short urban trips." (도시 단거리 이동에서의 교통수단 선택을 여러 연구 방법을 섞어 분석한 거예요.)
6. Jiwoo: "In plain English?" (쉬운 말로 하면요?)
7. Daniel: "Ha, fair. Basically, I asked people how they choose to walk, bike, or take the bus." (하, 그렇네요. 쉽게 말하면, 걸을지, 자전거를 탈지, 버스를 탈지 어떻게 고르는지 사람들에게 물었어요.)
8. Jiwoo: "That’s the gist! And what did you find?" (그게 요지예요! 그래서 뭘 알아냈어요?)
9. Daniel: "The short version is that people in my study chose bikes when the route felt safe, not just fast." (짧게 말하면, 제 연구에선 사람들이 길이 빠를 때만이 아니라 안전하게 느껴질 때 자전거를 골랐어요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Perfect. Put that on slide one. And jargon like “modal choice”? Cut it, or explain it once." (완벽해요. 그걸 첫 슬라이드에 넣어요. ‘modal choice’ 같은 전문 용어는 빼거나 한 번만 설명해요.)
11. Daniel: "But how do you know they won’t miss the details? What’s your evidence?" (그래도 심사위원들이 세부 내용을 아쉬워하면요? 근거가 뭐예요?)
12. Jiwoo: "You lost me at slide twelve. That’s my evidence. Long story short, twenty slides, one message." (12번째 슬라이드에서 제가 놓쳤어요. 그게 제 근거예요. 길게 말할 것 없이, 슬라이드 스무 장에 메시지 하나요.)
13. Daniel: "Fair point. In a nutshell, they want to see that I know my own work. The bottom line is clarity." (일리 있네요. 한마디로 제가 제 연구를 잘 아는지 보고 싶은 거죠. 결국 중요한 건 명료함이에요.)
Give one short, natural reaction to the scene (a few words) and say in one short sentence that you will now read it together. Do not ask any question about what happened yet: the quiz comes later, after the role reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

items: The committee hasn’t read Daniel’s thesis.
Jiwoo wants the main finding to come first.
steps.teach:
Quiz about the scene, now that the learner has heard it and read it in both roles. First ask two short, easy questions about what happens in it (who, what, where or how often), one per turn, with the answers in the lines below. Any answer that shows they understood is right, in any words or in Korean: say so and go on. If it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Never turn an answer into a repeat drill here: if their English has a slip, just say the right sentence back once in your reaction and go on. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too.
Then the true/false check. The statements on the learner's screen, each with its answer and the scene line that shows it. The answers are for you only: never say an answer or a line number before the learner has answered:
1. Daniel talked for thirty-five minutes. → True (line 2)
2. The committee hasn’t read Daniel’s thesis. → False (line 4)
3. Jiwoo wants the main finding to come first. → True (line 10)
The scene they are about:
1. Daniel: "… and finally, slide forty. Now I’ll elaborate on the implications." (… 마지막으로 40번째 슬라이드입니다. 이제 그 함의를 자세히 설명하겠습니다.)
2. Jiwoo: "Can I stop you there? That was thirty-five minutes. Isn’t the limit twenty?" (잠깐 끊어도 돼요? 35분 지났어요. 제한 시간이 20분 아니에요?)
3. Daniel: "It is. But every slide feels essential." (맞아요. 그런데 슬라이드가 하나같이 꼭 필요한 것 같아요.)
4. Jiwoo: "The committee has read your thesis. What’s it about, in one sentence?" (심사위원들은 논문을 읽었잖아요. 한 문장으로 하면 무엇에 관한 거예요?)
5. Daniel: "It’s a mixed-methods analysis of modal choice for short urban trips." (도시 단거리 이동에서의 교통수단 선택을 여러 연구 방법을 섞어 분석한 거예요.)
6. Jiwoo: "In plain English?" (쉬운 말로 하면요?)
7. Daniel: "Ha, fair. Basically, I asked people how they choose to walk, bike, or take the bus." (하, 그렇네요. 쉽게 말하면, 걸을지, 자전거를 탈지, 버스를 탈지 어떻게 고르는지 사람들에게 물었어요.)
8. Jiwoo: "That’s the gist! And what did you find?" (그게 요지예요! 그래서 뭘 알아냈어요?)
9. Daniel: "The short version is that people in my study chose bikes when the route felt safe, not just fast." (짧게 말하면, 제 연구에선 사람들이 길이 빠를 때만이 아니라 안전하게 느껴질 때 자전거를 골랐어요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Perfect. Put that on slide one. And jargon like “modal choice”? Cut it, or explain it once." (완벽해요. 그걸 첫 슬라이드에 넣어요. ‘modal choice’ 같은 전문 용어는 빼거나 한 번만 설명해요.)
11. Daniel: "But how do you know they won’t miss the details? What’s your evidence?" (그래도 심사위원들이 세부 내용을 아쉬워하면요? 근거가 뭐예요?)
12. Jiwoo: "You lost me at slide twelve. That’s my evidence. Long story short, twenty slides, one message." (12번째 슬라이드에서 제가 놓쳤어요. 그게 제 근거예요. 길게 말할 것 없이, 슬라이드 스무 장에 메시지 하나요.)
13. Daniel: "Fair point. In a nutshell, they want to see that I know my own work. The bottom line is clarity." (일리 있네요. 한마디로 제가 제 연구를 잘 아는지 보고 싶은 거죠. 결국 중요한 건 명료함이에요.)
Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). A one-word answer (True, False, 맞아요) is enough; never ask for a full sentence. Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: In a nutshell, …
Basically, …
The short version is that …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: In a nutshell, ___. / The short version is ___. Table (In a nutshell, … → Basically, …):
- the talk is too long. → we need fewer slides.
- the plan works. → it saves time and money.
- the meeting went well. → the client liked our ideas.
- the trip was fun. → it rained, but we laughed.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): In a nutshell, the talk is too long. Basically, even I got lost on slide twelve. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: 요약 표지 = 문장 맨 앞 + 쉼표

*In a nutshell*, the talk is too long. 한마디로 발표가 너무 길어요. 
긴 설명 *뒤*에 정리할 때도, *처음*에 결론부터 말할 때도 써요. 
*Put simply*, *Basically*, *Long story short*, 모두 같은 자리예요.
The short version is (that) … · boil down to + 명사

*The short version is that* we need more time. 짧게 말하면 시간이 더 필요해요. (말할 때는 that을 자주 빼요) 
It *boils down to* safety. 결국 안전 문제예요. (to 뒤에 명사·-ing)
errors: In a nutshell, it’s too long.
It boils down to we need time.
to 뒤에는 명사·-ing. 문장을 쓰려면 *The bottom line is …*
To cut a long story shortly, …
To cut a long story short, …
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 요약 표지 = 문장 맨 앞 + 쉼표: In a nutshell, the talk is too long. 한마디로 발표가 너무 길어요. / 긴 설명 뒤에 정리할 때도, 처음에 결론부터 말할 때도 써요. / Put simply, Basically, Long story short, 모두 같은 자리예요.
- The short version is (that) … · boil down to + 명사: The short version is that we need more time. 짧게 말하면 시간이 더 필요해요. (말할 때는 that을 자주 빼요) / It boils down to safety. 결국 안전 문제예요. (to 뒤에 명사·-ing)
Common mistakes on screen:
- In nutshell, it’s too long. → In a nutshell, it’s too long. (굳어진 표현이라 a를 빼지 않아요.)
- It boils down to we need time. → It boils down to time. (to 뒤에는 명사·-ing. 문장을 쓰려면 The bottom line is …)
- To cut a long story shortly, … → To cut a long story short, … (굳어진 표현이라 short 그대로.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): In a nutshell, my schedule is too full. Basically, I need a second Monday. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: 요약 표지 = 문장 맨 앞 + 쉼표: In a nutshell, the talk is too long. 한마디로 발표가 너무 길어요. 긴 설명 뒤에 정리할 때도, 처음에 결론부터 말할 때도 써요. Put simply, Basically, Long story short, 모두 같은 자리예요.
The short version is (that) … · boil down to + 명사: The short version is that we need more time. 짧게 말하면 시간이 더 필요해요. (말할 때는 that을 자주 빼요) It boils down to safety. 결국 안전 문제예요. (to 뒤에 명사·-ing)
mistakes: In nutshell, it’s too long. → In a nutshell, it’s too long.
It boils down to we need time. → It boils down to time.
To cut a long story shortly, … → To cut a long story short, …

steps.note: 예) the rehearsal / too long → A: So, how was the rehearsal? B: In a nutshell, it was too long.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) the rehearsal / too long → A: So, how was the rehearsal? B: In a nutshell, it was too long. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): the rehearsal / too long | the new plan / cheaper and faster | the meeting / a big success | my weekend / quiet and lazy.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "In a nutshell, …" (짧게 줄이기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "In a nutshell, ___." / "Basically, ___." / "The short version is ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: To cut a long story short, ___.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 짧게 말하기: "Long story short, ___." (길게 말할 것 없이, ~예요., 친근); "To cut a long story short, ___." (긴 이야기를 줄이자면, ~예요., 보통); "Put simply, ___." (간단히 말해, ~예요., 보통); "In plain English, ___." (쉬운 말로 하면, ~예요., 친근)
- 핵심 짚기: "The bottom line is ___." (결국 중요한 건 ~예요., 보통); "It boils down to ___." (결국 ~의 문제예요., 보통); "The gist is ___." (요지는 ~예요., 보통)
- 정리하기: "Let me sum it up." (제가 정리해 볼게요., 정중); "That’s it in a nutshell." (한마디로 그거예요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): The bottom line is I should sleep earlier. Every night, I become a philosopher at midnight and a zombie at seven. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 발표·심사에 쓰는 말

a thesis *defense* 논문 심사(발표) · the *committee* 심사위원회 
*rehearse* a talk 발표를 미리 연습하다 · a *backup* slide 예비 슬라이드 · *Q&A* 질의응답 
대니얼의 논문 내용은 수업을 위해 지어낸 가상 연구예요.
언제 어떤 요약 표지를 쓸까

Long story short는 친구에게 하는 이야기, The bottom line is는 일·결정에서 ‘결국’. 
업무 보고·이메일에서는 *In short*, … *To summarize*, …가 더 격식 있어요. 
Basically를 문장마다 쓰면 말버릇처럼 들려요.

낱말 상자: nutshell · version · line · boils
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 발표·심사에 쓰는 말: a thesis defense 논문 심사(발표) · the committee 심사위원회 / rehearse a talk 발표를 미리 연습하다 · a backup slide 예비 슬라이드 · Q&A 질의응답 / 대니얼의 논문 내용은 수업을 위해 지어낸 가상 연구예요.
- 언제 어떤 요약 표지를 쓸까: Long story short는 친구에게 하는 이야기, The bottom line is는 일·결정에서 ‘결국’. / 업무 보고·이메일에서는 In short, … To summarize, …가 더 격식 있어요. / Basically를 문장마다 쓰면 말버릇처럼 들려요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: How was the rehearsal? B: In a ___, it was too long. / A: What’s the short ___? B: The bottom ___ is, I need fewer slides. It ___ down to one message. / 낱말 상자: nutshell · version · line · boils
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

items.ko: 맨 아래, 바닥 · the bottom line 결국 중요한 것, 결론
전문 용어(그 분야 사람만 쉽게 아는 말)

steps.teach:
Picture words on screen. New: summarize (요약하다), concise (간결한(짧고 군더더기 없는)), brief (짧은, 간단한), essence (본질, 가장 중요한 부분), gist (요지, 대강의 내용), core ((사물의) 속, 중심; 핵심), simplify (단순하게 하다, 쉽게 만들다), condense ((글·말을) 압축하다, 줄이다), clarity (명료함, 분명함), bottom (맨 아래, 바닥 · the bottom line 결국 중요한 것, 결론), elaborate ((on) 자세히 설명하다), jargon (전문 용어(그 분야 사람만 쉽게 아는 말)).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I wanted to be concise in a text message. Three minutes later, I had written a tiny autobiography. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: Can you say it in one line?
a rehearsal in an empty room
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: summary (요약) — "Add a one-line summary."; line ((글의) 한 줄) — "Can you say it in one line?"; key (핵심적인, 가장 중요한) — "What’s the key finding?"; point (요점, 핵심) — "Get to the point."; thesis ((학위) 논문) — "Daniel is finishing his thesis."; committee (위원회, 심사위원회) — "The committee has read it."; rehearsal (예행연습, 리허설) — "a rehearsal in an empty room"; slide ((발표용) 슬라이드) — "Forty slides became twenty.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Get to the point is excellent advice for me. My mouth usually takes the scenic route first. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What do you do, in a nutshell?
Tell me about your last weekend. Now, what’s the short version?
What’s a show or book you like? What’s it about, basically?
The bottom line is ___. / It boils down to ___.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What do you do, in a nutshell?" (hint on screen: In a nutshell, I ___.)
- "Tell me about your last weekend. Now, what’s the short version?" (hint on screen: The short version is ___.)
- "What’s a show or book you like? What’s it about, basically?" (hint on screen: Basically, it’s about ___.)
- "What makes a good presentation?" (hint on screen: The bottom line is ___. / It boils down to ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): In a nutshell, I teach English and help people organize ideas. Then I spend ten minutes looking for my own marker. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Twenty Slides, One Message
steps.text: That evening, Daniel rewrote his talk. He gave each slide one key point and cut anything he couldn’t say in plain words. Forty slides became twenty. Jiwoo helped him simplify the charts, and he added a one-line summary to each section. “I thought being brief meant leaving things out,” he said. “Now I see it’s about clarity.” He kept a few backup slides *in case* the committee asked him to elaborate. The new talk was concise, and it took nineteen minutes. Jiwoo summarized the plan in one sentence: “*In short*, give them the essence and save the details for the Q&A.” Then Daniel wrote his first sentence on a card, the core of years of work condensed into one line. His defense was set for the end of August.
steps.gloss: rewrite 다시 쓰다 · leave out 빼다 · backup 예비의 · in case ~할 경우에 대비해 · in short 요컨대 · Q&A 질의응답 · be set for (날짜가) ~로 정해지다
questions: How many slides did Daniel’s new talk have?
How long did the new talk take?

Jiwoo summarized the plan in one sentence: “In short, give them the essence and save the details for the Q&A.” Then Daniel wrote his first sentence on a card, the core of years of work condensed into one line. His defense was set for the end of August." Words: rewrite 다시 쓰다 · leave out 빼다 · backup 예비의 · in case ~할 경우에 대비해 · in short 요컨대 · Q&A 질의응답 · be set for (날짜가) ~로 정해지다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "How many slides did Daniel’s new talk have?" / "How long did the new talk take?". items: ‘In a nutshell, ___.’로 긴 설명을 한 문장으로 줄일 수 있어요.
‘Basically, ___.’로 세부를 빼고 핵심만 말할 수 있어요.

steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘In a nutshell, ___.’로 긴 설명을 한 문장으로 줄일 수 있어요.
- ‘Basically, ___.’로 세부를 빼고 핵심만 말할 수 있어요.

First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that next time we will practise saying today's scene by heart, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 짧게 줄이기

steps.scene_desc: 8월 오후, 대학의 빈 강의실. 대니얼이 강단에서 리모컨을 들고 슬라이드(글자 없이 그래프 모양만)를 넘기며 발표 연습을 하고, 맨 앞줄에 앉은 지우가 손목시계를 가리키며 웃음. 책상 위에 지우의 노트와 물병. 칠판과 화면에 글자 없음
steps.label: 대화 외우기
steps.teach:
This is the start of Part 3 of "In a nutshell, …" (짧게 줄이기); it may be a different day. Today the learner practises saying the scene from this lesson by heart. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of one or two exchanges. React to what they say.
2) Then, in a new turn, say in one or two short sentences that today you will practise the scene ("Slide Forty · 8월 오후, 대학의 빈 강의실에서") until they can say it by heart: first listen once, then say their lines with fewer and fewer words on the screen. Do not ask if they are ready more than once.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays the scene once more — tell them to just listen.

steps.teach:
Memory practice 2: now the learner's lines show only the first letter of each word. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Daniel exactly as written. The full lines, for you only:
1. Daniel (you): "… and finally, slide forty. Now I’ll elaborate on the implications." (… 마지막으로 40번째 슬라이드입니다. 이제 그 함의를 자세히 설명하겠습니다.)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "Can I stop you there? That was thirty-five minutes. Isn’t the limit twenty?" (잠깐 끊어도 돼요? 35분 지났어요. 제한 시간이 20분 아니에요?)
3. Daniel (you): "It is. But every slide feels essential." (맞아요. 그런데 슬라이드가 하나같이 꼭 필요한 것 같아요.)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "The committee has read your thesis. What’s it about, in one sentence?" (심사위원들은 논문을 읽었잖아요. 한 문장으로 하면 무엇에 관한 거예요?)
5. Daniel (you): "It’s a mixed-methods analysis of modal choice for short urban trips." (도시 단거리 이동에서의 교통수단 선택을 여러 연구 방법을 섞어 분석한 거예요.)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "In plain English?" (쉬운 말로 하면요?)
7. Daniel (you): "Ha, fair. Basically, I asked people how they choose to walk, bike, or take the bus." (하, 그렇네요. 쉽게 말하면, 걸을지, 자전거를 탈지, 버스를 탈지 어떻게 고르는지 사람들에게 물었어요.)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "That’s the gist! And what did you find?" (그게 요지예요! 그래서 뭘 알아냈어요?)
9. Daniel (you): "The short version is that people in my study chose bikes when the route felt safe, not just fast." (짧게 말하면, 제 연구에선 사람들이 길이 빠를 때만이 아니라 안전하게 느껴질 때 자전거를 골랐어요.)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "Perfect. Put that on slide one. And jargon like “modal choice”? Cut it, or explain it once." (완벽해요. 그걸 첫 슬라이드에 넣어요. ‘modal choice’ 같은 전문 용어는 빼거나 한 번만 설명해요.)
11. Daniel (you): "But how do you know they won’t miss the details? What’s your evidence?" (그래도 심사위원들이 세부 내용을 아쉬워하면요? 근거가 뭐예요?)
12. Jiwoo (learner): "You lost me at slide twelve. That’s my evidence. Long story short, twenty slides, one message." (12번째 슬라이드에서 제가 놓쳤어요. 그게 제 근거예요. 길게 말할 것 없이, 슬라이드 스무 장에 메시지 하나요.)
13. Daniel (you): "Fair point. In a nutshell, they want to see that I know my own work. The bottom line is clarity." (일리 있네요. 한마디로 제가 제 연구를 잘 아는지 보고 싶은 거죠. 결국 중요한 건 명료함이에요.)
In one short sentence, say what is on the screen now and invite them to start. Do not say the learner's line before they try: remembering it is the point of this part, so this is the one exception to saying a sentence first. If they get stuck, give only the next word or two as a hint. If a word was missing or wrong, say the whole line once inside double quotes and let them try once more, then go on. Go in order, one line at a time. After the last line, react in a word or two, with no comment on how they sounded.
What comes next (after you call next_step): saying their lines from the Korean meaning only.

steps.teach: Wrap up like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how it felt to say the scene by heart, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today (for example a line they remembered well), say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 이야기에 긴장감
steps.goal: 반전 있는 이야기를 생생하게 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 8월 말 늦은 오후, 회사 건물 옥상 정원. 나무 벤치에 앉은 마야가 아이스커피를 들고 몸을 앞으로 기울여 듣고, 지우가 두 손을 활짝 펼치며 이야기함(화면이 ‘탁’ 꺼지는 손짓). 화분과 멀리 보이는 도시 빌딩. 글자·간판 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "So there I was, …" (이야기에 긴장감). Goal: 반전 있는 이야기를 생생하게 말하기. lines.en: I heard something happened at the client presentation last week. Spill!
lines.ko: 지난주 고객 발표 때 무슨 일 있었다면서요. 얘기해 봐요!

lines.en: Oh, the projector turned off. I drew on the whiteboard instead. It was fine.
lines.ko: 아, 프로젝터가 꺼졌어요. 대신 화이트보드에 그렸어요. 괜찮았어요.

7. Maya: "No! What did you do?" (안 돼! 어떻게 했어요?)
8. Jiwoo: "I check my laptop. To make matters worse, the battery’s at two percent. I kid you not." (노트북을 확인해요. 설상가상으로 배터리가 2%예요. 진짜라니까요.)
9. Maya: "Ha! Now pause. Make me wait." (하! 이제 잠깐 멈춰요. 저를 기다리게 해요.)
10. Jiwoo: "… And that’s when I see the whiteboard. So I grab a marker and start drawing the new screen." (… 바로 그때 화이트보드가 눈에 들어와요. 그래서 마커를 잡고 새 화면을 그리기 시작해요.)
11. Maya: "Love it. And how did the client react?" (좋아요. 그래서 고객은 어떻게 반응했어요?)
12. Jiwoo: "They loved the sketch. And here’s the kicker. They took a photo of it to show their own team." (스케치를 아주 좋아했어요. 그리고 결정적인 건요, 자기네 팀에 보여 주려고 그걸 사진으로 찍어 갔어요.)
13. Maya: "That’s your punchline! Now tell it once more, and say it like you mean it." (그게 이야기의 결정타네요! 이제 한 번 더 해 봐요. 진심을 담아서요.)
Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). A one-word answer (True, False, 맞아요) is enough; never ask for a full sentence. Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: So there I was, …
Out of nowhere, …
And that’s when …
rows: a neighbor offers me an umbrella.
I find cash in my coat.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: So there I was, ___. / And that’s when ___. Table (So there I was, … → Out of nowhere, …):
- on slide three. → the screen goes black.
- at the bus stop. → it starts to pour.
- in the elevator. → the lights go out.
- at the checkout. → my card doesn’t work.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): So there I was, on slide three, feeling strangely confident. And that's when the screen goes black, but I keep talking. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
지난 일을 *현재형*으로 말하면 눈앞의 일처럼 생생해요. 
So I’m standing there, and the screen *goes* black. 
친구에게 하는 이야기에서 써요. 보고·이메일은 과거형.

장면 → 문제 → 멈춤 → 전환점(And that’s when) 
*Just as I was about to* start, the screen went black. 막 시작하려던 참에 화면이 꺼졌어요. (be about to + 동사원형)
errors: Just as I was about to starting, …
Just as I was about to start, …
Out of nowhere, the screen go black.
Out of nowhere, the screen goes black.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 이야기 현재형 = 지금 보는 것처럼: 지난 일을 현재형으로 말하면 눈앞의 일처럼 생생해요. / So I’m standing there, and the screen goes black. / 친구에게 하는 이야기에서 써요. 보고·이메일은 과거형.
- 긴장감을 쌓는 순서: 장면 → 문제 → 멈춤 → 전환점(And that’s when) / Just as I was about to start, the screen went black. 막 시작하려던 참에 화면이 꺼졌어요. (be about to + 동사원형)
Common mistakes on screen:
- Little did I knew, … → Little did I know, … (did 뒤에는 동사원형.)
- Just as I was about to starting, … → Just as I was about to start, … (be about to 뒤에는 동사원형.)
- Out of nowhere, the screen go black. → Out of nowhere, the screen goes black. (이야기 현재형에서도 단수 주어는 -s.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): So I'm standing there, trying to look calm, and my phone starts ringing from the fridge. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: 이야기 현재형 = 지금 보는 것처럼: 지난 일을 현재형으로 말하면 눈앞의 일처럼 생생해요. So I’m standing there, and the screen goes black. 친구에게 하는 이야기에서 써요. 보고·이메일은 과거형.
긴장감을 쌓는 순서: 장면 → 문제 → 멈춤 → 전환점(And that’s when) Just as I was about to start, the screen went black. 막 시작하려던 참에 화면이 꺼졌어요. (be about to + 동사원형)
mistakes: Little did I knew, … → Little did I know, …
Just as I was about to starting, … → Just as I was about to start, …
Out of nowhere, the screen go black. → Out of nowhere, the screen goes black.

steps.note: 예) the screen goes black / I grab a marker → Out of nowhere, the screen goes black. And that’s when I grab a marker.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) the screen goes black / I grab a marker → Out of nowhere, the screen goes black. And that’s when I grab a marker. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): the screen goes black / I grab a marker | my umbrella breaks / a stranger shares one | the lights go out / my phone rings | I miss my stop / I see an old friend.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "So there I was, …" (이야기에 긴장감); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "So there I was, ___." / "Out of nowhere, ___." / "And that’s when ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: You’ll never guess what happened next.
다음에 무슨 일이 있었는지 상상도 못 할 거예요.
Just as I was about to ___, ___.
직접 봤어야 했는데(말로는 다 못 전해요).
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 긴장감 쌓기: "You’ll never guess what happened next." (다음에 무슨 일이 있었는지 상상도 못 할 거예요., 보통); "So I’m standing there, and ___." (그렇게 서 있는데, ~해요., 친근); "Little did I know, ___." (그때는 몰랐죠, ~라는 걸., 보통); "Just as I was about to ___, ___." (막 ~하려던 참에 ~했어요., 보통)
- 문제 키우기·반전: "To make matters worse, ___." (설상가상으로 ~했어요., 보통); "And here’s the kicker." (그리고 결정적인 건요., 친근); "I kid you not." (진짜라니까요, 농담 아니에요., 친근)
- 마무리하기: "Long story short, ___." (길게 말할 것 없이, ~했어요., 친근); "You had to be there." (직접 봤어야 했는데(말로는 다 못 전해요)., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Little did I know, my quick nap at six was actually my bedtime. I woke up feeling extremely responsible. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 이야기에 긴장감을 넣는 요령

결말을 먼저 말하지 않기 · 전환점 앞에서 잠깐 멈추기 · 생생한 세부 하나 (the battery’s at two percent) 
재미를 위해 조금 과장(exaggerate)해도 되지만, 일어난 일 자체를 바꾸지는 않아요. 
업무 보고에서는 결론부터 짧게 말해요.
이야기 구조를 말하는 낱말

*hook* 처음에 관심을 끄는 말 → *buildup* 긴장을 쌓는 부분 → *climax* 절정 → *twist* 반전 
*punchline* 웃음이 터지는 마지막 한마디 · *kicker* 끝에 나오는 뜻밖의 한 방

A: You’ll never ___ what happened next.   B: What? 
A: So there I ___, on stage. Out of ___, the lights go out. And that’s ___ I hear someone laugh.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 이야기에 긴장감을 넣는 요령: 결말을 먼저 말하지 않기 · 전환점 앞에서 잠깐 멈추기 · 생생한 세부 하나 (the battery’s at two percent) / 재미를 위해 조금 과장(exaggerate)해도 되지만, 일어난 일 자체를 바꾸지는 않아요. / 업무 보고에서는 결론부터 짧게 말해요.
- 이야기 구조를 말하는 낱말: hook 처음에 관심을 끄는 말 → buildup 긴장을 쌓는 부분 → climax 절정 → twist 반전 / punchline 웃음이 터지는 마지막 한마디 · kicker 끝에 나오는 뜻밖의 한 방
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: You’ll never ___ what happened next. B: What? / A: So there I ___, on stage. Out of ___, the lights go out. And that’s ___ I hear someone laugh. / 낱말 상자: guess · was · nowhere · when
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

items.ko: (농담·이야기의) 웃음이 터지는 마지막 한마디(= punch line)

steps.teach:
Picture words on screen. New: suspense ((다음이 궁금해) 조마조마함, 긴장감), twist ((이야기의) 반전), climax (절정, 가장 긴장되는 순간), punchline ((농담·이야기의) 웃음이 터지는 마지막 한마디(= punch line)), anecdote ((짧고 재미있는 실제) 일화), pause ((말을) 잠깐 멈춤; 잠깐 멈추다), vivid (생생한), buildup ((절정까지) 긴장을 쌓아 가는 부분), foreshadow ((앞으로 일어날 일을) 미리 암시하다), hook (갈고리; (이야기의) 관심을 끄는 시작), cliff (절벽), exaggerate (과장하다).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): The buildup was dramatic: dry soil, falling leaves, my worried face. The climax was realizing it was a plastic plant. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: 끝에 나오는 뜻밖의 한 방, 반전
Don’t reveal the ending too early.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: narrative (이야기, (이야기의) 흐름) — "Keep the narrative short."; kicker (끝에 나오는 뜻밖의 한 방, 반전) — "And here’s the kicker."; tension ((이야기의) 긴장감 (앞에서는 ‘(사람 사이의) 불편한 긴장’)) — "Build the tension slowly."; build ((점점) 쌓다, 키우다) — "Build some suspense."; reveal ((숨긴 것을) 드러내다; (이야기에서) 사실이 드러나는 순간) — "Don’t reveal the ending too early."; detail (세부 (내용)) — "one vivid detail"; pacing ((이야기의) 속도 조절, 전개 속도) — "The pacing was quick."; drama (극적인 일, 소동) — "I didn’t add any drama.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): The pacing was quick. I left home feeling organized, then ran back inside three times for my keys, wallet, and lunch. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Tell me about a time something went wrong. Where were you?
So there I was, ___. Out of nowhere, ___.
Long story short, ___. / And here’s the kicker. ___.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Tell me about a time something went wrong. Where were you?" (hint on screen: So there I was, ___. Out of nowhere, ___.)
- "Did anything make it worse?" (hint on screen: To make matters worse, ___.)
- "What was the turning point?" (hint on screen: And that’s when ___.)
- "How did it end?" (hint on screen: Long story short, ___. / And here’s the kicker. ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): So there I was, carrying groceries like a hero. To make matters worse, one bag ripped, and that's when an onion escaped downhill. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: Tell me about a time something went wrong. Where were you?
Did anything make it worse?
What was the turning point?
How did it end?

steps.title: The Whiteboard Story
steps.text: At the next team lunch, Maya asked Jiwoo to tell the projector story again. This time, Jiwoo started with a hook. “You’ll never guess what happened at our last client meeting.” She kept her narrative short and the pacing quick. She added one vivid detail, the two-percent battery, and paused right before the climax. Everyone leaned in. She even mentioned that the projector had flickered that morning, which foreshadowed everything. When she got to the kicker, the whole table laughed. “Did that really happen?” a teammate asked. “*I kid you not*,” Jiwoo said. Later, Maya told her, “You didn’t exaggerate or add drama. You just built the tension and saved the twist for the end.” That dark screen had felt like the edge of a cliff. Now it was her favorite story.
steps.gloss: hook 관심을 끄는 시작 · narrative 이야기 · pacing 전개 속도 · lean in 몸을 앞으로 기울이다 · flicker 깜빡거리다 · foreshadow 미리 암시하다 · the edge of a cliff 절벽 끝
questions: What vivid detail did Jiwoo add?
What did the projector do that morning?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "The Whiteboard Story". Text: "At the next team lunch, Maya asked Jiwoo to tell the projector story again. This time, Jiwoo started with a hook. “You’ll never guess what happened at our last client meeting.” She kept her narrative short and the pacing quick. She added one vivid detail, the two-percent battery, and paused right before the climax. Everyone leaned in. She even mentioned that the projector had flickered that morning, which foreshadowed everything. When she got to the kicker, the whole table laughed. “Did that really happen?” a teammate asked. “I kid you not,” Jiwoo said. Later, Maya told her, “You didn’t exaggerate or add drama. You just built the tension and saved the twist for the end.” That dark screen had felt like the edge of a cliff. Now it was her favorite story." Words: hook 관심을 끄는 시작 · narrative 이야기 · pacing 전개 속도 · lean in 몸을 앞으로 기울이다 · flicker 깜빡거리다 · foreshadow 미리 암시하다 · the edge of a cliff 절벽 끝.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What vivid detail did Jiwoo add?" / "What did the projector do that morning?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘So there I was, ___.’로 이야기의 장면을 세울 수 있어요.
‘Out of nowhere, ___.’로 갑자기 일어난 일을 생생하게 말할 수 있어요.
‘And that’s when ___.’로 이야기의 전환점을 꺼낼 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘So there I was, ___.’로 이야기의 장면을 세울 수 있어요.
- ‘Out of nowhere, ___.’로 갑자기 일어난 일을 생생하게 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘And that’s when ___.’로 이야기의 전환점을 꺼낼 수 있어요.
First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that next time we will practise saying today's scene by heart, and say a warm goodbye. steps.title: 이야기에 긴장감

steps.label: 대화 외우기
steps.teach:
This is the start of Part 3 of "So there I was, …" (이야기에 긴장감); it may be a different day. Today the learner practises saying the scene from this lesson by heart. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of one or two exchanges. React to what they say.
2) Then, in a new turn, say in one or two short sentences that today you will practise the scene ("The Projector Story · 8월 말 오후, 회사 옥상에서") until they can say it by heart: first listen once, then say their lines with fewer and fewer words on the screen. Do not ask if they are ready more than once.

What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays the scene once more — tell them to just listen.

steps.teach:
Memory practice 2: now the learner's lines show only the first letter of each word. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Maya exactly as written. The full lines, for you only:
1. Maya (you): "I heard something happened at the client presentation last week. Spill!" (지난주 고객 발표 때 무슨 일 있었다면서요. 얘기해 봐요!)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "Oh, the projector turned off. I drew on the whiteboard instead. It was fine." (아, 프로젝터가 꺼졌어요. 대신 화이트보드에 그렸어요. 괜찮았어요.)
3. Maya (you): "That’s it? That’s a great anecdote, and you gave away the ending! Tell it again. Build some suspense." (그게 다예요? 좋은 일화인데 결말을 먼저 말해 버렸잖아요! 다시 해 봐요. 긴장감을 좀 쌓아서요.)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "OK … So there I was, on slide three, in front of eight people from the client’s team." (좋아요 … 그렇게 저는 세 번째 슬라이드에서 고객사 팀 여덟 명 앞에 서 있었어요.)
5. Maya (you): "Good. Now try the present tense. It feels like it’s happening right now." (좋아요. 이제 현재형으로 해 봐요. 지금 일어나는 일처럼 느껴지거든요.)

7. Maya (you): "No! What did you do?" (안 돼! 어떻게 했어요?)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "I check my laptop. To make matters worse, the battery’s at two percent. I kid you not." (노트북을 확인해요. 설상가상으로 배터리가 2%예요. 진짜라니까요.)
9. Maya (you): "Ha! Now pause. Make me wait." (하! 이제 잠깐 멈춰요. 저를 기다리게 해요.)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "… And that’s when I see the whiteboard. So I grab a marker and start drawing the new screen." (… 바로 그때 화이트보드가 눈에 들어와요. 그래서 마커를 잡고 새 화면을 그리기 시작해요.)
11. Maya (you): "Love it. And how did the client react?" (좋아요. 그래서 고객은 어떻게 반응했어요?)
12. Jiwoo (learner): "They loved the sketch. And here’s the kicker. They took a photo of it to show their own team." (스케치를 아주 좋아했어요. 그리고 결정적인 건요, 자기네 팀에 보여 주려고 그걸 사진으로 찍어 갔어요.)
13. Maya (you): "That’s your punchline! Now tell it once more, and say it like you mean it." (그게 이야기의 결정타네요! 이제 한 번 더 해 봐요. 진심을 담아서요.)
In one short sentence, say what is on the screen now and invite them to start. Do not say the learner's line before they try: remembering it is the point of this part, so this is the one exception to saying a sentence first. If they get stuck, give only the next word or two as a hint. If a word was missing or wrong, say the whole line once inside double quotes and let them try once more, then go on. Go in order, one line at a time. After the last line, react in a word or two, with no comment on how they sounded.
What comes next (after you call next_step): saying their lines from the Korean meaning only.

steps.label: 마무리
steps.teach: Wrap up like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how it felt to say the scene by heart, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today (for example a line they remembered well), say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 스포일러 없이
steps.goal: 결말을 숨기며 영화·책을 소개하기
steps.scene_desc: 9월 금요일 저녁, 클로이 집 거실. 담요를 두르고 소파에 앉은 클로이가 손으로 입에 지퍼를 채우는 시늉을 하고, 옆의 지우가 웃으며 두 손으로 귀를 막고 있음. 꺼진 텔레비전(화면 글자 없이), 탁자 위에 팝콘 그릇과 찻잔 두 개. 글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Without giving too much away, …" (스포일러 없이). Goal: 결말을 숨기며 영화·책을 소개하기. Today's scene: 9월 금요일 저녁, 클로이 집 거실. 담요를 두르고 소파에 앉은 클로이가 손으로 입에 지퍼를 채우는 시늉을 하고, 옆의 지우가 웃으며 두 손으로 귀를 막고 있음. 꺼진 텔레비전, 탁자 위에 팝콘 그릇과 찻잔 두 개. 글자 없음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Chloe, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Without giving too much away, ___.".

steps.when: 작품을 소개하되 *중요한 내용은 숨길 때* 써요. give away = (결말·비밀을) 누설하다.
steps.extra: Without giving too much away, episode nine changes everything.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Without giving too much away, ___." (너무 많이 말하지 않고 말하면, ~예요.). When to use it: 작품을 소개하되 중요한 내용은 숨길 때 써요. give away = (결말·비밀을) 누설하다. Note: Without giving too much away, episode nine changes everything.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Without giving too much away, this book kept me up all night. Not from suspense; I spilled tea on the last chapter. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Let’s just say ___.".

steps.when: 자세히 말하지 않고 *힌트만* 줄 때. 웃으며 말하면 ‘더는 말 못 해요’라는 느낌이에요.
steps.extra: Let’s just say you won’t trust anyone after episode six.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "Let’s just say ___." (~라고만 해 둘게요.). When to use it: 자세히 말하지 않고 힌트만 줄 때. 웃으며 말하면 ‘더는 말 못 해요’라는 느낌이에요. Note: Let’s just say you won’t trust anyone after episode six.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Let’s just say my cooking is very confident. The smoke alarm always hears about dinner first. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "You’ll have to see for yourself.".

head: It’s a …
Without giving too much away, …
Let’s just say …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: Without giving too much away, ___. / Let’s just say ___. Table (It’s a … → Without giving too much away, …):
- mystery. → the letters matter.
- comedy. → a family trip goes wrong.
- thriller. → someone is lying.
- family drama. → there’s a big secret.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Without giving too much away, a family trip goes wrong. We went out for milk and came home with a lamp. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: give away · spoil = 결말을 말해 버리다

Don’t *give away* the ending! 결말 말하지 마요! 
*Without giving* too much *away*, … without 뒤에는 *-ing*. too much는 give와 away 사이에 와요. 
I won’t *spoil* it *for* you. 스포일러 안 할게요.

*Let’s just say* it’s not a happy ending. 해피엔딩은 아니라고만 해 둘게요. 
뒤에 완전한 문장. *just*는 짧고 가볍게, 끝은 내려 말해요. 
You’ll have to see *for yourself*. 직접 봐야 알아요.
errors: I won’t spoil it for you.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- give away · spoil = 결말을 말해 버리다: Don’t give away the ending! 결말 말하지 마요! / Without giving too much away, … without 뒤에는 -ing. too much는 give와 away 사이에 와요. / I won’t spoil it for you. 스포일러 안 할게요.
- Let’s just say + 문장: Let’s just say it’s not a happy ending. 해피엔딩은 아니라고만 해 둘게요. / 뒤에 완전한 문장. just는 짧고 가볍게, 끝은 내려 말해요. / You’ll have to see for yourself. 직접 봐야 알아요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Without give too much away, … → Without giving too much away, … (without 뒤에는 -ing.)
- I won’t spoil you it. → I won’t spoil it for you. (spoil + 작품 + for + 사람.)
- Let’s just saying it’s sad. → Let’s just say it’s sad. (Let’s 뒤에는 동사원형.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I won’t spoil it for you. Let’s just say my lunch looked better before the microwave got involved. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: give away · spoil = 결말을 말해 버리다: Don’t give away the ending! 결말 말하지 마요! Without giving too much away, … without 뒤에는 -ing. too much는 give와 away 사이에 와요. I won’t spoil it for you. 스포일러 안 할게요.
Let’s just say + 문장: Let’s just say it’s not a happy ending. 해피엔딩은 아니라고만 해 둘게요. 뒤에 완전한 문장. just는 짧고 가볍게, 끝은 내려 말해요. You’ll have to see for yourself. 직접 봐야 알아요.
mistakes: Without give too much away, … → Without giving too much away, …
I won’t spoil you it. → I won’t spoil it for you.
Let’s just saying it’s sad. → Let’s just say it’s sad.

steps.note: 예) the ending / it’s not happy → A: How does it end? B: Without giving too much away, let’s just say it’s not happy.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) the ending / it’s not happy → A: How does it end? B: Without giving too much away, let’s just say it’s not happy. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): the ending / it’s not happy | the main character / she has a secret | episode nine / it changes everything | the last scene / bring tissues.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: You’ll have to see for yourself.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Without giving too much away, …" (스포일러 없이); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Without giving too much away, ___." / "Let’s just say ___." / "You’ll have to see for yourself.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I won’t spoil it for you.
I don’t want to say more.
The first half is a slow burn.

아무것도 모르고 보는 게 제일 좋아요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 스포일러 피하기: "I won’t spoil it for you." (스포일러 안 할게요., 보통); "I don’t want to say more." (더는 말하고 싶지 않아요., 보통); "Watch it, then let’s talk." (다 보고 나서 얘기해요., 친근)
- 분위기만 알려 주기: "The first half is a slow burn." (앞부분은 천천히 달아올라요., 보통); "It keeps you guessing." (계속 추리하게 만들어요., 보통); "It’s not what you expect." (예상과 달라요., 보통); "It’ll stay with you." (오래 마음에 남을 거예요., 보통)

Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): It’s best to go in blind. I watched one trailer last week and somehow learned the plot, the twist, and the dog’s name. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 작품을 소개하는 낱말: premise 기본 설정 · synopsis 줄거리 요약 · trailer 예고편 / arc (인물이) 변해 가는 흐름 · finale (시리즈의) 마지막 회 / cliffhanger 다음이 궁금한 채로 끝나는 장면 / 이 과의 드라마는 수업을 위해 지어낸 이야기예요.

Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.

Word list on screen: plot (줄거리) — "The plot is simple at first."; reveal ((숨긴 것을) 드러내다; (이야기에서) 사실이 드러나는 순간) — "Each reveal surprised her."; ending (결말) — "The ending divided people."; tone ((작품의) 분위기 (앞에서는 ‘말투, 어조’)) — "The tone is quiet but sharp."; pacing ((이야기의) 속도 조절, 전개 속도) — "The pacing picks up later."; subtle (미묘한, 은근한) — "a subtle hint in episode two"; ambiguous (애매한, 여러 뜻으로 읽히는) — "The last scene is ambiguous."; review (리뷰, 평) — "The review said too much.".

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What’s a show, movie, or book you’d recommend?" (hint on screen: It’s a ___. Without giving too much away, ___.)
- "What’s the premise?" (hint on screen: It’s about ___. Let’s just say ___.)
- "Do you read reviews before you watch something?" (hint on screen: Yes, but ___. / No. It’s best to go in blind.)
- "Has anyone ever spoiled an ending for you?" (hint on screen: Yes. ___ / Luckily, no. I always ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Luckily, no. I always watch first and read reviews later. Critics use big words; I’m still looking for my remote. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.

steps.title: Episode Nine
steps.text: Jiwoo watched episode nine that night, and Chloe was right. The premise sounds simple. A mail carrier on a small island finds a box of letters that were never delivered. But halfway through, the protagonist’s arc takes a sharp turn. The pacing picks up, and every episode ends on a cliffhanger. Jiwoo hadn’t watched the trailer or read a synopsis, so each reveal surprised her. One critic called the tone “quiet but sharp,” and Jiwoo agreed. By Sunday night, she had reached the finale. She texted Chloe: “Done. We need to talk.” They talked on the phone for an hour. Was the ending happy or sad? Was the last scene a hint or just ambiguous? They still couldn’t agree. But they agreed on one thing. The story would *stay with* them for a long time.
steps.gloss: mail carrier 집배원 · deliver 배달하다 · take a sharp turn 확 바뀌다 · pick up (속도가) 빨라지다 · reveal 사실이 드러나는 순간 · stay with (마음에) 오래 남다
questions: What is the premise of the drama?
How long did Jiwoo and Chloe talk on the phone?

The pacing picks up, and every episode ends on a cliffhanger. Jiwoo hadn’t watched the trailer or read a synopsis, so each reveal surprised her. Was the ending happy or sad? Was the last scene a hint or just ambiguous? They still couldn’t agree. But they agreed on one thing. The story would stay with them for a long time." Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:

First ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence, and stop there to wait. React and praise specifically. Only then, in a later turn, end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to it, say that next time we will practise saying today's scene by heart, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 스포일러 없이
steps.goal: 오늘 장면의 대화를 외워서 말해 보기
steps.scene_desc: 9월 금요일 저녁, 클로이 집 거실. 담요를 두르고 소파에 앉은 클로이가 손으로 입에 지퍼를 채우는 시늉을 하고, 옆의 지우가 웃으며 두 손으로 귀를 막고 있음. 꺼진 텔레비전(화면 글자 없이), 탁자 위에 팝콘 그릇과 찻잔 두 개. 글자 없음
steps.label: 대화 외우기
steps.teach:
This is the start of Part 3 of "Without giving too much away, …" (스포일러 없이); it may be a different day. Today the learner practises saying the scene from this lesson by heart. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of one or two exchanges. React to what they say.
2) Then, in a new turn, say in one or two short sentences that today you will practise the scene ("Episode Eight · 9월 금요일 저녁, 클로이 집에서") until they can say it by heart: first listen once, then say their lines with fewer and fewer words on the screen. Do not ask if they are ready more than once.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays the scene once more — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Episode Eight · 9월 금요일 저녁, 클로이 집에서

steps.label: 장면 다시 듣기
steps.teach:
The app has just played the scene again in the characters' own voices:
1. Chloe: "Done! I just finished the last episode. All sixteen." (다 봤어요! 방금 마지막 화 끝냈어요. 열여섯 화 전부요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Already? I’m only on episode eight. Don’t tell me anything!" (벌써요? 저는 이제 8화예요. 아무 말도 하지 마요!)
3. Chloe: "I won’t spoil it for you. I promise. My lips are sealed." (스포일러 안 할게요. 약속해요. 입 꾹 다물게요.)
4. Jiwoo: "But is it worth finishing? The middle feels kind of slow." (그런데 끝까지 볼 만해요? 중간이 좀 느린 것 같아서요.)

6. Jiwoo: "Changes how? Is the mail carrier hiding something?" (어떻게 바뀌는데요? 그 집배원이 뭘 숨기고 있어요?)

12. Jiwoo: "OK, no more questions. Let’s just say I know what I’m doing tonight." (알았어요, 더 안 물을게요. 오늘 밤 뭘 할지는 정해졌다고만 해 둘게요.)
