steps.title: 비꼼 알아듣기
steps.goal: 억양으로 반어를 알아듣고 쓰기
steps.scene_desc: 9월 말 비 오는 저녁, 동네 버스 정류장. 버스 한 대가 물웅덩이를 튀기며 떠나가고, 우산을 든 벤이 무표정한 얼굴로 떠나는 버스를 바라봄. 옆에서 지우가 바람에 뒤집힌 우산을 들고 웃음을 참음. 정류장 안내판·노선도에 글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "Oh, great." (비꼼 알아듣기). Goal: 억양으로 반어를 알아듣고 쓰기. Today's scene: 9월 말 비 오는 저녁, 동네 버스 정류장. 버스 한 대가 물웅덩이를 튀기며 떠나가고, 우산을 든 벤이 무표정한 얼굴로 떠나는 버스를 바라봄. 옆에서 지우가 바람에 뒤집힌 우산을 들고 웃음을 참음. 정류장 안내판·노선도에 글자 없음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Ben, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Oh, great.".

steps.when: 말은 ‘좋다’지만 *낮고 평평하게, 길게* 말하면 반대 뜻(실망·짜증)이 되기 쉬워요. *밝게, 끝을 올려* 말하면 진짜 기쁨으로 들려요. 실제 뜻은 표정·상황도 함께 봐요.
steps.extra: The bus just left. Oh, great.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Oh, great." ((비꼼) 아, 잘됐네. / (진심) 와, 잘됐다!). When to use it: 말은 ‘좋다’지만 낮고 평평하게, 길게 말하면 반대 뜻(실망·짜증)이 되기 쉬워요. 밝게, 끝을 올려 말하면 진짜 기쁨으로 들려요. 실제 뜻은 표정·상황도 함께 봐요. Note: The bus just left. Oh, great.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): The bus just left. Oh, great. Now I get to speed-walk to work like it's an Olympic event. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.

Sincere (bright ↗)
rows: it rained on my day off.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: ___. Oh, great. / “___.” “Yeah, right.”. Table (Phrase → Sarcastic (low, flat ↘)):
- Oh, great. → the bus just left.
- That’s just what I needed. → my umbrella broke.
- Lucky me. → it rained on my day off.
- I can hardly wait. → there’s a two-hour meeting at six.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): There's a two-hour meeting at six. I can hardly wait. My evening was getting far too exciting. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 억양이 뜻을 바꿔요: 진심: Oh, great! ↗ 높고 밝게, 끝을 올려요. / 비꼼: Oh, grea-a-at. ↘ 낮고 평평하게, 길게 끌고 끝을 내려요. 얼굴은 무표정(deadpan)이거나 눈을 굴려요(eye-roll). / ↗ 올림 · ↘ 내림 · 이 대화의 연습 패턴이에요
- 반어를 알아채는 단서: ① 말과 상황이 반대(버스를 놓쳤는데 great) ② 지나친 과장 (Could this day get any better?) ③ 느리고 평평한 말투 / 맞장구: Tell me about it. 내 말이요(누가 아니래요).
Common mistakes on screen:
- That’s just what I needed it. → That’s just what I needed. (what이 목적어라 it을 또 쓰지 않아요.)
- Could this day get any more better? → Could this day get any better? (better가 이미 비교급이라 more를 쓰지 않아요.)
- I can hardly to wait. → I can hardly wait. (can 뒤에는 동사원형.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I watered my plant, and it fell off the shelf. That's just what I needed. The floor looked far too clean. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.

The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "Oh, great." (비꼼 알아듣기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Oh, great." / "Yeah, right." / "That’s just what I needed.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Lost in Tone
steps.text: On the bus, Ben told Jiwoo about his first year in Seoul. A coworker showed him the new schedule for a very busy month, and Ben said, “Oh, great,” in a flat voice. He meant it as a dry joke about how busy he would be, but his coworker misread it. She thought he was mocking her work. “That’s the problem with sarcasm,” Ben said. “The real meaning is implied, not said. If people don’t know you well, they may think the joke is aimed at them.” The next day, he apologized and explained. Now they laugh about it together. Ben added that text messages are even riskier, because no one can hear your intonation. Jiwoo decided to save her sarcasm for rainy days, broken umbrellas, and late buses. “And for myself,” she said with a smirk. “Nice going, Jiwoo.”

steps.label: 장면 다시 듣기
steps.teach:
The app has just played the scene again in the characters' own voices:
1. Ben: "Run, Jiwoo! … And it’s gone. Oh, great." (뛰어요, 지우 씨! … 가 버렸네요. 아, 잘됐네요.)
2. Jiwoo: "“Great”? We just missed the bus!" (‘잘됐다’고요? 방금 버스 놓쳤잖아요!)
3. Ben: "Exactly. Listen to my tone. “Oh, great.” Low, flat, and slow. That means it’s not great at all." (바로 그거예요. 제 말투를 들어 봐요. “Oh, great.” 낮고, 평평하고, 느리게. 전혀 좋지 않다는 뜻이에요.)

5. Ben: "Twenty-five minutes in the rain. I can hardly wait." (빗속에서 25분이라. 기대돼 죽겠네요.)
6. Jiwoo: "The app says it might come early, though." (그래도 앱에서는 일찍 올 수도 있대요.)
7. Ben: "Yeah, right. When has that ever happened?" (퍽이나요. 그런 적이 언제 있었어요?)
8. Jiwoo: "Oh no, my umbrella just flipped inside out. That’s just what I needed." (아, 우산이 방금 뒤집혔어요. 딱 이게 필요했죠.)
9. Ben: "Ha! Perfect. You stretched out “needed” and kept a straight face. Very deadpan." (하! 완벽해요. needed를 길게 끌고 무표정을 유지했어요. 아주 능청스러워요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Thanks! But can I use sarcasm with anyone?" (고마워요! 그런데 비꼬는 말은 아무한테나 써도 돼요?)
11. Ben: "Use it on the weather, the bus, or yourself. Aimed at a person, it can really hurt." (날씨나 버스, 아니면 자기 자신한테 써요. 사람을 겨냥하면 정말 상처가 될 수 있어요.)
12. Jiwoo: "Got it. Oh, look! That’s our bus, and it’s early! Oh, great!" (알겠어요. 어, 봐요! 우리 버스예요, 일찍 왔어요! 와, 잘됐다!)
13. Ben: "Now that’s a real “Oh, great!” Bright and rising. Could this day get any better? This time, I mean it." (이번 건 진짜 “Oh, great!”네요. 밝고 끝이 올라가요. 오늘 이보다 더 좋을 수 있을까요? 이번엔 진심이에요.)

lines.en: 뛰어요, 지우 씨! … 가 버렸네요. 아, 잘됐네요.
“Great”? We just missed the bus!
lines.ko: ‘잘됐다’고요? 방금 버스 놓쳤잖아요!

lines.en: 바로 그거예요. 제 말투를 들어 봐요. “Oh, great.” 낮고, 평평하고, 느리게. 전혀 좋지 않다는 뜻이에요.
Ah, it’s sarcasm. Let me check the app … The next one is in twenty-five minutes.
lines.ko: 아, 비꼬는 말이군요. 앱 좀 볼게요 … 다음 버스는 25분 뒤예요.

lines.en: 빗속에서 25분이라. 기대돼 죽겠네요.
The app says it might come early, though.
lines.ko: 그래도 앱에서는 일찍 올 수도 있대요.

lines.en: 퍽이나요. 그런 적이 언제 있었어요?
Oh no, my umbrella just flipped inside out. {{That’s just what I needed}}.
lines.ko: 아, 우산이 방금 뒤집혔어요. 딱 이게 필요했죠.

lines.en: 하! 완벽해요. needed를 길게 끌고 무표정을 유지했어요. 아주 능청스러워요.
Thanks! But can I use sarcasm with anyone?
lines.ko: 고마워요! 그런데 비꼬는 말은 아무한테나 써도 돼요?

lines.en: 날씨나 버스, 아니면 자기 자신한테 써요. 사람을 겨냥하면 정말 상처가 될 수 있어요.
Got it. Oh, look! That’s our bus, and it’s early! Oh, great!
lines.ko: 알겠어요. 어, 봐요! 우리 버스예요, 일찍 왔어요! 와, 잘됐다!

lines.en: 이번 건 진짜 “Oh, great!”네요. 밝고 끝이 올라가요. 오늘 이보다 더 좋을 수 있을까요? 이번엔 진심이에요.

steps.hint: 이번엔 상대 역할이에요. 한국어 뜻만 보고 영어로 말해요
steps.teach:
Last round, with the roles switched: the learner now says the other person's lines, seeing only their Korean meaning, and you read Jiwoo's lines. The learner is Ben; you read the lines of Jiwoo exactly as written. The full lines, for you only:
1. Ben (learner): "Run, Jiwoo! … And it’s gone. Oh, great." (뛰어요, 지우 씨! … 가 버렸네요. 아, 잘됐네요.)
2. Jiwoo (you): "“Great”? We just missed the bus!" (‘잘됐다’고요? 방금 버스 놓쳤잖아요!)
3. Ben (learner): "Exactly. Listen to my tone. “Oh, great.” Low, flat, and slow. That means it’s not great at all." (바로 그거예요. 제 말투를 들어 봐요. “Oh, great.” 낮고, 평평하고, 느리게. 전혀 좋지 않다는 뜻이에요.)
4. Jiwoo (you): "Ah, it’s sarcasm. Let me check the app … The next one is in twenty-five minutes." (아, 비꼬는 말이군요. 앱 좀 볼게요 … 다음 버스는 25분 뒤예요.)
5. Ben (learner): "Twenty-five minutes in the rain. I can hardly wait." (빗속에서 25분이라. 기대돼 죽겠네요.)
6. Jiwoo (you): "The app says it might come early, though." (그래도 앱에서는 일찍 올 수도 있대요.)
7. Ben (learner): "Yeah, right. When has that ever happened?" (퍽이나요. 그런 적이 언제 있었어요?)
8. Jiwoo (you): "Oh no, my umbrella just flipped inside out. That’s just what I needed." (아, 우산이 방금 뒤집혔어요. 딱 이게 필요했죠.)
9. Ben (learner): "Ha! Perfect. You stretched out “needed” and kept a straight face. Very deadpan." (하! 완벽해요. needed를 길게 끌고 무표정을 유지했어요. 아주 능청스러워요.)
10. Jiwoo (you): "Thanks! But can I use sarcasm with anyone?" (고마워요! 그런데 비꼬는 말은 아무한테나 써도 돼요?)
11. Ben (learner): "Use it on the weather, the bus, or yourself. Aimed at a person, it can really hurt." (날씨나 버스, 아니면 자기 자신한테 써요. 사람을 겨냥하면 정말 상처가 될 수 있어요.)
12. Jiwoo (you): "Got it. Oh, look! That’s our bus, and it’s early! Oh, great!" (알겠어요. 어, 봐요! 우리 버스예요, 일찍 왔어요! 와, 잘됐다!)
13. Ben (learner): "Now that’s a real “Oh, great!” Bright and rising. Could this day get any better? This time, I mean it." (이번 건 진짜 “Oh, great!”네요. 밝고 끝이 올라가요. 오늘 이보다 더 좋을 수 있을까요? 이번엔 진심이에요.)
In one short sentence, say what is on the screen now and invite them to start. Do not say the learner's line before they try: remembering it is the point of this part, so this is the one exception to saying a sentence first. If they get stuck, give only the next word or two as a hint. If a word was missing or wrong, say the whole line once inside double quotes and let them try once more, then go on. Go in order, one line at a time. After the last line, react in a word or two, with no comment on how they sounded.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

steps.label: 마무리
steps.teach: Wrap up like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how it felt to say the scene by heart, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today (for example a line they remembered well), say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

lessons.title: 농담 설명
lessons.goal: 한국어 말장난을 영어로 설명하고 비슷한 웃음 찾기

steps.title: 농담 설명
steps.goal: 한국어 말장난을 영어로 설명하고 비슷한 웃음 찾기
steps.scene_desc: 10월 첫 토요일 저녁, 동네 식당의 긴 나무 식탁. 지우가 두 손을 펼쳐 무언가를 열심히 설명하고, 맞은편 클로이가 고개를 갸웃하다가 막 웃음을 터뜨리려 함. 식탁 위에 찌개·전·복숭아 접시(글자 없이). 식탁 끝에서 그레이스가 아직 웃고 있고, 벤·대니얼·마야도 웃으며 듣고 있음. 간판·메뉴판에 글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "It’s funnier in Korean." (농담 설명). Goal: 한국어 말장난을 영어로 설명하고 비슷한 웃음 찾기. Today's scene: 10월 첫 토요일 저녁, 동네 식당의 긴 나무 식탁. 지우가 두 손을 펼쳐 무언가를 열심히 설명하고, 맞은편 클로이가 고개를 갸웃하다가 막 웃음을 터뜨리려 함. 식탁 위에 찌개·전·복숭아 접시. 식탁 끝에서 그레이스가 아직 웃고 있고, 벤·대니얼·마야도 웃으며 듣고 있음. 간판·메뉴판에 글자 없음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Chloe, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "It doesn’t really translate, but ___.".

steps.when: 다른 언어로 옮기면 맛이 사라지는 말을 설명하기 *전에* 미리 알려요. 주어가 말·농담이면 translate는 ‘번역되다’.
steps.extra: It doesn’t really translate, but I’ll try.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "It doesn’t really translate, but ___." (딱 맞게 번역되지는 않지만, ~). When to use it: 다른 언어로 옮기면 맛이 사라지는 말을 설명하기 전에 미리 알려요. 주어가 말·농담이면 translate는 ‘번역되다’. Note: It doesn’t really translate, but I’ll try.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): It doesn’t really translate, but my handwriting doesn’t really translate either. Even I read it like a surprise. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "The joke is that ___.".

steps.when: 농담이 왜 웃긴지 *핵심*을 짚어요. that 뒤에 문장.
steps.extra: The joke is that 언덕 also means “hill.”
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "The joke is that ___." (웃긴 포인트는 ~라는 거예요.). When to use it: 농담이 왜 웃긴지 핵심을 짚어요. that 뒤에 문장. Note: The joke is that 언덕 also means “hill.”.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): The joke is that I set an early alarm. My body treated it like a polite suggestion. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "It’s funnier in Korean.".

steps.when: 설명하고 나서 웃음이 줄었을 때 가볍게 덧붙여요. *FUN*nier에 힘을 줘요.
steps.extra: Trust me, it’s funnier in Korean.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "It’s funnier in Korean." (한국어로 하면 더 웃겨요.). When to use it: 설명하고 나서 웃음이 줄었을 때 가볍게 덧붙여요. FUNnier에 힘을 줘요. Note: Trust me, it’s funnier in Korean.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): It’s funnier in Korean. In English, it sounds less like a joke and more like bus information. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("A Very Cold Duck · 10월 첫 토요일 저녁, 동네 식당 모임에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: A Very Cold Duck · 10월 첫 토요일 저녁, 동네 식당 모임에서

lines.en: What did I miss? Grace is still laughing.
lines.ko: 제가 뭘 놓쳤어요? 그레이스가 아직도 웃고 있네요.

lines.en: I told her a Korean joke. {{It doesn’t really translate, but}} I’ll try. What happens to a duck when it freezes?
lines.ko: 그레이스한테 한국 농담을 했어요. 딱 맞게 번역되지는 않지만 해 볼게요. 오리가 얼면 어떻게 될까요?

lines.en: Um … it turns into a duck popsicle?
lines.ko: 음… 오리 아이스바가 돼요?

lines.en: It turns into 언덕! {{Let me try to explain.}} “언” means “frozen,” and “duck” is just “duck.” {{The joke is that}} 언덕 is a real Korean word, too. It means “hill.”
lines.ko: 언덕이 돼요! 설명해 볼게요. ‘언’은 ‘얼어 버린’이라는 뜻이고, duck은 그냥 영어 duck이에요. 웃긴 포인트는 ‘언덕’이 진짜 한국어 낱말이기도 하다는 거예요. ‘hill’이라는 뜻이에요.

lines.en: So a frozen duck becomes a hill! {{I get it now!}} Half Korean, half English. {{That’s actually hilarious.}}
lines.ko: 그러니까 얼어 버린 오리가 언덕이 되는 거네요! 이제 알겠어요! 반은 한국어, 반은 영어. 이거 진짜 웃기네요.

lines.en: {{It’s funnier in Korean}}, trust me. One more. What’s the hottest fruit in the world? … 천도복숭아!
lines.ko: 한국어로 하면 더 웃겨요, 정말이에요. 하나 더요. 세상에서 가장 뜨거운 과일은? … 천도복숭아!

lines.en: A peach? Why is a peach hot?
lines.ko: 복숭아요? 복숭아가 왜 뜨거워요?

lines.en: 천도 is a kind of peach. But {{the word}} 천도 also {{sounds like}} 천 도, “a thousand degrees.”
lines.ko: 천도는 복숭아의 한 종류예요. 그런데 ‘천도’는 ‘천 도’, 그러니까 ‘1,000도’처럼 들리기도 해요.

lines.en: Ha! {{It’s a play on words.}} And you paused right before the punch line. Great timing!
lines.ko: 하! 말장난이네요. 그리고 마지막 한마디 바로 앞에서 잠깐 쉬었죠. 타이밍 좋았어요!

lines.en: I practiced! My team has a potato joke, too, but {{you kind of had to be there}}. {{It’s an inside joke.}} … {{Never mind, it’s not that funny.}}
lines.ko: 연습했거든요! 저희 팀에도 감자 농담이 있는데, 그 자리에 있어야 웃겨요. 우리끼리만 통하는 농담이에요. …아니에요, 그렇게 웃기지도 않아요.

lines.en: Fair. {{Explaining a joke kills it.}} But your two jokes both worked!
lines.ko: 그렇죠. 농담은 설명하면 재미가 없어지죠. 그래도 지우 씨 농담 두 개는 둘 다 통했어요!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "A Very Cold Duck · 10월 첫 토요일 저녁, 동네 식당 모임에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Chloe: "What did I miss? Grace is still laughing." (제가 뭘 놓쳤어요? 그레이스가 아직도 웃고 있네요.)
2. Jiwoo: "I told her a Korean joke. It doesn’t really translate, but I’ll try. What happens to a duck when it freezes?" (그레이스한테 한국 농담을 했어요. 딱 맞게 번역되지는 않지만 해 볼게요. 오리가 얼면 어떻게 될까요?)
3. Chloe: "Um … it turns into a duck popsicle?" (음… 오리 아이스바가 돼요?)
4. Jiwoo: "It turns into 언덕! Let me try to explain. “언” means “frozen,” and “duck” is just “duck.” The joke is that 언덕 is a real Korean word, too. It means “hill.”" (언덕이 돼요! 설명해 볼게요. ‘언’은 ‘얼어 버린’이라는 뜻이고, duck은 그냥 영어 duck이에요. 웃긴 포인트는 ‘언덕’이 진짜 한국어 낱말이기도 하다는 거예요. ‘hill’이라는 뜻이에요.)
5. Chloe: "So a frozen duck becomes a hill! I get it now! Half Korean, half English. That’s actually hilarious." (그러니까 얼어 버린 오리가 언덕이 되는 거네요! 이제 알겠어요! 반은 한국어, 반은 영어. 이거 진짜 웃기네요.)
6. Jiwoo: "It’s funnier in Korean, trust me. One more. What’s the hottest fruit in the world? … 천도복숭아!" (한국어로 하면 더 웃겨요, 정말이에요. 하나 더요. 세상에서 가장 뜨거운 과일은? … 천도복숭아!)
7. Chloe: "A peach? Why is a peach hot?" (복숭아요? 복숭아가 왜 뜨거워요?)
8. Jiwoo: "천도 is a kind of peach. But the word 천도 also sounds like 천 도, “a thousand degrees.”" (천도는 복숭아의 한 종류예요. 그런데 ‘천도’는 ‘천 도’, 그러니까 ‘1,000도’처럼 들리기도 해요.)
9. Chloe: "Ha! It’s a play on words. And you paused right before the punch line. Great timing!" (하! 말장난이네요. 그리고 마지막 한마디 바로 앞에서 잠깐 쉬었죠. 타이밍 좋았어요!)
10. Jiwoo: "I practiced! My team has a potato joke, too, but you kind of had to be there. It’s an inside joke. … Never mind, it’s not that funny." (연습했거든요! 저희 팀에도 감자 농담이 있는데, 그 자리에 있어야 웃겨요. 우리끼리만 통하는 농담이에요. …아니에요, 그렇게 웃기지도 않아요.)
11. Chloe: "Fair. Explaining a joke kills it. But your two jokes both worked!" (그렇죠. 농담은 설명하면 재미가 없어지죠. 그래도 지우 씨 농담 두 개는 둘 다 통했어요!)
Give one short, natural reaction to the scene (a few words) and say in one short sentence that you will now read it together. Do not ask any question about what happened yet: the quiz comes later, after the role reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

steps.title: A Very Cold Duck · 10월 첫 토요일 저녁, 동네 식당 모임에서

lines.en: What did I miss? Grace is still laughing.
lines.ko: 제가 뭘 놓쳤어요? 그레이스가 아직도 웃고 있네요.

lines.en: I told her a Korean joke. {{It doesn’t really translate, but}} I’ll try. What happens to a duck when it freezes?
lines.ko: 그레이스한테 한국 농담을 했어요. 딱 맞게 번역되지는 않지만 해 볼게요. 오리가 얼면 어떻게 될까요?

lines.en: Um … it turns into a duck popsicle?
lines.ko: 음… 오리 아이스바가 돼요?

lines.en: It turns into 언덕! {{Let me try to explain.}} “언” means “frozen,” and “duck” is just “duck.” {{The joke is that}} 언덕 is a real Korean word, too. It means “hill.”
lines.ko: 언덕이 돼요! 설명해 볼게요. ‘언’은 ‘얼어 버린’이라는 뜻이고, duck은 그냥 영어 duck이에요. 웃긴 포인트는 ‘언덕’이 진짜 한국어 낱말이기도 하다는 거예요. ‘hill’이라는 뜻이에요.

lines.en: So a frozen duck becomes a hill! {{I get it now!}} Half Korean, half English. {{That’s actually hilarious.}}
lines.ko: 그러니까 얼어 버린 오리가 언덕이 되는 거네요! 이제 알겠어요! 반은 한국어, 반은 영어. 이거 진짜 웃기네요.

lines.en: {{It’s funnier in Korean}}, trust me. One more. What’s the hottest fruit in the world? … 천도복숭아!
lines.ko: 한국어로 하면 더 웃겨요, 정말이에요. 하나 더요. 세상에서 가장 뜨거운 과일은? … 천도복숭아!

lines.en: A peach? Why is a peach hot?
lines.ko: 복숭아요? 복숭아가 왜 뜨거워요?

lines.en: 천도 is a kind of peach. But {{the word}} 천도 also {{sounds like}} 천 도, “a thousand degrees.”
lines.ko: 천도는 복숭아의 한 종류예요. 그런데 ‘천도’는 ‘천 도’, 그러니까 ‘1,000도’처럼 들리기도 해요.

lines.en: Ha! {{It’s a play on words.}} And you paused right before the punch line. Great timing!
lines.ko: 하! 말장난이네요. 그리고 마지막 한마디 바로 앞에서 잠깐 쉬었죠. 타이밍 좋았어요!

lines.en: I practiced! My team has a potato joke, too, but {{you kind of had to be there}}. {{It’s an inside joke.}} … {{Never mind, it’s not that funny.}}
lines.ko: 연습했거든요! 저희 팀에도 감자 농담이 있는데, 그 자리에 있어야 웃겨요. 우리끼리만 통하는 농담이에요. …아니에요, 그렇게 웃기지도 않아요.

lines.en: Fair. {{Explaining a joke kills it.}} But your two jokes both worked!
lines.ko: 그렇죠. 농담은 설명하면 재미가 없어지죠. 그래도 지우 씨 농담 두 개는 둘 다 통했어요!

steps.teach:
Role reading of the same scene. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Chloe exactly as written, word for word. Never change, add or skip a line, and never read the learner's lines for them first.
1. Chloe (you): "What did I miss? Grace is still laughing." (제가 뭘 놓쳤어요? 그레이스가 아직도 웃고 있네요.)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "I told her a Korean joke. It doesn’t really translate, but I’ll try. What happens to a duck when it freezes?" (그레이스한테 한국 농담을 했어요. 딱 맞게 번역되지는 않지만 해 볼게요. 오리가 얼면 어떻게 될까요?)
3. Chloe (you): "Um … it turns into a duck popsicle?" (음… 오리 아이스바가 돼요?)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "It turns into 언덕! Let me try to explain. “언” means “frozen,” and “duck” is just “duck.” The joke is that 언덕 is a real Korean word, too. It means “hill.”" (언덕이 돼요! 설명해 볼게요. ‘언’은 ‘얼어 버린’이라는 뜻이고, duck은 그냥 영어 duck이에요. 웃긴 포인트는 ‘언덕’이 진짜 한국어 낱말이기도 하다는 거예요. ‘hill’이라는 뜻이에요.)
5. Chloe (you): "So a frozen duck becomes a hill! I get it now! Half Korean, half English. That’s actually hilarious." (그러니까 얼어 버린 오리가 언덕이 되는 거네요! 이제 알겠어요! 반은 한국어, 반은 영어. 이거 진짜 웃기네요.)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "It’s funnier in Korean, trust me. One more. What’s the hottest fruit in the world? … 천도복숭아!" (한국어로 하면 더 웃겨요, 정말이에요. 하나 더요. 세상에서 가장 뜨거운 과일은? … 천도복숭아!)
7. Chloe (you): "A peach? Why is a peach hot?" (복숭아요? 복숭아가 왜 뜨거워요?)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "천도 is a kind of peach. But the word 천도 also sounds like 천 도, “a thousand degrees.”" (천도는 복숭아의 한 종류예요. 그런데 ‘천도’는 ‘천 도’, 그러니까 ‘1,000도’처럼 들리기도 해요.)
9. Chloe (you): "Ha! It’s a play on words. And you paused right before the punch line. Great timing!" (하! 말장난이네요. 그리고 마지막 한마디 바로 앞에서 잠깐 쉬었죠. 타이밍 좋았어요!)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "I practiced! My team has a potato joke, too, but you kind of had to be there. It’s an inside joke. … Never mind, it’s not that funny." (연습했거든요! 저희 팀에도 감자 농담이 있는데, 그 자리에 있어야 웃겨요. 우리끼리만 통하는 농담이에요. …아니에요, 그렇게 웃기지도 않아요.)
11. Chloe (you): "Fair. Explaining a joke kills it. But your two jokes both worked!" (그렇죠. 농담은 설명하면 재미가 없어지죠. 그래도 지우 씨 농담 두 개는 둘 다 통했어요!)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Chloe. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, react to the scene in a word or two (not a comment on how they sounded), then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short quiz about the scene.

items: Jiwoo told Grace a Korean joke before Chloe asked about it.
The joke combines the Korean word 언 with the English word duck.
Jiwoo explains her team’s potato joke to Chloe.
steps.teach:
Quiz about the scene, now that the learner has heard it and read it in both roles. First ask two short, easy questions about what happens in it (who, what, where or how often), one per turn, with the answers in the lines below. Any answer that shows they understood is right, in any words or in Korean: say so and go on. If it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Never turn an answer into a repeat drill here: if their English has a slip, just say the right sentence back once in your reaction and go on. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too.
Then the true/false check. The statements on the learner's screen, each with its answer and the scene line that shows it. The answers are for you only: never say an answer or a line number before the learner has answered:
1. Jiwoo told Grace a Korean joke before Chloe asked about it. → True (line 1, 2)
2. The joke combines the Korean word 언 with the English word duck. → True (line 4)
3. Jiwoo explains her team’s potato joke to Chloe. → False (line 10)
The scene they are about:
1. Chloe: "What did I miss? Grace is still laughing." (제가 뭘 놓쳤어요? 그레이스가 아직도 웃고 있네요.)

6. Jiwoo: "It’s funnier in Korean, trust me. One more. What’s the hottest fruit in the world? … 천도복숭아!" (한국어로 하면 더 웃겨요, 정말이에요. 하나 더요. 세상에서 가장 뜨거운 과일은? … 천도복숭아!)

9. Chloe: "Ha! It’s a play on words. And you paused right before the punch line. Great timing!" (하! 말장난이네요. 그리고 마지막 한마디 바로 앞에서 잠깐 쉬었죠. 타이밍 좋았어요!)
10. Jiwoo: "I practiced! My team has a potato joke, too, but you kind of had to be there. It’s an inside joke. … Never mind, it’s not that funny." (연습했거든요! 저희 팀에도 감자 농담이 있는데, 그 자리에 있어야 웃겨요. 우리끼리만 통하는 농담이에요. …아니에요, 그렇게 웃기지도 않아요.)

Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). A one-word answer (True, False, 맞아요) is enough; never ask for a full sentence. Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: The word …
sounds like …
The joke is that …
rows: a frozen duck becomes a hill.
a peach is the hottest fruit.
sea salt lasts a thousand days.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: It doesn’t really translate, but ___. / The joke is that ___. Table (The word … → sounds like …):
- 언덕 → “언 duck,” a frozen duck.
- 천도 → 천 도, “a thousand degrees.”
- 십구만 (190,000) → 쉽구만, “Oh, that’s easy.”
- 천일염 (sea salt) → 천 일, “a thousand days.”
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): One word sounds like a thousand degrees. That is also how my soup feels when I am already late. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: The joke is that … · sounds like …

*The joke is that* 언덕 also means “hill.” 웃긴 포인트는 언덕이 ‘hill’이라는 뜻도 된다는 거예요. 
*The word* 천도 *sounds like* 천 도, which means “a thousand degrees.” sound like + 명사(구) = ~처럼 들리다

It doesn’t really *translate*. (말이) 잘 번역되지 않아요. 주어가 말·농담이면 ‘번역되다’. 
It’s *funnier* in Korean. funny → funnier (y → ier)
errors: This word sounds an English word.
This word sounds like an English word.
I don’t get it the joke.
get 뒤 목적어는 하나만. it이나 the joke 중 하나.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- The joke is that … · sounds like …: The joke is that 언덕 also means “hill.” 웃긴 포인트는 언덕이 ‘hill’이라는 뜻도 된다는 거예요. / The word 천도 sounds like 천 도, which means “a thousand degrees.” sound like + 명사(구) = ~처럼 들리다
- It doesn’t really translate · funnier: It doesn’t really translate. (말이) 잘 번역되지 않아요. 주어가 말·농담이면 ‘번역되다’. / It’s funnier in Korean. funny → funnier (y → ier)
Common mistakes on screen:
- This word sounds an English word. → This word sounds like an English word. (명사 앞에서는 sounds like.)
- I don’t get it the joke. → I don’t get the joke. (get 뒤 목적어는 하나만. it이나 the joke 중 하나.)
- Explaining a joke kill it. → Explaining a joke kills it. (-ing 주어는 단수 취급이라 kills.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Explaining a joke kills it. I still explain it like I am presenting quarterly results. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: The joke is that … · sounds like …: The joke is that 언덕 also means “hill.” 웃긴 포인트는 언덕이 ‘hill’이라는 뜻도 된다는 거예요. The word 천도 sounds like 천 도, which means “a thousand degrees.” sound like + 명사(구) = ~처럼 들리다
It doesn’t really translate · funnier: It doesn’t really translate. (말이) 잘 번역되지 않아요. 주어가 말·농담이면 ‘번역되다’. It’s funnier in Korean. funny → funnier (y → ier)
mistakes: This word sounds an English word. → This word sounds like an English word.
I don’t get it the joke. → I don’t get the joke.
Explaining a joke kill it. → Explaining a joke kills it.

steps.note: 예) 눈치 / reading the room → A: What does 눈치 mean? B: It doesn’t really translate, but it’s kind of like reading the room.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) 눈치 / reading the room → A: What does 눈치 mean? B: It doesn’t really translate, but it’s kind of like reading the room. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): 눈치 / reading the room | 정 / a warm bond | 답답하다 / stuck and frustrated | 아재 개그 / corny dad jokes.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

This is the start of session 2 of "It’s funnier in Korean." (농담 설명); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "It doesn’t really translate, but ___." / "The joke is that ___." / "It’s funnier in Korean.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: You kind of had to be there.
Never mind, it’s not that funny.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 설명 시작하기: "Let me try to explain." (설명해 볼게요., 보통); "It’s a play on words." (말장난이에요., 보통); "The word ___ sounds like ___." (~라는 말이 ~처럼 들려요., 보통)
- 잘 안 전해질 때: "You kind of had to be there." (그 자리에 있어야 웃긴 거예요., 친근); "It’s an inside joke." (우리끼리만 통하는 농담이에요., 친근); "Never mind, it’s not that funny." (아니에요, 그렇게 웃기지도 않아요., 친근); "Explaining a joke kills it." (농담은 설명하면 재미가 없어져요., 친근)
- 알아들었을 때: "I get it now!" (이제 알겠어요!, 친근); "That’s actually hilarious." (이거 진짜 웃기네요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Let me try to explain. It’s a play on words. After two minutes, even I need subtitles. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 농담의 짜임과 말하는 법

*setup* 앞부분(질문·상황) → (한 박자 쉼) → *punch line* 웃음이 터지는 마지막 한마디 
What’s the hottest fruit in the world? … *천도복숭아!* 마지막 말 앞에서 쉬고, 마지막 말에 힘을 줘요. 
같은 농담도 *timing*(쉬는 때)과 *delivery*(말하는 방식)에 따라 달라요.
웃음에 쓰는 말

a *homophone* 소리는 같고 뜻이 다른 말(pair · pear)

steps.title: Jokes from Home
steps.text: After dessert, everyone tried to explain a joke from home. Ben told one about baseball, but it depended on a cultural reference nobody else knew. “You kind of had to grow up in Boston,” he admitted. Daniel’s pun used two English words that are homophones, so it worked right away, and the whole table groaned. Then Grace asked Jiwoo about the potato joke. Jiwoo laughed and *shook her head*. “Some jokes are untranslatable,” she said. Chloe said a joke is like a good drama scene. The words matter, but so do the timing and the delivery. “Your duck joke had both,” Maya told Jiwoo. On the way home, Jiwoo wrote down three more Korean puns. Next time, she wanted to explain them faster and *let the punch line do the work*.

steps.title: 농담 설명
steps.goal: 오늘 장면의 대화를 외워서 말해 보기
steps.scene_desc: 10월 첫 토요일 저녁, 동네 식당의 긴 나무 식탁. 지우가 두 손을 펼쳐 무언가를 열심히 설명하고, 맞은편 클로이가 고개를 갸웃하다가 막 웃음을 터뜨리려 함. 식탁 위에 찌개·전·복숭아 접시(글자 없이). 식탁 끝에서 그레이스가 아직 웃고 있고, 벤·대니얼·마야도 웃으며 듣고 있음. 간판·메뉴판에 글자 없음
steps.label: 대화 외우기
steps.teach:
This is the start of Part 3 of "It’s funnier in Korean." (농담 설명); it may be a different day. Today the learner practises saying the scene from this lesson by heart. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of one or two exchanges. React to what they say.
2) Then, in a new turn, say in one or two short sentences that today you will practise the scene ("A Very Cold Duck · 10월 첫 토요일 저녁, 동네 식당 모임에서") until they can say it by heart: first listen once, then say their lines with fewer and fewer words on the screen. Do not ask if they are ready more than once.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays the scene once more — tell them to just listen.

steps.label: 장면 다시 듣기
steps.teach:
The app has just played the scene again in the characters' own voices:
1. Chloe: "What did I miss? Grace is still laughing." (제가 뭘 놓쳤어요? 그레이스가 아직도 웃고 있네요.)
2. Jiwoo: "I told her a Korean joke. It doesn’t really translate, but I’ll try. What happens to a duck when it freezes?" (그레이스한테 한국 농담을 했어요. 딱 맞게 번역되지는 않지만 해 볼게요. 오리가 얼면 어떻게 될까요?)

7. Chloe: "A peach? Why is a peach hot?" (복숭아요? 복숭아가 왜 뜨거워요?)
8. Jiwoo: "천도 is a kind of peach. But the word 천도 also sounds like 천 도, “a thousand degrees.”" (천도는 복숭아의 한 종류예요. 그런데 ‘천도’는 ‘천 도’, 그러니까 ‘1,000도’처럼 들리기도 해요.)
9. Chloe: "Ha! It’s a play on words. And you paused right before the punch line. Great timing!" (하! 말장난이네요. 그리고 마지막 한마디 바로 앞에서 잠깐 쉬었죠. 타이밍 좋았어요!)
10. Jiwoo: "I practiced! My team has a potato joke, too, but you kind of had to be there. It’s an inside joke. … Never mind, it’s not that funny." (연습했거든요! 저희 팀에도 감자 농담이 있는데, 그 자리에 있어야 웃겨요. 우리끼리만 통하는 농담이에요. …아니에요, 그렇게 웃기지도 않아요.)
11. Chloe: "Fair. Explaining a joke kills it. But your two jokes both worked!" (그렇죠. 농담은 설명하면 재미가 없어지죠. 그래도 지우 씨 농담 두 개는 둘 다 통했어요!)

steps.goal: 말장난에 반응하고 농담을 주고받기
steps.scene_desc: 10월 마지막 금요일 저녁, 벤의 집(3층) 식탁. 벤이 갓 구운 롤빵 바구니를 들고 장난스럽게 씩 웃고, 지우와 그레이스가 한 손으로 이마를 짚은 채 웃음 섞인 신음을 함. 식탁 위에 피자·샐러드·작은 롤빵(글자·상표 없이). 창밖은 어두움
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "I see what you did there." (말장난). Goal: 말장난에 반응하고 농담을 주고받기. Today's scene: 10월 마지막 금요일 저녁, 벤의 집(3층) 식탁. 벤이 갓 구운 롤빵 바구니를 들고 장난스럽게 씩 웃고, 지우와 그레이스가 한 손으로 이마를 짚은 채 웃음 섞인 신음을 함. 식탁 위에 피자·샐러드·작은 롤빵. 창밖은 어두움. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Ben, Grace, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I see what you did there.".

steps.when: 상대가 슬쩍 넣은 *말장난·재치*를 알아챘다고 웃으며 알려요. *SEE*에 힘을 주고 끝을 내려요.
steps.extra: “It’s a little cheesy.” Ha! I see what you did there.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I see what you did there." (무슨 말장난인지 알겠어요.). When to use it: 상대가 슬쩍 넣은 말장난·재치를 알아챘다고 웃으며 알려요. SEE에 힘을 주고 끝을 내려요. Note: “It’s a little cheesy.” Ha! I see what you did there.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): My coworker looked at my desk and called it historical. I see what you did there. Some papers might be from last winter. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "No pun intended.".

lines.en: Pizza’s ready! I’d tell you a joke about pizza, but it’s a little cheesy.
lines.ko: 피자 나왔어요! 피자 농담을 하나 하고 싶은데, 좀 치즈 같아서요(썰렁해서요).

lines.ko: 또 시작이네요. 벤 집 저녁에는 늘 말장난이 공짜로 따라와요.

lines.en: Ugh, Ben. {{It’s so bad it’s good.}}
lines.ko: 으, 벤. 너무 썰렁해서 오히려 웃겨요.

lines.en: Thank you. Here, have some bread, too.
lines.ko: 고마워요. 자, 빵도 좀 먹어요.

lines.en: Thanks. Are these rolls homemade?

lines.en: They are. I’m on a roll tonight.
lines.ko: 그럼요. 오늘 밤 제가 아주 물이 올랐거든요(롤이 잘 나왔거든요).

lines.en: {{I walked right into that one.}}
lines.ko: 제가 딱 걸려들었네요.

lines.en: Ben, {{don’t quit your day job}}.
lines.ko: 벤, 본업은 그만두지 마요.

lines.en: {{I’ll be here all week.}} {{Ba-dum-tss.}} So, Jiwoo, how’s the bike app going?
lines.ko: 이번 주 내내 공연합니다. 둥둥 칫! 그래서 지우 씨, 자전거 앱은 어떻게 돼 가요?

lines.en: Slow. The second-stage launch keeps getting pushed back. We’re just spinning our wheels, {{no pun intended}}.
lines.ko: 느려요. 2단계 출시가 계속 밀려요. 바퀴만 헛돌고 있어요(제자리걸음이에요). 말장난하려던 건 아니고요.

lines.en: Spinning your wheels on a bike app? {{I see what you did there.}}

lines.en: Ha! “Draw laughs.” {{Okay, that was clever.}}

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: I see what you did there. / ___, no pun intended. Table (Someone says … → The two meanings):
- I’d tell you a pizza joke, but it’s a little cheesy. → full of cheese / corny
- I’m on a roll tonight. → bread roll / doing well
- Eggs don’t tell jokes. They’d crack each other up. → break / make laugh
- The moon café has great food but no atmosphere. → air / mood
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I told an egg joke at breakfast. My friend said it cracked her up. I see what you did there. I nearly dropped the pan. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: I see what you did there — 주어 + 동사 순서

I see *what you did* there. 거기서 뭘 했는지 알겠어요 → 말장난을 알아챘어요. 
문장 안에 들어간 의문문은 *주어 + 동사* 순서: I know *what you mean*.

*No pun intended.* 일부러 한 말장난이 아니에요. 
*Pun intended.* 일부러 한 거예요(웃으며 인정). 
intended는 ‘의도된’이라는 과거분사.
errors: I see what did you there.

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- I see what you did there — 주어 + 동사 순서: I see what you did there. 거기서 뭘 했는지 알겠어요 → 말장난을 알아챘어요. / 문장 안에 들어간 의문문은 주어 + 동사 순서: I know what you mean.
- (No) pun intended: No pun intended. 일부러 한 말장난이 아니에요. / Pun intended. 일부러 한 거예요(웃으며 인정). / intended는 ‘의도된’이라는 과거분사.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I see what did you there. → I see what you did there. (문장 안의 의문문은 주어 + 동사 순서.)
- No pun intending. → No pun intended. (‘의도된’이라 과거분사 intended.)
- His jokes always make me to groan. → His jokes always make me groan. (make + 사람 + 동사원형.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I know what you mean. I know what my alarm means too, but we still disagree every morning. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. steps.note: 예) cheesy / full of cheese, corny → A: My pizza joke is a little cheesy. B: Ha! I see what you did there. “Cheesy” means full of cheese, and it also means corny.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) cheesy / full of cheese, corny → A: My pizza joke is a little cheesy. B: Ha! I see what you did there. “Cheesy” means full of cheese, and it also means corny. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): cheesy / full of cheese / corny | roll / bread / a lucky streak | crack up / break / laugh hard | atmosphere / air / mood.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: I see what you did there.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "I see what you did there." (말장난); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I see what you did there." / "No pun intended." / "It’s so bad it’s good.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

steps.title: The Pun Jar
steps.text: After dinner, Ben brought out a glass jar and some paper slips. “The Pun Jar,” he announced. “Write your best one-liner, and we’ll read them at the next dinner.” Grace said good banter feels like *a game of catch*. One person throws a quip, and the other sends back a quick comeback. Ben admitted that his jokes are corny on purpose. “If people groan, I win,” he said. Jiwoo asked about teasing. Ben said it’s fine only when everyone is laughing, including the person being teased. “And never about looks or where someone’s from,” Grace added. Jiwoo wrote her “draw laughs” line on a slip. Ben grinned. “That one’s *a keeper*,” he said. On the way upstairs, Jiwoo was already thinking of her next wisecrack.

steps.label: 대화 외우기
steps.teach:
This is the start of Part 3 of "I see what you did there." (말장난); it may be a different day. Today the learner practises saying the scene from this lesson by heart. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of one or two exchanges. React to what they say.
2) Then, in a new turn, say in one or two short sentences that today you will practise the scene ("Dinner at Ben’s · 10월 마지막 금요일 저녁, 벤의 집에서") until they can say it by heart: first listen once, then say their lines with fewer and fewer words on the screen. steps.label: 장면 다시 듣기
steps.teach:
The app has just played the scene again in the characters' own voices:
1. Ben: "Pizza’s ready! I’d tell you a joke about pizza, but it’s a little cheesy." (피자 나왔어요! 피자 농담을 하나 하고 싶은데, 좀 치즈 같아서요(썰렁해서요).)
2. Grace: "Here we go. Dinner at Ben’s always comes with free puns." (또 시작이네요. 벤 집 저녁에는 늘 말장난이 공짜로 따라와요.)
3. Jiwoo: "Ugh, Ben. It’s so bad it’s good." (으, 벤. 너무 썰렁해서 오히려 웃겨요.)
4. Ben: "Thank you. Here, have some bread, too." (고마워요. 자, 빵도 좀 먹어요.)
5. Jiwoo: "Thanks. Are these rolls homemade?" (고마워요. 이 롤빵 직접 만든 거예요?)
6. Ben: "They are. I’m on a roll tonight." (그럼요. 오늘 밤 제가 아주 물이 올랐거든요(롤이 잘 나왔거든요).)
7. Jiwoo: "I walked right into that one." (제가 딱 걸려들었네요.)
8. Grace: "Ben, don’t quit your day job." (벤, 본업은 그만두지 마요.)
9. Ben: "I’ll be here all week. Ba-dum-tss. So, Jiwoo, how’s the bike app going?" (이번 주 내내 공연합니다. 둥둥 칫! 그래서 지우 씨, 자전거 앱은 어떻게 돼 가요?)
10. Jiwoo: "Slow. The second-stage launch keeps getting pushed back. We’re just spinning our wheels, no pun intended." (느려요. 2단계 출시가 계속 밀려요. 바퀴만 헛돌고 있어요(제자리걸음이에요). 말장난하려던 건 아니고요.)
11. Ben: "Spinning your wheels on a bike app? I see what you did there." (자전거 앱에서 바퀴가 헛돈다? 무슨 말장난인지 알겠네요.)
12. Jiwoo: "I honestly didn’t plan it! But here’s one on purpose. I’m a designer, so I don’t tell jokes. I just draw laughs." (정말 일부러 한 거 아니에요! 그래도 이번엔 일부러 하나 할게요. 저는 디자이너라 농담은 안 해요. 웃음을 그릴(끌어낼) 뿐이죠.)
13. Ben: "Ha! “Draw laughs.” Okay, that was clever." (하! ‘draw laughs’라. 오, 그건 재치 있었어요.)
14. Grace: "Oh, you’re on a roll today, Jiwoo." (오, 오늘 지우 씨 물이 올랐네요.)
Give one short reaction in a few words and say in one short sentence that now they will practise their lines. Ask no question about it. Then call next_step.

steps.scene_desc: 11월 첫 토요일 저녁, 저녁 모임 2주년을 앞둔 그레이스 집 거실. 식탁 위에 피자 두 판(한 판에는 파인애플 조각)과 작은 케이크. 대니얼이 손가락으로 지우를 가리키며 웃고, 지우는 파인애플 피자 한 조각을 든 채 난처하게 웃으며 말하고 있음. 그레이스·벤·클로이·마야가 소파와 바닥에 앉아 재미있다는 듯 구경함. 글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "For the sake of argument" (반대편 변호). Goal: 내 생각과 반대인 쪽을 연습 삼아 변호하기. Today's scene: 11월 첫 토요일 저녁, 저녁 모임 2주년을 앞둔 그레이스 집 거실. 식탁 위에 피자 두 판(한 판에는 파인애플 조각)과 작은 케이크. 대니얼이 손가락으로 지우를 가리키며 웃고, 지우는 파인애플 피자 한 조각을 든 채 난처하게 웃으며 말하고 있음. 그레이스·벤·클로이·마야가 소파와 바닥에 앉아 재미있다는 듯 구경함. 글자 없음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Daniel, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "For the sake of argument, ___.".

steps.when: 내 생각과 상관없이 *일단 가정*하고 이야기를 이어 가요. 뒤에 let’s say …가 자주 와요.
steps.extra: For the sake of argument, let’s say tomatoes don’t count.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "For the sake of argument, ___." ((논의를 위해) 일단 ~라고 쳐 볼게요.). When to use it: 내 생각과 상관없이 일단 가정하고 이야기를 이어 가요. 뒤에 let’s say …가 자주 와요. Note: For the sake of argument, let’s say tomatoes don’t count.
Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) The learner says it with their own real word in the blank (for example their own name). Show it first with your own real word; nobody ever says the blank itself. Any word of theirs that makes a correct sentence is right, even when the book uses another one.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): For the sake of argument, let’s say I can cook. Last night, even the eggs looked nervous. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Let’s assume for a moment that ___.".

steps.title: Devil’s Advocate · 11월 첫 토요일 저녁, 2주년을 앞둔 그레이스 집 모임에서

lines.en: Almost two years of Saturday dinners! Let’s play a game. You argue the side you disagree with.
lines.ko: 토요일 저녁 모임이 곧 2년이에요! 게임 해요. 자기와 반대되는 쪽을 변호하는 거예요.

lines.en: So we play devil’s advocate? Fun. What’s the topic?
lines.ko: 일부러 반대편을 드는 거네요? 재밌겠다. 주제는요?

lines.en: Pineapple on pizza. You love it, so you’re against it. I’ll defend it.
lines.ko: 피자 위 파인애플이요. 지우 씨는 좋아하니까 반대편이에요. 저는 변호할게요.

lines.en: Oh no. Okay. {{I don’t actually believe this, but}} fruit doesn’t belong on pizza.
lines.ko: 이런. 좋아요. 진짜 제 생각은 아니지만, 과일은 피자에 어울리지 않아요.

lines.en: {{Technically speaking}}, tomatoes are fruit.
lines.ko: 엄밀히 말하면 토마토도 과일이에요.

lines.en: Fine. {{For the sake of argument}}, let’s say tomatoes don’t count. They’re not sweet. Pineapple is basically dessert.
lines.ko: 좋아요. 일단 토마토는 빼고 치죠. 달지 않으니까요. 파인애플은 거의 디저트예요.

lines.en: {{By that logic}}, sweet-and-sour pork is dessert, too.
lines.ko: 그 논리대로라면 탕수육도 디저트네요.

lines.en: Hmm. Then {{let’s assume for a moment that}} good crust should stay crispy. Pineapple is so juicy that it makes the crust soggy. {{You can’t deny that.}}
lines.ko: 음. 그럼 잠깐 좋은 피자 도우는 바삭해야 한다고 가정해 봐요. 파인애플은 즙이 많아서 도우를 눅눅하게 해요. 그건 부정 못 하죠.

lines.en: A soggy crust is sad, I admit. {{Okay, the other side has a point.}}
lines.ko: 눅눅한 도우는 슬프죠, 인정해요. 좋아요, 반대쪽 말도 일리가 있네요.

lines.en: {{Now I’m starting to convince myself!}}
lines.ko: 이제 저 스스로도 설득되기 시작했어요!

lines.en: Not so fast. {{Hear me out.}} {{If you think about it}}, the sweet pineapple balances the salty cheese.
lines.ko: 아직 일러요. 제 말 들어 봐요. 생각해 보면 달콤한 파인애플이 짭짤한 치즈와 균형을 맞춰 줘요.

lines.en: Wait, that’s my real argument! Wow, {{that was harder than I thought}}.
lines.ko: 잠깐, 그건 제 진짜 주장이잖아요! 와, 생각보다 어렵네요.

lines.en: Then {{let’s switch sides}}. Finally! Pineapple has no place on pizza!
lines.ko: 그럼 편을 바꿔요. 드디어! 파인애플은 피자에 올라갈 자리가 없어요!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Devil’s Advocate · 11월 첫 토요일 저녁, 2주년을 앞둔 그레이스 집 모임에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Daniel: "Almost two years of Saturday dinners! Let’s play a game. You argue the side you disagree with." (토요일 저녁 모임이 곧 2년이에요! 게임 해요. 자기와 반대되는 쪽을 변호하는 거예요.)
2. Jiwoo: "So we play devil’s advocate? Fun. What’s the topic?" (일부러 반대편을 드는 거네요? 재밌겠다. 주제는요?)
3. Daniel: "Pineapple on pizza. You love it, so you’re against it. I’ll defend it." (피자 위 파인애플이요. 지우 씨는 좋아하니까 반대편이에요. 저는 변호할게요.)
4. Jiwoo: "Oh no. Okay. I don’t actually believe this, but fruit doesn’t belong on pizza." (이런. 좋아요. 진짜 제 생각은 아니지만, 과일은 피자에 어울리지 않아요.)
5. Daniel: "Technically speaking, tomatoes are fruit." (엄밀히 말하면 토마토도 과일이에요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Fine. For the sake of argument, let’s say tomatoes don’t count. They’re not sweet. Pineapple is basically dessert." (좋아요. 일단 토마토는 빼고 치죠. 달지 않으니까요. 파인애플은 거의 디저트예요.)
7. Daniel: "By that logic, sweet-and-sour pork is dessert, too." (그 논리대로라면 탕수육도 디저트네요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Hmm. Then let’s assume for a moment that good crust should stay crispy. Pineapple is so juicy that it makes the crust soggy. You can’t deny that." (음. 그럼 잠깐 좋은 피자 도우는 바삭해야 한다고 가정해 봐요. 파인애플은 즙이 많아서 도우를 눅눅하게 해요. 그건 부정 못 하죠.)
9. Daniel: "A soggy crust is sad, I admit. Okay, the other side has a point." (눅눅한 도우는 슬프죠, 인정해요. 좋아요, 반대쪽 말도 일리가 있네요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Now I’m starting to convince myself!" (이제 저 스스로도 설득되기 시작했어요!)
11. Daniel: "Not so fast. Hear me out. If you think about it, the sweet pineapple balances the salty cheese." (아직 일러요. 제 말 들어 봐요. 생각해 보면 달콤한 파인애플이 짭짤한 치즈와 균형을 맞춰 줘요.)
12. Jiwoo: "Wait, that’s my real argument! Wow, that was harder than I thought." (잠깐, 그건 제 진짜 주장이잖아요! 와, 생각보다 어렵네요.)
13. Daniel: "Then let’s switch sides. Finally! Pineapple has no place on pizza!" (그럼 편을 바꿔요. 드디어! 파인애플은 피자에 올라갈 자리가 없어요!)
Give one short, natural reaction to the scene (a few words) and say in one short sentence that you will now read it together. Do not ask any question about what happened yet: the quiz comes later, after the role reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.
