12. Jiwoo (learner): "Wait, that’s my real argument! Wow, that was harder than I thought." (잠깐, 그건 제 진짜 주장이잖아요! 와, 생각보다 어렵네요.)
13. Daniel (you): "Then let’s switch sides. Finally! Pineapple has no place on pizza!" (그럼 편을 바꿔요. 드디어! 파인애플은 피자에 올라갈 자리가 없어요!)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Daniel. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, react to the scene in a word or two (not a comment on how they sounded), then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short quiz about the scene.

items: In real life, Jiwoo likes pineapple on pizza.
Jiwoo argues that pineapple makes the crust soggy.
At the end, Daniel wants to keep defending pineapple on pizza.
steps.teach:
Quiz about the scene, now that the learner has heard it and read it in both roles. First ask two short, easy questions about what happens in it (who, what, where or how often), one per turn, with the answers in the lines below. Any answer that shows they understood is right, in any words or in Korean: say so and go on. If it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Never turn an answer into a repeat drill here: if their English has a slip, just say the right sentence back once in your reaction and go on. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too.
Then the true/false check. The statements on the learner's screen, each with its answer and the scene line that shows it. The answers are for you only: never say an answer or a line number before the learner has answered:
1. In real life, Jiwoo likes pineapple on pizza. → True (line 3, 12)
2. Jiwoo argues that pineapple makes the crust soggy. → True (line 8)
3. At the end, Daniel wants to keep defending pineapple on pizza. → False (line 13)
The scene they are about:
1. Daniel: "Almost two years of Saturday dinners! Let’s play a game. You argue the side you disagree with." (토요일 저녁 모임이 곧 2년이에요! 게임 해요. 자기와 반대되는 쪽을 변호하는 거예요.)
2. Jiwoo: "So we play devil’s advocate? Fun. What’s the topic?" (일부러 반대편을 드는 거네요? 재밌겠다. 주제는요?)
3. Daniel: "Pineapple on pizza. You love it, so you’re against it. I’ll defend it." (피자 위 파인애플이요. 지우 씨는 좋아하니까 반대편이에요. 저는 변호할게요.)
4. Jiwoo: "Oh no. Okay. I don’t actually believe this, but fruit doesn’t belong on pizza." (이런. 좋아요. 진짜 제 생각은 아니지만, 과일은 피자에 어울리지 않아요.)
5. Daniel: "Technically speaking, tomatoes are fruit." (엄밀히 말하면 토마토도 과일이에요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Fine. For the sake of argument, let’s say tomatoes don’t count. They’re not sweet. Pineapple is basically dessert." (좋아요. 일단 토마토는 빼고 치죠. 달지 않으니까요. 파인애플은 거의 디저트예요.)
7. Daniel: "By that logic, sweet-and-sour pork is dessert, too." (그 논리대로라면 탕수육도 디저트네요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Hmm. Then let’s assume for a moment that good crust should stay crispy. Pineapple is so juicy that it makes the crust soggy. You can’t deny that." (음. 그럼 잠깐 좋은 피자 도우는 바삭해야 한다고 가정해 봐요. 파인애플은 즙이 많아서 도우를 눅눅하게 해요. 그건 부정 못 하죠.)
9. Daniel: "A soggy crust is sad, I admit. Okay, the other side has a point." (눅눅한 도우는 슬프죠, 인정해요. 좋아요, 반대쪽 말도 일리가 있네요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Now I’m starting to convince myself!" (이제 저 스스로도 설득되기 시작했어요!)
11. Daniel: "Not so fast. Hear me out. If you think about it, the sweet pineapple balances the salty cheese." (아직 일러요. 제 말 들어 봐요. 생각해 보면 달콤한 파인애플이 짭짤한 치즈와 균형을 맞춰 줘요.)
12. Jiwoo: "Wait, that’s my real argument! Wow, that was harder than I thought." (잠깐, 그건 제 진짜 주장이잖아요! 와, 생각보다 어렵네요.)
13. Daniel: "Then let’s switch sides. Finally! Pineapple has no place on pizza!" (그럼 편을 바꿔요. 드디어! 파인애플은 피자에 올라갈 자리가 없어요!)
Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). A one-word answer (True, False, 맞아요) is enough; never ask for a full sentence. Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: I don’t actually believe this, but ___.
head: Topic
I don’t actually believe this, but …
If you think about it, …
rows: the quietest hours are after midnight.
one phone can hold a whole library.
they never ask for a walk in the rain.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: For the sake of argument, ___. / I don’t actually believe this, but ___. Table (Topic → I don’t actually believe this, but …):
- Morning or night? → night owls have it better.
- Paper or e-books? → e-books win.
- Cats or dogs? → cats are better company.
- Summer or winter? → winter is the best season.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I don’t actually believe this, but e-books win. At least they never fall on my face in bed. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*For the sake of argument*, let’s say it’s true. 일단 그렇다고 쳐요. 
*Let’s assume for a moment that* crust should be crispy. 잠깐 ~라고 가정해 봐요(that + 문장).

*By that logic*, sweet-and-sour pork is dessert. 그 논리대로라면 ~ (허점 보이기) 
*Technically speaking*, tomatoes are fruit. 엄밀히 말하면 ~
errors: For the sake of argue, let’s say yes.
For the sake of argument, let’s say yes.
Let’s assume that it belong on pizza.
Let’s assume that it belongs on pizza.
By that logic, every fruit are dessert.
By that logic, every fruit is dessert.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 가정하는 말: For the sake of argument, let’s say it’s true. 일단 그렇다고 쳐요. / Let’s assume for a moment that crust should be crispy. 잠깐 ~라고 가정해 봐요(that + 문장).
- 논리를 잇는 말: By that logic, sweet-and-sour pork is dessert. 그 논리대로라면 ~ (허점 보이기) / Technically speaking, tomatoes are fruit. 엄밀히 말하면 ~
Common mistakes on screen:
- For the sake of argue, let’s say yes. → For the sake of argument, let’s say yes. (of + 명사 argument.)
- Let’s assume that it belong on pizza. → Let’s assume that it belongs on pizza. (it(단수) → belongs.)
- By that logic, every fruit are dessert. → By that logic, every fruit is dessert. (every + 단수 → is.)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): For the sake of argument, let’s say I’m calm before coffee. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: 가정하는 말: For the sake of argument, let’s say it’s true. 일단 그렇다고 쳐요. Let’s assume for a moment that crust should be crispy. 잠깐 ~라고 가정해 봐요(that + 문장).
논리를 잇는 말: By that logic, sweet-and-sour pork is dessert. 그 논리대로라면 ~ (허점 보이기) Technically speaking, tomatoes are fruit. 엄밀히 말하면 ~

Let’s assume that it belong on pizza. → Let’s assume that it belongs on pizza.
By that logic, every fruit are dessert. → By that logic, every fruit is dessert.

steps.note: 예) morning people / mornings are overrated → A: Argue the other side. B: I don’t actually believe this, but mornings are overrated.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) morning people / mornings are overrated → A: Argue the other side. B: I don’t actually believe this, but mornings are overrated. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): pineapple pizza / it ruins pizza | morning people / mornings are overrated | e-books / paper is better | winter / it’s the best season.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: Let’s assume for a moment that ___.
I don’t actually believe this, but ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "For the sake of argument" (반대편 변호); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "For the sake of argument, ___." / "Let’s assume for a moment that ___." / "I don’t actually believe this, but ___.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Now I’m starting to convince myself.
Okay, the other side has a point.
That was harder than I thought.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 가정하고 논리 펴기: "Hear me out." (제 말 좀 들어 봐요., 친근); "Technically speaking, ___." (엄밀히 말하면, ~, 보통); "By that logic, ___." (그 논리대로라면, ~, 보통); "If you think about it, ___." (생각해 보면, ~, 보통); "You can’t deny that ___." (~라는 건 부정할 수 없어요., 보통)
- 게임 하면서: "Now I’m starting to convince myself." (이제 저 스스로도 설득되기 시작했어요., 친근); "Okay, the other side has a point." (좋아요, 반대쪽 말도 일리가 있네요., 보통); "That was harder than I thought." (생각보다 어렵네요., 보통); "Let’s switch sides." (편을 바꿔요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): By that logic, folding laundry once a month is efficient. I only have to feel disappointed twelve times a year. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 토론에서 쓰는 말

*strawman* 상대 주장을 일부러 약하게 바꿔 놓고 공격하기(허수아비 논법) 
*steelman* 상대 주장을 가장 강한 모습으로 다시 말해 주기 
a logical *fallacy* 논리의 오류 · a *rebuttal* 반박 · a *counterargument* 반론
강세로 보여 주는 ‘게임일 뿐’

I don’t *AC*tually believe this, but … actually에 힘을 주면 ‘진심은 아니에요’라는 신호 
Let’s *SWITCH* sides. 
반대편 변호는 놀이예요. 정치·종교처럼 마음 다칠 수 있는 주제는 피해요.
steps.blank:
A: Let’s play devil’s advocate.   B: Okay. I don’t ___ believe this, but mornings are overrated. 
A: For the ___ of argument, let’s say you’re right. By that ___, nobody should get up before noon!   B: Ha! You have a point. 
낱말 상자: actually · sake · logic
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 토론에서 쓰는 말: strawman 상대 주장을 일부러 약하게 바꿔 놓고 공격하기(허수아비 논법) / steelman 상대 주장을 가장 강한 모습으로 다시 말해 주기 / a logical fallacy 논리의 오류 · a rebuttal 반박 · a counterargument 반론
- 강세로 보여 주는 ‘게임일 뿐’: I don’t ACtually believe this, but … actually에 힘을 주면 ‘진심은 아니에요’라는 신호 / Let’s SWITCH sides. / 반대편 변호는 놀이예요. 정치·종교처럼 마음 다칠 수 있는 주제는 피해요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Let’s play devil’s advocate. B: Okay. I don’t ___ believe this, but mornings are overrated. / A: For the ___ of argument, let’s say you’re right. By that ___, nobody should get up before noon! B: Ha! You have a point. / 낱말 상자: actually · sake · logic
Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

items.ko: 악마 · devil’s advocate 일부러 반대편을 드는 사람
수사(설득하려고 말을 꾸미는 기술), 그럴듯하게 꾸민 말
상대 주장을 가장 강한 모습으로 다시 말하다
허수아비 논법(상대 주장을 약하게 바꿔 공격하기)

steps.teach:
Picture words on screen. New: logic (논리), technically (엄밀히 말하면, 따지고 보면), devil (악마 · devil’s advocate 일부러 반대편을 드는 사람), rhetoric (수사(설득하려고 말을 꾸미는 기술), 그럴듯하게 꾸민 말), counterargument (반론), absurd (터무니없는, 말도 안 되는), concede ((맞다고) 인정하다, 양보하다), hypothetical (가정의, 가상의; 가정해 본 상황), steelman (상대 주장을 가장 강한 모습으로 다시 말하다), strawman (허수아비 논법(상대 주장을 약하게 바꿔 공격하기)), fallacy ((논리의) 오류, 잘못된 생각), rebuttal (반박).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): My logic is simple: if I buy healthy snacks, I become healthy by association. The cookies nearby ruin the plan. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: argument (논거, 주장; 말다툼) — "a strong argument"; assume ((사실이라고) 가정하다, 생각하다) — "Let’s assume it’s true."; assumption (가정, 전제) — "a wrong assumption"; premise ((논증의) 전제(앞에서는 ‘(이야기의) 기본 설정’)) — "a false premise"; definition (정의, 뜻풀이) — "by definition"; advocate (옹호자, 지지자; 옹호하다) — "play devil’s advocate"; persuade (설득하다) — "persuade a friend"; debate (토론; 토론하다) — "a friendly debate"; position (입장) — "defend a position".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): By definition, a clean kitchen should exist after dinner. Mine becomes a historical site in about twenty minutes. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Are you a morning person or a night owl? Now defend the other side.
I’m a ___. I don’t actually believe this, but ___.
Pick a food you don’t like. Argue for it.
For the sake of argument, ___. If you think about it, ___.
Let’s assume for a moment that weekends are three days long. What changes?
Let’s assume for a moment that ___. Then ___.
Was it hard to argue the other side? Why?
That was harder than I thought, because ___.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Are you a morning person or a night owl? Now defend the other side." (hint on screen: I’m a ___. I don’t actually believe this, but ___.)
- "Pick a food you don’t like. Argue for it." (hint on screen: For the sake of argument, ___. If you think about it, ___.)
- "Let’s assume for a moment that weekends are three days long. What changes?" (hint on screen: Let’s assume for a moment that ___. Then ___.)
- "Was it hard to argue the other side? Why?" (hint on screen: That was harder than I thought, because ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Let’s assume for a moment that weekends are three days long. Then I finally finish resting from the first two. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). steps.title: Almost Two Years of Saturdays
steps.text: The game went on all evening. Ben argued that winter beats summer, and he did it so well that Grace conceded. Chloe’s rebuttal to Maya was so absurd that everyone laughed, including Maya. Then Grace *raised her glass* to Daniel. In late August, he had passed his thesis defense, and he would graduate next spring. Ben started calling him “Doctor Daniel” right away. “I couldn’t have finished my thesis without these Saturdays,” Daniel said. “You all taught me to argue with a smile.” He shared his favorite debate rule. Before you disagree, steelman the other side. “Say their best argument first. Never attack a strawman.” Jiwoo liked that. At work, she sometimes heard rhetoric instead of reasons. Next time, she would steelman first.
steps.gloss: concede 인정하다 · rebuttal 반박 · raise one’s glass 잔을 들다 · thesis defense 논문 심사 · steelman 가장 강하게 다시 말하다 · strawman 허수아비 논법
questions: What did Daniel do in late August?
What is Daniel’s favorite debate rule?

steps.title: 반대편 변호
steps.goal: 오늘 장면의 대화를 외워서 말해 보기
steps.scene_desc: 11월 첫 토요일 저녁, 저녁 모임 2주년을 앞둔 그레이스 집 거실. 식탁 위에 피자 두 판(한 판에는 파인애플 조각)과 작은 케이크. 대니얼이 손가락으로 지우를 가리키며 웃고, 지우는 파인애플 피자 한 조각을 든 채 난처하게 웃으며 말하고 있음. 그레이스·벤·클로이·마야가 소파와 바닥에 앉아 재미있다는 듯 구경함. 글자 없음
steps.label: 대화 외우기
steps.teach:

1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of one or two exchanges. React to what they say.

steps.title: Devil’s Advocate · 11월 첫 토요일 저녁, 2주년을 앞둔 그레이스 집 모임에서

lines.en: Almost two years of Saturday dinners! Let’s play a game. You argue the side you disagree with.
lines.ko: 토요일 저녁 모임이 곧 2년이에요! 게임 해요. 자기와 반대되는 쪽을 변호하는 거예요.

lines.en: So we play devil’s advocate? Fun. What’s the topic?
lines.ko: 일부러 반대편을 드는 거네요? 재밌겠다. 주제는요?

lines.en: Pineapple on pizza. You love it, so you’re against it. I’ll defend it.
lines.ko: 피자 위 파인애플이요. 지우 씨는 좋아하니까 반대편이에요. 저는 변호할게요.

lines.en: Oh no. Okay. {{I don’t actually believe this, but}} fruit doesn’t belong on pizza.
lines.ko: 이런. 좋아요. 진짜 제 생각은 아니지만, 과일은 피자에 어울리지 않아요.

lines.en: {{Technically speaking}}, tomatoes are fruit.
lines.ko: 엄밀히 말하면 토마토도 과일이에요.

lines.en: Fine. {{For the sake of argument}}, let’s say tomatoes don’t count. They’re not sweet. Pineapple is basically dessert.
lines.ko: 좋아요. 일단 토마토는 빼고 치죠. 달지 않으니까요. 파인애플은 거의 디저트예요.

lines.en: {{By that logic}}, sweet-and-sour pork is dessert, too.
lines.ko: 그 논리대로라면 탕수육도 디저트네요.

lines.en: Hmm. Then {{let’s assume for a moment that}} good crust should stay crispy. Pineapple is so juicy that it makes the crust soggy. {{You can’t deny that.}}
lines.ko: 음. 그럼 잠깐 좋은 피자 도우는 바삭해야 한다고 가정해 봐요. 파인애플은 즙이 많아서 도우를 눅눅하게 해요. 그건 부정 못 하죠.

lines.en: A soggy crust is sad, I admit. {{Okay, the other side has a point.}}
lines.ko: 눅눅한 도우는 슬프죠, 인정해요. 좋아요, 반대쪽 말도 일리가 있네요.

lines.en: {{Now I’m starting to convince myself!}}
lines.ko: 이제 저 스스로도 설득되기 시작했어요!

lines.ko: 그럼 편을 바꿔요. 드디어! 파인애플은 피자에 올라갈 자리가 없어요!

steps.label: 장면 다시 듣기
steps.teach:
The app has just played the scene again in the characters' own voices:
1. Daniel: "Almost two years of Saturday dinners! Let’s play a game. You argue the side you disagree with." (토요일 저녁 모임이 곧 2년이에요! 게임 해요. 자기와 반대되는 쪽을 변호하는 거예요.)
2. Jiwoo: "So we play devil’s advocate? Fun. What’s the topic?" (일부러 반대편을 드는 거네요? 재밌겠다. 주제는요?)
3. Daniel: "Pineapple on pizza. You love it, so you’re against it. I’ll defend it." (피자 위 파인애플이요. 지우 씨는 좋아하니까 반대편이에요. 저는 변호할게요.)
4. Jiwoo: "Oh no. Okay. I don’t actually believe this, but fruit doesn’t belong on pizza." (이런. 좋아요. 진짜 제 생각은 아니지만, 과일은 피자에 어울리지 않아요.)
5. Daniel: "Technically speaking, tomatoes are fruit." (엄밀히 말하면 토마토도 과일이에요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Fine. For the sake of argument, let’s say tomatoes don’t count. They’re not sweet. Pineapple is basically dessert." (좋아요. 일단 토마토는 빼고 치죠. 달지 않으니까요. 파인애플은 거의 디저트예요.)
7. Daniel: "By that logic, sweet-and-sour pork is dessert, too." (그 논리대로라면 탕수육도 디저트네요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Hmm. Then let’s assume for a moment that good crust should stay crispy. Pineapple is so juicy that it makes the crust soggy. You can’t deny that." (음. 그럼 잠깐 좋은 피자 도우는 바삭해야 한다고 가정해 봐요. 파인애플은 즙이 많아서 도우를 눅눅하게 해요. 그건 부정 못 하죠.)
9. Daniel: "A soggy crust is sad, I admit. Okay, the other side has a point." (눅눅한 도우는 슬프죠, 인정해요. 좋아요, 반대쪽 말도 일리가 있네요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Now I’m starting to convince myself!" (이제 저 스스로도 설득되기 시작했어요!)
11. Daniel: "Not so fast. Hear me out. If you think about it, the sweet pineapple balances the salty cheese." (아직 일러요. 제 말 들어 봐요. 생각해 보면 달콤한 파인애플이 짭짤한 치즈와 균형을 맞춰 줘요.)
12. Jiwoo: "Wait, that’s my real argument! Wow, that was harder than I thought." (잠깐, 그건 제 진짜 주장이잖아요! 와, 생각보다 어렵네요.)
13. Daniel: "Then let’s switch sides. Finally! Pineapple has no place on pizza!" (그럼 편을 바꿔요. 드디어! 파인애플은 피자에 올라갈 자리가 없어요!)

Do not say the learner's line before they try: remembering it is the point of this part, so this is the one exception to saying a sentence first. If they get stuck, give only the next word or two as a hint. If a word was missing or wrong, say the whole line once inside double quotes and let them try once more, then go on. What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

steps.label: 마무리
steps.teach: Wrap up like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how it felt to say the scene by heart, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today (for example a line they remembered well), say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

steps.title: 말 많은 토론
steps.goal: 가벼운 주제로 유머와 근거를 섞어 우기기
steps.scene_desc: 같은 날 밤(11월 첫 토요일), 그레이스 집 거실. 마야가 핫도그 하나를 변호사처럼 높이 들고 당당하게 말하고, 지우는 맞은편에서 팔짱을 낀 채 웃고 있음. 식탁 위에 핫도그와 샌드위치 접시. 그레이스·벤·클로이·대니얼이 판사처럼 손을 들어 투표하는 중. 글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.

Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat, one question per turn: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally. The warm-up is long enough only when the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions (one is enough if your class notes say you already had a class with them today); do not mention today's topic or ask if they are ready before that.
2) Then, in a new turn, bring up today's topic in your own words: "I rest my case." (말 많은 토론). Goal: 가벼운 주제로 유머와 근거를 섞어 우기기. Today's scene: 같은 날 밤(11월 첫 토요일), 그레이스 집 거실. 마야가 핫도그 하나를 변호사처럼 높이 들고 당당하게 말하고, 지우는 맞은편에서 팔짱을 낀 채 웃고 있음. 식탁 위에 핫도그와 샌드위치 접시. 그레이스·벤·클로이·대니얼이 판사처럼 손을 들어 투표하는 중. 글자 없음. People in the scene (say the names exactly like this): Maya, Jiwoo. Say in one or two short sentences what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene, and in a few words where the scene happens and who meets (from Today's scene above). Bring up the topic only once and ask if they are ready only once. When the learner says they are ready, answer with one short, warm sentence like a person would (for example: Great, let's start.) and nothing more.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Hear me out on this one.".

steps.teach:

Teach it like a person, in three small turns. One thing per turn, and wait for the learner each time. Never name these turns or say what kind of practice comes next; just talk:
(1) Say it once inside a real everyday moment (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can) and let the learner say it.
(2) Give a different everyday moment where they need it, and let them say it there.
(3) Have a tiny real exchange with it, like in a normal conversation: ask the learner something that this expression answers, or let them say it to you, and give your own real answer (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way).
Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.

Taking the bus is faster than driving, if I ignore the twenty minutes I spent missing it. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.

Fix at most one thing, gently, and only if it is really wrong. If you need a word for it, say this expression or this sentence. This expression is finished only when the learner has said it in three separate turns and you have replied to the last one. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): By definition, exercise is movement. I moved my chair three times today, so I am basically training for something. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.

steps.when: 법정 말투를 빌려 *근거를 다 댔다*며 의기양양하게 마무리해요. *CASE*에 힘을 줘요.

Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("The Hot Dog Debate · 같은 날 밤, 그레이스 집에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: The Hot Dog Debate · 같은 날 밤, 그레이스 집에서

lines.en: One last debate tonight, and this time we argue what we really think. Is a hot dog a sandwich?
lines.ko: 오늘 밤 마지막 토론이에요. 이번엔 진짜 생각대로 말해요. 핫도그는 샌드위치일까요?

lines.en: Easy. No. A hot dog is a hot dog.
lines.ko: 쉽네요. 아니요. 핫도그는 핫도그예요.

lines.en: {{Hear me out on this one.}} Bread, filling, bread. {{By definition}}, that’s a sandwich.
lines.ko: 이번 건 끝까지 들어 봐요. 빵, 속, 빵. 정의상 그건 샌드위치예요.

lines.en: But a hot dog bun is one piece of bread. It’s connected at the bottom.
lines.ko: 그런데 핫도그 빵은 한 덩어리예요. 아래가 붙어 있잖아요.

lines.en: So is a sub roll, and that’s a sandwich. {{The facts are on my side.}}
lines.ko: 긴 샌드위치 빵도 그렇잖아요. 그건 샌드위치고요. 사실은 제 편이에요.

lines.en: {{That’s a stretch.}} Nobody orders a “hot dog sandwich.”
lines.ko: 그건 좀 억지예요. ‘핫도그 샌드위치’ 주세요, 하는 사람은 없잖아요.

lines.en: {{Now you’re just splitting hairs.}} What we call it is just semantics.
lines.ko: 이제 별걸 다 따지네요. 뭐라고 부르는지는 그냥 말뜻 문제예요.

lines.en: {{You’re overthinking this.}} By your logic, a taco is a sandwich, too.
lines.ko: 너무 깊이 생각하네요. 마야 씨 논리대로라면 타코도 샌드위치예요.

lines.en: {{Let’s not get carried away.}} Tacos are their own category.
lines.ko: 너무 나가지는 말아요. 타코는 따로 한 종류예요.

lines.en: Exactly! So hot dogs are their own category, too.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요! 그러니까 핫도그도 따로 한 종류예요.

lines.en: {{Okay, I’ll give you that.}} But a hot dog is still a sandwich. {{That’s a hill I’m willing to die on.}}
lines.ko: 좋아요, 그건 인정할게요. 그래도 핫도그는 샌드위치예요. 이건 절대 양보 못 해요.

lines.en: {{This is the most important debate of our time}}, isn’t it? {{Agree to disagree?}}
lines.ko: 이게 우리 시대 가장 중요한 토론이네요, 그렇죠? 서로 다르다는 걸 인정할까요?

lines.en: Never. Let’s vote. Hands up for “sandwich.” … Four to two. {{I rest my case.}}
lines.ko: 절대 안 돼요. 투표해요. ‘샌드위치’ 손 드세요. … 4 대 2. 제 변론은 여기까지예요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "The Hot Dog Debate · 같은 날 밤, 그레이스 집에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Maya: "One last debate tonight, and this time we argue what we really think. Is a hot dog a sandwich?" (오늘 밤 마지막 토론이에요. 이번엔 진짜 생각대로 말해요. 핫도그는 샌드위치일까요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Easy. No. A hot dog is a hot dog." (쉽네요. 아니요. 핫도그는 핫도그예요.)
3. Maya: "Hear me out on this one. Bread, filling, bread. By definition, that’s a sandwich." (이번 건 끝까지 들어 봐요. 빵, 속, 빵. 정의상 그건 샌드위치예요.)
4. Jiwoo: "But a hot dog bun is one piece of bread. It’s connected at the bottom." (그런데 핫도그 빵은 한 덩어리예요. 아래가 붙어 있잖아요.)
5. Maya: "So is a sub roll, and that’s a sandwich. The facts are on my side." (긴 샌드위치 빵도 그렇잖아요. 그건 샌드위치고요. 사실은 제 편이에요.)
6. Jiwoo: "That’s a stretch. Nobody orders a “hot dog sandwich.”" (그건 좀 억지예요. ‘핫도그 샌드위치’ 주세요, 하는 사람은 없잖아요.)
7. Maya: "Now you’re just splitting hairs. What we call it is just semantics." (이제 별걸 다 따지네요. 뭐라고 부르는지는 그냥 말뜻 문제예요.)
8. Jiwoo: "You’re overthinking this. By your logic, a taco is a sandwich, too." (너무 깊이 생각하네요. 마야 씨 논리대로라면 타코도 샌드위치예요.)
9. Maya: "Let’s not get carried away. Tacos are their own category." (너무 나가지는 말아요. 타코는 따로 한 종류예요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Exactly! So hot dogs are their own category, too." (바로 그거예요! 그러니까 핫도그도 따로 한 종류예요.)
11. Maya: "Okay, I’ll give you that. But a hot dog is still a sandwich. That’s a hill I’m willing to die on." (좋아요, 그건 인정할게요. 그래도 핫도그는 샌드위치예요. 이건 절대 양보 못 해요.)
12. Jiwoo: "This is the most important debate of our time, isn’t it? Agree to disagree?" (이게 우리 시대 가장 중요한 토론이네요, 그렇죠? 서로 다르다는 걸 인정할까요?)
13. Maya: "Never. Let’s vote. Hands up for “sandwich.” … Four to two. I rest my case." (절대 안 돼요. 투표해요. ‘샌드위치’ 손 드세요. … 4 대 2. 제 변론은 여기까지예요.)
Give one short, natural reaction to the scene (a few words) and say in one short sentence that you will now read it together. Do not ask any question about what happened yet: the quiz comes later, after the role reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

13. Maya (you): "Never. Let’s vote. Hands up for “sandwich.” … Four to two. I rest my case." (절대 안 돼요. 투표해요. ‘샌드위치’ 손 드세요. … 4 대 2. 제 변론은 여기까지예요.)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Maya. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say most of it or a good part of a long line, accept it warmly and go on; only if what they say is clearly not their line, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, react to the scene in a word or two (not a comment on how they sounded), then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short quiz about the scene.

items: Maya thinks a hot dog is a sandwich.
Jiwoo says a hot dog bun is two pieces of bread.
In the vote, most people say a hot dog is a sandwich.
steps.teach:
Quiz about the scene, now that the learner has heard it and read it in both roles. First ask two short, easy questions about what happens in it (who, what, where or how often), one per turn, with the answers in the lines below. Any answer that shows they understood is right, in any words or in Korean: say so and go on. If it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Never turn an answer into a repeat drill here: if their English has a slip, just say the right sentence back once in your reaction and go on. The learner plays Jiwoo in this lesson, so an answer in the first person (I'm new here instead of Jiwoo is new here) is right too.
Then the true/false check. The statements on the learner's screen, each with its answer and the scene line that shows it. The answers are for you only: never say an answer or a line number before the learner has answered:
1. Maya thinks a hot dog is a sandwich. → True (line 3, 11)
2. Jiwoo says a hot dog bun is two pieces of bread. → False (line 4)
3. In the vote, most people say a hot dog is a sandwich. → True (line 13)
The scene they are about:
1. Maya: "One last debate tonight, and this time we argue what we really think. Is a hot dog a sandwich?" (오늘 밤 마지막 토론이에요. 이번엔 진짜 생각대로 말해요. 핫도그는 샌드위치일까요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Easy. No. A hot dog is a hot dog." (쉽네요. 아니요. 핫도그는 핫도그예요.)
3. Maya: "Hear me out on this one. Bread, filling, bread. By definition, that’s a sandwich." (이번 건 끝까지 들어 봐요. 빵, 속, 빵. 정의상 그건 샌드위치예요.)
4. Jiwoo: "But a hot dog bun is one piece of bread. It’s connected at the bottom." (그런데 핫도그 빵은 한 덩어리예요. 아래가 붙어 있잖아요.)
5. Maya: "So is a sub roll, and that’s a sandwich. The facts are on my side." (긴 샌드위치 빵도 그렇잖아요. 그건 샌드위치고요. 사실은 제 편이에요.)
6. Jiwoo: "That’s a stretch. Nobody orders a “hot dog sandwich.”" (그건 좀 억지예요. ‘핫도그 샌드위치’ 주세요, 하는 사람은 없잖아요.)
7. Maya: "Now you’re just splitting hairs. What we call it is just semantics." (이제 별걸 다 따지네요. 뭐라고 부르는지는 그냥 말뜻 문제예요.)
8. Jiwoo: "You’re overthinking this. By your logic, a taco is a sandwich, too." (너무 깊이 생각하네요. 마야 씨 논리대로라면 타코도 샌드위치예요.)
9. Maya: "Let’s not get carried away. Tacos are their own category." (너무 나가지는 말아요. 타코는 따로 한 종류예요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Exactly! So hot dogs are their own category, too." (바로 그거예요! 그러니까 핫도그도 따로 한 종류예요.)
11. Maya: "Okay, I’ll give you that. But a hot dog is still a sandwich. That’s a hill I’m willing to die on." (좋아요, 그건 인정할게요. 그래도 핫도그는 샌드위치예요. 이건 절대 양보 못 해요.)
12. Jiwoo: "This is the most important debate of our time, isn’t it? Agree to disagree?" (이게 우리 시대 가장 중요한 토론이네요, 그렇죠? 서로 다르다는 걸 인정할까요?)
13. Maya: "Never. Let’s vote. Hands up for “sandwich.” … Four to two. I rest my case." (절대 안 돼요. 투표해요. ‘샌드위치’ 손 드세요. … 4 대 2. 제 변론은 여기까지예요.)
Go by the answers above, not by what the learner says: if their answer is the other one, say so kindly and show the line. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/아니에요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Give the verdict in the language you are using with this learner. Only when you are speaking Korean to them, say it as 정답은 True예요 / 정답은 False예요. There are 3 statements: ask every one and wait for an answer to each (Oh or Hmm is not an answer). A one-word answer (True, False, 맞아요) is enough; never ask for a full sentence. Only after you have checked the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

By definition, ___. I rest my case.

rows: soup is food in a liquid.
A hot dog is a sandwich.
a sandwich is a filling in bread.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key sentences: Hear me out on this one. ___. / By definition, ___. I rest my case. Table (Hear me out on this one. → By definition, …):
- Cereal is soup. → soup is food in a liquid.
- A hot dog is a sandwich. → a sandwich is a filling in bread.
- A pizza is a pie. → a pie has a crust and a filling.
- Water is wet. → wet means covered in a liquid.
Make three quick real-life moments out of the key sentences and the rows, one per turn (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. If their sentence is correct and natural, accept it even when the table uses other words. Do not read labels or arrows aloud, and never say a blank: use real words. This part is finished only when the learner has answered three of these moments. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): Hear me out on this one. By definition, breakfast is food in the morning. I ate cake at seven. I rest my case. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: By definition · I rest my case

*By definition*, a sandwich has bread. 정의상(뜻 그대로 따지면) 
Bread, filling, bread. *I rest my case.* 법정에서 변호사가 ‘변론을 마칩니다’ 하는 말. 일상에서는 장난스럽게 써요.

The facts are on my side. + This is the most important debate of our time. 
과장은 주제가 *가벼울 때만* 웃겨요. 진지한 주제에서는 무례하게 들릴 수 있어요.
errors: Hear me out on this one.
By definition, a sandwich have bread.
By definition, a sandwich has bread.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- By definition · I rest my case: By definition, a sandwich has bread. 정의상(뜻 그대로 따지면) / Bread, filling, bread. I rest my case. 법정에서 변호사가 ‘변론을 마칩니다’ 하는 말. 일상에서는 장난스럽게 써요.
- 근거 하나 + 과장 하나: The facts are on my side. + This is the most important debate of our time. / 과장은 주제가 가벼울 때만 웃겨요. 진지한 주제에서는 무례하게 들릴 수 있어요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Hear me out this one. → Hear me out on this one. (‘이번 건’은 on this one.)
- By definition, a sandwich have bread. → By definition, a sandwich has bread. (단수 주어 → has.)
- Now you’re just split hairs. → Now you’re just splitting hairs. (be + -ing(진행형).)
There are 2 grammar points and 3 mistakes. Go through them as a conversation, one new thing per turn, never as a lecture. Start with the first point right away, with no opening sentence about how you will do this:
- Each grammar point: say its main idea in one or two plain, easy sentences with one short example with real words (do not go through every detail of the point), then ask the learner to make one short sentence of their own with it. When they answer, react to their sentence in a few words, and go on to the next thing in the same reply.
- Then the mistakes, one at a time: say the wrong sentence and ask the learner to fix it. When they answer, first confirm the right sentence and say why in a few words, then give the next wrong sentence in the same reply. Do every mistake on screen this way.
Never give two new points or two new mistakes in one turn, and never skip the confirmation. After the last mistake is fixed and confirmed, call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): By definition, a sandwich has bread. My lunch had one lonely slice, so it was arguing with itself. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

근거 하나 + 과장 하나: The facts are on my side. + This is the most important debate of our time. 과장은 주제가 가벼울 때만 웃겨요. 진지한 주제에서는 무례하게 들릴 수 있어요.

steps.note: 예) cereal / soup → A: Hear me out on this one. Cereal is soup. B: That’s a stretch. A: By definition, soup is food in a liquid. I rest my case.
steps.teach:
Quick practice. How it works (written on the learner's screen; do not read it out): 예) cereal / soup → A: Hear me out on this one. Cereal is soup. B: That’s a stretch. A: By definition, soup is food in a liquid. I rest my case. The items (the words the learner gets for each one): cereal / soup | a hot dog / a sandwich | pizza / a pie | a taco / a sandwich.
The sample on screen shows what is said for one item and who says it (sometimes the learner speaks as the named person, for example they pretend to be Daniel and introduce themselves as Daniel; sometimes it is a two-person exchange). If the sample has a dash (—), the words before the dash are one speaker and the words after it are the other: split it like a real conversation, the learner says one side and you say the other. The learner should get to use the given words. If both words belong to one side, the learner says that side and you say the other. If the words are split between the two sides (for example a question with the first word and an answer with the second), take turns across the items: for one item you ask and the learner answers with the second word, for the next the learner asks with the first word and you answer. When you set up an item, say which side the learner takes and give them only the word that goes into it. Never make the learner say both sides in one go. If their sentence is correct English and uses the given word, it is right: say so and go on, and never ask for extra words from the sample. Do not say the sample or the answer before the learner tries: from the first item they build it themselves. Set up each item in one short English sentence so the expected answer is clear, in different words each time, let the learner answer, and react like a person. Recast once if needed. There are 4 items: do every one, one per turn, in order. Only after the last answer, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and stop there to wait for their answer. In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.

cards: Hear me out on this one.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "I rest my case." (말 많은 토론); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say. Start the review only after the learner has answered at least two of your small-talk questions.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Hear me out on this one." / "By definition, ___." / "I rest my case.". One at a time: give a tiny real situation, wait for their answer and react naturally, then the next. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: That’s a hill I’m willing to die on.
이건 절대 양보 못 해요.(장난스러운 과장)
The facts are on my side.
This is the most important debate of our time.
이게 우리 시대 가장 중요한 토론이에요.(장난스러운 과장)
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 우기기: "That’s a hill I’m willing to die on." (이건 절대 양보 못 해요.(장난스러운 과장), 친근); "The facts are on my side." (사실은 제 편이에요., 보통); "This is the most important debate of our time." (이게 우리 시대 가장 중요한 토론이에요.(장난스러운 과장), 친근)
- 받아치기: "Let’s not get carried away." (너무 나가지는 말아요., 보통); "You’re overthinking this." (너무 깊이 생각하네요., 친근); "That’s a stretch." (그건 좀 억지예요., 보통); "Now you’re just splitting hairs." (이제 별걸 다 따지네요., 보통)
- 마무리하기: "Okay, I’ll give you that." (좋아요, 그건 인정할게요., 보통); "Agree to disagree?" (서로 다르다는 걸 인정할까요?, 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life and take them one per turn: say one, wait for the learner to say it and react, then the next. Then use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): That’s a hill I’m willing to die on: weekend alarms should be illegal. Mine rang at seven, and I stayed offended until lunch. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 법정 말투로 장난치기: a case (법정의) 사건, 주장 · I rest my case. 변론을 마칩니다 / the verdict 평결 → 모임에서는 투표 결과 · a loophole (규칙의) 허점 / I rest my CASE. 마지막 낱말에 힘을 주고 끝을 내려요.

Go through every point in each tip box (for example every greeting with its time of day), one or two short sentences each, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, one blank per turn: stop at the blank, wait for them to fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

items.ko: 머리카락 · split hairs 별걸 다 따지다

steps.teach:
Picture words on screen. New: category (범주, 종류), classify (분류하다), overthink (지나치게 깊이 생각하다), verdict (평결, (최종) 판정), ridiculous (말도 안 되는, 우스꽝스러운), settle ((논쟁을) 끝내다, 결론 내다), semantics (말뜻 따지기; 의미론), nitpick (사소한 흠을 잡다), contrarian (일부러 반대 의견을 내는 사람), loophole ((규칙의) 허점, 빠져나갈 구멍), hot take (일부러 튀는 의견), hair (머리카락 · split hairs 별걸 다 따지다).
Go through about six, new ones first, one word per turn: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and wait for the learner to say it before the next word. Never give several words in one turn. After every two or three words, ask one tiny real question with the word you just did (for example: Are you a morning person?), wait for the answer and react; do this at least twice in this part. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I overthink simple choices. Yesterday I tried to classify my socks by color, season, and mood. The verdict was ridiculous. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: definition (정의, 뜻풀이) — "by definition"; technically (엄밀히 말하면) — "Technically, it’s a sandwich."; absurd (터무니없는) — "an absurd argument"; stretch (늘이다; 억지, 무리한 해석) — "That’s a stretch."; split (쪼개다, 나누다) — "split a pizza"; case ((법정의) 사건; 주장, 논거) — "make a strong case"; rest (쉬다; (변론을) 마치다) — "I rest my case."; evidence (증거, 근거) — "Where’s your evidence?"; argue (주장하다; 언쟁하다) — "argue for fun".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): I can make a strong case for buying plants. I cannot make a strong case for keeping them alive. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Is cereal soup? Take a side and argue." (hint on screen: Hear me out on this one. ___. By definition, ___.)
- "What silly topic would you love to debate with friends?" (hint on screen: I’d love to debate whether ___.)

Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
A small funny moment for this part (your private idea, not a sentence for the learner to repeat): When I started, I could only say hello and ask simple questions. Now I can call customer service and still solve nothing. Haha. Say it once, as your own little story, at a natural moment in this part (often right after your first example). Keep its first sentence as written, because the joke depends on it; never put its ending after a different sentence. It replaces some of your other words, so your turn does not get longer. Use it only if it fits: if the learner is stuck, you are correcting them, or they just told you something, react to them first and skip it or save it for later.

steps.title: To the Next Chapter
steps.text: The vote *settled* it: a hot dog is a sandwich. Only Daniel voted with Jiwoo. He called Maya’s argument “a loophole in the definition.” Ben, the group’s favorite contrarian, demanded a recount just for fun. When the laughter died down, Jiwoo stood up and raised her glass. “When I first moved in, the first thing I said to Grace was ‘Yes. Hi!’ Tonight, I argued about hot dogs in English, and I lost *with style*. Thank you for every Saturday, every question, and every terrible pun. To the next chapter!” For a moment, nobody spoke. Then Grace smiled. “That sounded just like you.” “Totally you,” Chloe agreed. Daniel nodded. “Clear, honest, and funny.” Ben added, “No script needed.” Maya raised her glass, too. “Formal or casual, you sound like you,” she said. “I rest my case.”

steps.title: The Hot Dog Debate · 같은 날 밤, 그레이스 집에서

lines.en: One last debate tonight, and this time we argue what we really think. Is a hot dog a sandwich?
lines.ko: 오늘 밤 마지막 토론이에요. 이번엔 진짜 생각대로 말해요. 핫도그는 샌드위치일까요?

lines.en: Easy. No. A hot dog is a hot dog.
lines.ko: 쉽네요. 아니요. 핫도그는 핫도그예요.

lines.en: {{Hear me out on this one.}} Bread, filling, bread. {{By definition}}, that’s a sandwich.
lines.ko: 이번 건 끝까지 들어 봐요. 빵, 속, 빵. 정의상 그건 샌드위치예요.

lines.en: But a hot dog bun is one piece of bread. It’s connected at the bottom.
lines.ko: 그런데 핫도그 빵은 한 덩어리예요. 아래가 붙어 있잖아요.

lines.en: So is a sub roll, and that’s a sandwich. {{The facts are on my side.}}
lines.ko: 긴 샌드위치 빵도 그렇잖아요. 그건 샌드위치고요. 사실은 제 편이에요.

lines.en: {{That’s a stretch.}} Nobody orders a “hot dog sandwich.”
lines.ko: 그건 좀 억지예요. ‘핫도그 샌드위치’ 주세요, 하는 사람은 없잖아요.

lines.en: {{Now you’re just splitting hairs.}} What we call it is just semantics.
lines.ko: 이제 별걸 다 따지네요. 뭐라고 부르는지는 그냥 말뜻 문제예요.

lines.en: {{You’re overthinking this.}} By your logic, a taco is a sandwich, too.
lines.ko: 너무 깊이 생각하네요. 마야 씨 논리대로라면 타코도 샌드위치예요.

lines.en: {{Let’s not get carried away.}} Tacos are their own category.
lines.ko: 너무 나가지는 말아요. 타코는 따로 한 종류예요.

lines.en: Exactly! So hot dogs are their own category, too.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요! 그러니까 핫도그도 따로 한 종류예요.

lines.en: {{Okay, I’ll give you that.}} But a hot dog is still a sandwich. {{That’s a hill I’m willing to die on.}}
lines.ko: 좋아요, 그건 인정할게요. 그래도 핫도그는 샌드위치예요. 이건 절대 양보 못 해요.

lines.en: {{This is the most important debate of our time}}, isn’t it? {{Agree to disagree?}}
lines.ko: 이게 우리 시대 가장 중요한 토론이네요, 그렇죠? 서로 다르다는 걸 인정할까요?

lines.en: Never. Let’s vote. Hands up for “sandwich.” … Four to two. {{I rest my case.}}
lines.ko: 절대 안 돼요. 투표해요. ‘샌드위치’ 손 드세요. … 4 대 2. 제 변론은 여기까지예요.

steps.teach:
Memory practice 2: now the learner's lines show only the first letter of each word. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Maya exactly as written. The full lines, for you only:
1. Maya (you): "One last debate tonight, and this time we argue what we really think. Is a hot dog a sandwich?" (오늘 밤 마지막 토론이에요. 이번엔 진짜 생각대로 말해요. 핫도그는 샌드위치일까요?)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "Easy. No. A hot dog is a hot dog." (쉽네요. 아니요. 핫도그는 핫도그예요.)
3. Maya (you): "Hear me out on this one. Bread, filling, bread. By definition, that’s a sandwich." (이번 건 끝까지 들어 봐요. 빵, 속, 빵. 정의상 그건 샌드위치예요.)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "But a hot dog bun is one piece of bread. It’s connected at the bottom." (그런데 핫도그 빵은 한 덩어리예요. 아래가 붙어 있잖아요.)
5. Maya (you): "So is a sub roll, and that’s a sandwich. The facts are on my side." (긴 샌드위치 빵도 그렇잖아요. 그건 샌드위치고요. 사실은 제 편이에요.)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "That’s a stretch. Nobody orders a “hot dog sandwich.”" (그건 좀 억지예요. ‘핫도그 샌드위치’ 주세요, 하는 사람은 없잖아요.)
7. Maya (you): "Now you’re just splitting hairs. What we call it is just semantics." (이제 별걸 다 따지네요. 뭐라고 부르는지는 그냥 말뜻 문제예요.)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "You’re overthinking this. By your logic, a taco is a sandwich, too." (너무 깊이 생각하네요. 마야 씨 논리대로라면 타코도 샌드위치예요.)
9. Maya (you): "Let’s not get carried away. Tacos are their own category." (너무 나가지는 말아요. 타코는 따로 한 종류예요.)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "Exactly! So hot dogs are their own category, too." (바로 그거예요! 그러니까 핫도그도 따로 한 종류예요.)
11. Maya (you): "Okay, I’ll give you that. But a hot dog is still a sandwich. That’s a hill I’m willing to die on." (좋아요, 그건 인정할게요. 그래도 핫도그는 샌드위치예요. 이건 절대 양보 못 해요.)
12. Jiwoo (learner): "This is the most important debate of our time, isn’t it? Agree to disagree?" (이게 우리 시대 가장 중요한 토론이네요, 그렇죠? 서로 다르다는 걸 인정할까요?)
13. Maya (you): "Never. Let’s vote. Hands up for “sandwich.” … Four to two. I rest my case." (절대 안 돼요. 투표해요. ‘샌드위치’ 손 드세요. … 4 대 2. 제 변론은 여기까지예요.)

Do not say the learner's line before they try: remembering it is the point of this part, so this is the one exception to saying a sentence first. If they get stuck, give only the next word or two as a hint. If a word was missing or wrong, say the whole line once inside double quotes and let them try once more, then go on. Go in order, one line at a time. After the last line, react in a word or two, with no comment on how they sounded.

In your next reply, react to their answer, praise one specific thing they did today (for example a line they remembered well), say that the next lesson is waiting for next time, and say a warm goodbye. Call finish_session only at the end of that goodbye reply, after you have said all of it.
